short.hook: A clean plate hovers in front of a full cabinet shelf with nowhere to go, and that pause is the whole check.
short.standalone_note: Name the trigger, unloading the dishwasher, and the limit rule immediately, or the hovering plate reads as ordinary.

close.standard_beat: Hold the finished cabinet: daily dishes between shoulder and eye height, one category per stack, no plate stack more than about six, every mug liftable without moving another, top shelf holding only what you use less than monthly. Then the trigger, the dishwasher opened and emptied against the labelled edges.
close.next_zone_teaser: Now go down, to the cabinet where the pans live three deep and you lift two to reach the third.

shot_list: Overhead locked off on the counter grid for the mug count
Three-quarter at cabinet height for placement and lifting moves
Close inside the cabinet, bounce card lit, for the dust band and shelf edges
Low angle from below the cabinet for the greasy underside
Macro on chips, crazed glaze, and shelf edge labels
Three-quarter on the step stool in use, framed below the ankles
Close on a second pair of hands unloading the dishwasher, wrists down
High three-quarter from a raised tripod onto the top shelf
videos.description_hook: Most kitchens keep two sets of dishes at the height they reach into every day, then blame the cabinet for being full. Six passes, Sort through Sustain, including how to decide the second set honestly.

videos.title: 6S for Pots and Pans: Resetting the Lower Cookware Cabinet
videos.cold_open_problem: Three frying pans pulled out of a low cabinet and set side by side on the floor, one of them the expensive one nobody ever liked cooking on. Name the problem: the money is already spent and keeping the pan does not bring any of it back, it only costs you the easiest shelf in the kitchen. The call this zone turns on is the cap, the most pans you had going at once in a normal week, plus one.

segments.covers: Everything comes out onto the floor, which is the only way the third saucepan is ever found.
beats: Empty the entire cabinet onto the floor and lay it out so every piece is visible at once, including the wok bought for one weekend.
Keep only what actually cooked something in the past year, handling each piece while the decision is made.
Show the nonstick pan worn through to the metal in the middle and call it finished rather than a spare, headed for metal recycling instead of the back of the shelf.
Do the cap count out loud, the most pans going at once in a normal week plus one, then release the guest pieces that a roasting tray you already own would cover.
shots: Three-quarter, cabinet doors open on the full contents
Overhead, everything laid out on the floor in one frame
Macro, nonstick worn through to bare metal
Close, hands setting the keep pile out against the cap count
on_screen_text: All of it, onto the floor
Most at once in a week, plus one

short.hook: A low kitchen cabinet empties onto the floor and a third saucepan appears that nobody knew was still in there.
short.standalone_note: State the cap rule, most pans going at once in a week plus one, up front, since the floor lay-out only means something against a number.

segments.covers: Every pan comes out and goes back in one motion, with nothing lifted to reach anything else.
beats: Nest by size but cap any stack at three, with a cloth or a sheet of paper between coated faces.
Stand the lids in a rack or on a rail inside the door, cut against loose lids sliding out over the threshold.
Put the baking sheets on edge in a divider so you stop lifting three to reach the fourth.
Place the two pans you cook with nightly at the front of the cabinet nearest the hob, and run the one motion test on each.
shots: Close, three pans nested with paper between coated faces
Three-quarter, lids going into a door rail
Overhead, baking sheets standing on edge in a divider
Close, a nightly pan out and back in a single unbroken motion
on_screen_text: Out and back in one motion

short.hook: The same frying pan is fetched from a low cabinet twice: once by lifting two pans out of the way, once in a single motion.
short.standalone_note: Establish that this is the low cookware cabinet and that out and back in one motion is the standard being tested.

segments.covers: Clean to inspect: the shelf floor holds oil, and the handles get checked while everything is out.
beats: Wipe the shelf floor itself, showing the tacky film where oil has crept down the outsides of pan bases and held dust, and why a dry cloth will not shift it.
Twist every pan handle in turn and tighten any rivet or screw that moves, which is only possible while the cabinet is empty.
Return the pieces only once the shelf is dry, so the film does not start again the same day.
shots: Macro, raking light on the tacky film on the shelf floor
Close, damp cloth pass showing the difference
Macro, a handle twisted loose and a screw driven tight
on_screen_text: Oil creeps down and holds dust
Twist every handle while it is out

short.hook: A saucepan handle twists loose in the hand, and a screwdriver fixes in seconds what would otherwise have failed while carrying something hot.
short.standalone_note: Note that this check only happens while the cookware cabinet is emptied, which is why it belongs to this pass.

segments.covers: Weight goes low, stacks survive a slammed door, and blades never sit loose in a bowl. This is the 4th S.
beats: Move the cast iron and the full stockpot to the cabinet floor, never above waist height, and lift from a squat rather than a bend over the open door.
Close the door hard on purpose and watch the stack. If it slides, rebuild it until it survives a slam, since one day it will land on a foot.
Find the food processor and blender blades stored loose inside a bowl in the dark, and give them a closed container or a high shelf away from reaching fingers.
Restate the finished rule on camera: heaviest pieces on the cabinet floor, nothing sharp loose in the dark.
shots: Three-quarter, stockpot lowered to the cabinet floor, lift from a squat, wrists and below only
Close, door closed hard and the stack holding still
Macro, a loose blade found inside a bowl in a dark cabinet
Close, blades going into a closed container
on_screen_text: Build the stack to survive a slam

short.hook: A cabinet door is slammed on purpose to see whether the stack of pans behind it moves, because one day it will get slammed anyway.
short.standalone_note: State that Safety is the fourth of six passes and make clear the slam is a deliberate test of the stack, not carelessness.

segments.covers: Slots get sized to the pans you kept and named, so a slot cannot quietly change job.
beats: Size the divider slots to the pans you kept, fitting the skillet, the two saucepans, and the baking sheets as the dividers go in rather than after.
Write the pan on the front edge of each slot so the wide skillet slot cannot become the place lids get dropped.
Offer a lid to the named skillet slot on camera and have the name turn it away to the door rail.
shots: Overhead, dividers set against the actual pans
Macro, pan names written on slot front edges
Close, a lid offered to the skillet slot and redirected to the rail
on_screen_text: Size the slot to the pan
Name it on the front edge

short.hook: A divider slot in a pan cabinet gets the word skillet written on its front edge, and the lid that tries to move in gets turned away.
short.standalone_note: Show the named slots first so the redirect at the end reads as a rule and not as a preference.

segments.covers: The trigger is the drying rack: pans go back to named slots when they come off it.
beats: Take the pans off the drying rack and return each to its named slot as one continuous action rather than a later job.
Show the pan that has lived on the hob overnight and read it as evidence that its slot is too hard to reach, then fix the slot.
Make the general point that a standard failing in the same place every time is a design problem in the zone, not a discipline problem in the house.
shots: Close, dry pans lifted off the rack
Three-quarter, each pan going into its named slot
Overhead, a lone pan left on the hob in morning light
on_screen_text: Off the rack, into its slot
A pan left out means fix the slot

short.hook: A frying pan has slept on the hob again, and the fix is not a reminder, it is the slot it was supposed to go back into.
short.standalone_note: Name the trigger, pans coming off the drying rack, and the named slot standard, since the diagnosis needs both.

close.standard_beat: Hold the finished cabinet: stacks capped at three, lids racked or railed, baking sheets on edge, heaviest pieces on the cabinet floor, and the two nightly pans at the front nearest the hob. Then the one motion test run on three different pieces in a row, and the trigger, pans coming off the drying rack straight into named slots.
close.next_zone_teaser: Straight above the pans, the shallow drawers, where two can openers and a loose paring knife are sharing a space.

shot_list: Wide overhead on the floor lay-out of the whole cabinet
Three-quarter at floor level for lifting and stacking moves
Close inside the cabinet, bounce card lit, for slot fitting and the shelf film
Macro on worn nonstick, loose rivets, and loose blades
Close on the one motion retrieval test, repeatable on several pans
Locked off on the closed door for the slam test
Macro on slot names written on front edges
Close on the drying rack handoff into named slots
videos.description_hook: If you lift two pans to reach the third, the cabinet is not full, it is stacked wrong. Six passes, Sort through Sustain, including an honest cap on how many frying pans a kitchen needs.

videos.title: 6S for Kitchen Drawers: Flatware, Wraps, and the Drawer Everyone Calls Junk
videos.cold_open_problem: A drawer that no longer opens fully, jammed on an envelope of screws and the manual for a dead printer. Name the problem: a kitchen is allowed one drawer of small useful things, but the call this zone turns on is whether that drawer gets a name and a divider or stays an amnesty. Everything in it has to be something you would come to the kitchen looking for.

segments.covers: One drawer at a time onto a towel, and only what you have used since the season changed goes back.
beats: Tip a single drawer onto a tea towel with the others kept shut, so the job stays finishable in one sitting.
Put back only what has been used since the season changed, handling each item once.
Run the duplicates rule on camera: two can openers on the towel means one leaves.

Set aside the takeaway chopsticks, the rubber bands, the unlabelled key, and the loose batteries, none of which are cooking tools, and date the box for anything you cannot name a use for while holding it.
shots: Overhead, one drawer tipped onto a tea towel
Macro, two identical can openers side by side
Close, non-kitchen items being separated out
Close, the box being dated on its lid
on_screen_text: Two of a thing means one leaves

short.hook: One kitchen drawer tips onto a tea towel and two identical can openers land next to each other.
short.standalone_note: Establish the one drawer at a time rule and the used since the season changed test, both of which the Short depends on.

segments.covers: Dividers go in before anything else, and the drawer gets named before it gets filled.
beats: Fit the dividers into the empty drawer first, then name the drawer, then fill it, in that order.
Place the flatware nearest the dishwasher and the cooking tools nearest the hob, showing the walk each placement removes.
Put the measuring spoons and the scale beside the baking cupboard.
Stand the foil, the cling film, and the baking paper on end so the boxes read from above, in the drawer you can pull open with one hand while the other holds a dish.
shots: Overhead, dividers going into an empty drawer
Close, the drawer named before a single item enters
Overhead, wrap boxes standing on end and readable from above
Three-quarter, a drawer pulled open one handed while the other hand holds a dish
on_screen_text: Divider first, name second, fill third
Boxes on end, read from above

short.hook: A kitchen drawer gets its dividers fitted and its name written before a single object is allowed back in.
short.standalone_note: Say the order out loud, divider, name, fill, since doing it in reverse is the common mistake.

segments.covers: Lift the insert out, because the grit that jams the drawer is underneath it.
beats: Show the drawer failing to close flush, then lift the divider insert right out and tip the crumbs and grit that were sitting under it onto paper.
Wipe both runners and the drawer box itself, including the track the grit has been packing into.
Push the drawer once and check it closes flush before refilling it, which is the actual test of this pass.
shots: Close, insert lifted out and grit tipped onto paper
Macro, runner track before and after wiping
Close, drawer pushed once and closing flush
on_screen_text: The grit lives under the insert

short.hook: A kitchen drawer will not close flush, and the divider insert lifts out to show the crumbs that have been jamming it.
short.standalone_note: Show the drawer failing to close first, so what comes out from under the insert answers a question.

segments.covers: Every blade gets a sheath, a sleeve, or its own tray at the front. This is the 4th S.
beats: Show what a hand meets rummaging in this drawer without looking: the peeler, the loose mandoline blade, and the paring knife lying among the spatulas.
Give each blade a sheath, a sleeve, or its own shallow tray at the front of the drawer, where it is seen before anything is reached past it.
Collect the loose button batteries out of the utility drawer, framed as the poison, choke, or strangle question, since at this height they are swallowed easily and do serious internal damage fast.
Move the batteries into a closed container out of a child's reach, and make that placement part of the drawer's written name.
shots: Close, a hand entering a drawer without looking, wrists and below only
Macro, mandoline blade and paring knife loose among spatulas
Close, each blade sheathed and set into a front tray
Macro, button batteries collected into a closed container
on_screen_text: Button batteries do not live loose

short.hook: A hand goes into a kitchen drawer without looking, and the camera holds on the loose paring knife and mandoline blade waiting in there.
short.standalone_note: State that Safety is the fourth of six passes and name both hazards plainly, loose blades and button batteries.

segments.covers: The name is the rule, written inside the drawer front.
beats: Write the name inside each drawer front: flatware, cooking tools, wraps and bags, utility.
Offer an item that does not match the name at the drawer and have it turned away, which is the whole function of a name.
Write the utility drawer's list on the same label, tape, string, a torch, batteries, a working pen, the menus you actually order from, so it stays a category rather than an amnesty.
shots: Macro, name written inside a drawer front
Overhead, four drawers open with four names visible
Close, an unmatched item refused at the drawer and carried away

short.hook: Four kitchen drawers open in sequence, each with its job written inside the front edge: flatware, cooking tools, wraps and bags, utility.
short.standalone_note: Read the four names on screen so the closing refusal has something to be refused against.

segments.covers: The trigger is the shopping being put away.
beats: Put the shopping away and stand the new roll of foil in on end as part of the same trip.
Walk back whatever has migrated during the week, the whisk that landed in the flatware insert and the scissors in the wraps drawer, in the same pass.
Return to the dated box and hold its deadline: nothing pulled out of it by the end of the season and it leaves unopened.
shots: Three-quarter, shopping bag unpacked with foil going in on end
Close, a whisk lifted out of the flatware insert and placed in the cooking tools drawer
Close, the dated box on its shelf, then leaving unopened
on_screen_text: Nothing used by season end, it leaves

short.hook: A new roll of foil goes into a drawer standing on end, and a whisk that has been living in the flatware insert gets walked back to its own drawer.
short.standalone_note: Name the trigger, putting the shopping away, and the drawer naming standard it enforces.

close.standard_beat: Open all four drawers in sequence on the finished state: one category per drawer, named inside the front edge, flatware in a divided insert with nothing loose beside it, wraps standing on end and readable, blades sheathed at the front, every drawer closing flush with one push. Then the trigger, the shopping put away and one migrated item walked home.
close.next_zone_teaser: One appliance left in this kitchen, the refrigerator, and it wants a morning with real time in it.

shot_list: Overhead locked off on the counter for the tipped drawer contents
Overhead directly down into each open drawer, for before and after
Macro on blades, button batteries, and runner grit
Close on the divider insert lifting out
Close on the drawer closing flush with one push
Macro on names being written inside drawer fronts
Three-quarter on shopping being unpacked into named drawers
Close on the dated box, written and shelved
videos.description_hook: A kitchen gets one drawer of small useful things, but it needs a category and a divider, not an amnesty. Six passes, Sort through Sustain, on the shallow drawers that jam.

videos.title: 6S Refrigerator and Freezer Reset: Label, Date, and the Eat-First Bin
videos.cold_open_problem: Close on a container of perfectly good leftovers being moved to the front of a shelf, again. Name the problem: this is the container you have now shifted forward three times, and the call this zone turns on is a three part question asked at the door, which meal, which day, who eats it. Without an answer, what is being stored is not food, it is the guilt of having cooked too much.

segments.covers: One shelf at a time, judged by the date on the lid rather than by smell.
beats: Work a single shelf at a time with the rest of the door shut, so nothing sits out warming while decisions are being made.
Clear anything frozen past recognition and unlabelled, on the grounds that an unidentifiable block is not an ingredient.
Judge every opened jar, sauce, and dressing against the date on its lid, since these keep smelling fine long after they should have gone.
Make the leftover call on camera, naming the meal, the day, and the person, or it goes today, then fix the cause by portioning into a lunch container the same evening you cook.
shots: Three-quarter, one shelf cleared while the rest stay untouched
Macro, an unlabelled frozen block held up
Close, the date on a dressing lid read under a bounce card
Close, leftovers portioned into a lunch container and dated
on_screen_text: Read the lid, not the smell

short.hook: A container of good leftovers gets moved to the front of a fridge shelf for the third time, and the camera just holds on the move.
short.standalone_note: Ask the three part question, which meal, which day, who eats it, in the opening seconds, since that is the whole Short.

segments.covers: Position inside the fridge is decided by food safety and by what has to be seen first.
beats: Put the raw proteins on the lowest shelf, where a leaking package cannot drip onto anything below it.
Move the dairy out of the door and into the body of the fridge, since the door temperature swings every time somebody opens it.
Put the produce in the drawers and actually set the humidity slider, which on most fridges has never been moved.
Set the eat-first bin at the front at eye level, where the door opens straight onto it.
shots: Three-quarter, raw meat sealed and placed on the lowest shelf
Close, dairy moving from the door shelf into the body
Macro, humidity slider being set on a crisper drawer
Overhead through the open door onto the eat-first bin at eye level

short.hook: The humidity slider on a fridge crisper drawer gets moved for the first time since the fridge was delivered.
short.standalone_note: Explain what the slider does and where on the drawer it sits, since the detail is invisible otherwise.

segments.covers: Clean to inspect: drawers out, coils vacuumed, gasket folds wiped.

Vacuum the condenser coils at the back or underneath, and show what a blanket of dust there means for the machine.
Wipe the door gasket inside its folds, making the point that a gasket usually fails from grime long before it fails from age.
Dry everything before it goes back, so the reset is finished rather than merely wet.

segments.covers: Raw below ready-to-eat, vents clear, and a thermometer so you know instead of assume. This is the 4th S.
beats: Place the sealed raw meat below the ready-to-eat food and hold the vertical order in frame, the single move that carries most of cross contamination prevention.
Show what that order prevents, juices reaching the bagged salad on the shelf beneath, which nobody is going to cook again.
Clear the rear vents of anything pressed up against them so the compartment holds its temperature.
Put a cheap thermometer on the middle shelf and read it on camera, so the running temperature is known rather than assumed.
Move the heavy glass jars off the top door shelf and the top shelf, since they fall onto tile at foot level.

segments.covers: Nothing goes in without a name and a date, and the tools to do that live on the fridge.

Label and date a container before it goes in, filmed as one unbroken action from lid to shelf.
Land the rule that a container without a name and a date is not stored, it is abandoned. Cross-reference Chapter 24, the checklist.

segments.covers: The trigger is the shopping list, written from the gaps.
beats: Before the shopping list gets written, empty the eat-first bin of anything past.
Write the list from the gaps that leaves, with the open fridge and the list in the same frame so the link is obvious.
Make the case for the order: the list already gets written every week, and doing it this way round stops you buying what you already own.

close.standard_beat: Hold the finished state with the door open: raw meat sealed on the lowest shelf, leftovers in clear containers at eye level each named and dated, one eat-first bin at the front where the door opens onto it, rear vents clear, the door holding condiments only, nothing in the freezer without a label. rooms.room_note: A pantry is a small, dim, deep box, and that is the shooting problem. Work the contents out onto a kitchen counter or a folding table just outside the door so the sorting happens in daylight, and reserve the in-pantry camera position for matched before and after states only. Window light is the only source, with a white bounce card on the shadow side because pantry interiors go black two shelves in. One tripod covers everything: a clamp head on the door frame for the three-quarter angle, and the centre column reversed over the counter for overheads. No second operator, no lights, no moving camera, so every shot is either a lock-off or a hand-led reveal inside a static frame. Shoot each shelf fully empty once so Straighten and Shine both have a clean plate to cut to. On set: the two-step stool stays in shot and in use for any top shelf reach, glass is handled at chest height or lower with dry hands, any bulging or leaking can is bagged sealed and binned on camera rather than opened for a better shot, and every shelf is wiped and dried fully before anything goes back.

videos.cold_open_problem: Hands set four part-used bags from the back of the shelf down on the counter in daylight: buckwheat, coarse polenta, rice flour, and one with the date rubbed off. The decision this zone turns on is named plainly, the bag opened for a single recipe and kept ever since because binning food feels wrong and you do still intend to use it. The gap between intending and cooking is stated, and the fourteen day rule is set up as the thing that settles it.

segments.covers: Every bag comes down off this shelf, the already-opened ones get opened and smelled, and the fourteen day rule decides what leaves today.
beats: Strip the shelf bare onto the counter and show why it has to come off in one go, since the buckwheat only surfaces when the cereal boxes in front of it move.
Roll open the part-used bags and smell the flour and the oats, cutting to what stale grain and fine webbing look like beside clean grain.
Apply the fourteen day rule to each opened bag, opened stock with no named meal inside two weeks leaves now.
Split the leavers two ways, unopened and in date into a give-away box while it is still worth having, opened and over a year old straight into the bin.

Opened and over a year: bin

segments.covers: Height on this shelf is assigned by how often you actually cook the grain, so the reach itself becomes the signal.

short.standalone_note: Establish that these are sealed dry staple containers already sorted, so the only open question inside the Short is what goes at which height.

segments.covers: The empty dry goods shelf gets cleaned dry first and dried fully after, because grain dust plus damp is how a pantry starts to smell.
beats: With the shelf bare, vacuum the back corners and the front lip where flour and oat dust settle, before any cloth touches it.
Wipe with mild soap, then dry the shelf fully, with a container held back at the edge of frame until the surface is dry.
Clean to inspect: rake window light across the corners of the flour, oat and rice containers looking for fine webbing or a moth.

Macro on flour dust lifting off the shelf edge

short.standalone_note: Open on the bare shelf and state it has just been emptied of grain containers, so the dry-first order makes sense on its own.

segments.covers: Weight and glass come off the high shelf, because on a grain shelf the crush risk sits at head height.
beats: Show the hazard honestly, cereal boxes and full grain containers stacked above shoulder height, and what the stack does when the bottom one is tugged.
Rebuild to the rule on camera, heavy containers low, light boxes high, nothing stacked more than two deep.
Bring glass grain jars down to chest height or lower and send lidded plastic up top, with wet hands on a full jar shown as the reason.
Stand a two-step stool inside the pantry and give the test, if the stool is not there, that shelf is too high for anything you need weekly.

segments.covers: One container style and one label per container, so a low rice level and an old opening date both read from the doorway.
beats: Swap the mixed jars and boxes for one container style, with the point made that this is not about matching, it is that a half-empty oats container reads the same as a half-empty rice one.
Write a label carrying the item and the date the bag was opened, and fix it facing the doorway.
Quote the rule line, "A standard is the best way you know today, written down," over the finished shelf.
Run the readability test from the doorway, levels and dates read without a single container being lifted. See Chapter 14, visual controls.

segments.covers: Loading order is the habit that keeps this shelf honest, and it rides on putting the shopping away.

Show the correct move, new stock sliding in behind the open bag as the shopping is unpacked.

Land the finished state, every opened bag sealed and dated or gone, two clear blocks, every level readable from the doorway.

Then show the trigger happening for real, shopping bags landing on the counter and new stock loading in behind the open bag, so the standard is seen being kept rather than described.
close.next_zone_teaser: Next along the same wall, the cans and jars, where the argument is with a best-before date you keep overruling.

videos.title: Pantry Cans and Jars: Reading Every Date and Rebuilding the Rows
videos.cold_open_problem: Hands turn three cans one after another hunting for the stamp: soup two years past, chickpeas with the date rubbed clean off, a gift jar being saved for an occasion that has not arrived. The argument this zone runs on is named, the best-before you keep overruling on a technicality while never actually eating the thing. The difference is set out plainly, best-before is about quality and use-by is about safety, and the seven day test is put on the table.

segments.covers: Every can and jar comes off this shelf, gets turned until the date shows, and the duplicates get counted into rows.
beats: Empty the shelf onto the counter and turn each can until the stamp comes into view, showing how much of this pass is simply rotation.
Send dented seams, rust and domed lids straight into the bin rather than back on the shelf, and make clear they do not go to a food bank either.
Count the duplicates into a visible row, four jars of the same pasta sauce, read as a record of what you keep buying blind.
Run the seven day test on anything past best-before, into a meal this week or out this week, and put anything past a use-by date out now.

segments.covers: Rows are built by the meal they belong to rather than by can size, and nothing is allowed to hide behind anything.
beats: Group by how they cook, tomatoes coconut milk and stock in one row because they end up in the same pan, beans and tuna in another because they are lunch.
Show the size-sorted version failing, a short can of tomatoes vanishing behind a tall passata jar, then rebuild tall behind short.
Spin every label to face the front and set the oldest date at the front of its row.

segments.covers: The sticky rings under the honey and the sauce jars come off, because a sticky shelf edge is how ants find the pantry.
beats: Lift the honey jar to reveal the ring it has been sitting in, then find the same under the sauce lids.
Wash the threads of the jars you open most, showing the residue that collects under the rim.
Wipe the shelf edge as well as the surface, since the edge is where a running drip ends up and where ants travel.

segments.covers: Spoilage signs are treated as a hard stop, and the dense can rows come down off the high shelf.

Quote the rule line, "Find it, and fix it now," as the bin lid closes.
Bring the dense can row and the glass sauce jars down below shoulder height, with the two outcomes named, a tin on a bare foot and glass on tile.

videos.title: Pantry Baking Shelf: Testing Leaveners and Settling the Kit
videos.cold_open_problem: Hands lift a piping set, a block of fondant, a third tart tin and a bag of specialty bread flour out onto the counter. Why this is the hardest shelf in the pantry gets named, letting the kit go feels like a statement about who you are rather than about what you bake. The test is set out before any of it moves, keep the tools for what you have baked twice and let go of the tools for what you have baked once, with both numbers explained.

segments.covers: The leaveners get tested rather than guessed at, and the twice-not-once test decides the decorating kit and the tins.
beats: Test on camera in two clear glasses, a spoon of baking powder into hot water should fizz hard and yeast in warm sugared water should foam, and the flat ones go.
Show the other obvious leavers off this shelf, the brick of hardened brown sugar and the cocoa gone grey.
Run the twice-not-once test across the piping set, the fondant and the third tart tin, with twice read as a thing you do and once read as an afternoon that has already happened.
Route what leaves to somebody who bakes this month rather than into a box in the garage.

The shift is set out, choose once in daylight what a child may take without asking, put exactly that in the bin, and let the shelf answer instead of you.

segments.covers: Lids get matched to containers, orphans leave in both directions, and the rattling snack boxes get combined.
beats: Pair every lid to a tub across the counter, letting the unpaired pile build in shot.
Bin the orphans in both directions, lidless tubs and lids for tubs that died, treated as one decision rather than two.
Tip out the snack boxes with two bars rattling in the bottom, combine them, and flatten the empty cartons.
Set the surviving container count against the number of lunches you genuinely pack in a week, not the number you might.

beats: Load the pre-approved snacks into an open bin the child reaches without a stool.

videos.title: Pantry Backstock and Bulk: Setting an Honest Maximum on the Shelf Edge

The belief this zone runs on gets named, that the big pack was a saving because the unit price was better. Then the honest question replaces it, whether you have ever finished one of these before it turned, and that answer becomes a number written on the shelf edge.

Set the rule, anything you hold more than one spare of moves forward into the working shelves this month or it leaves.
Route what sits over the line into meals this month or out to a food bank while it is still in date.
Close the pass on the point that a cupboard of food you will not eat is money already spent rather than value stored.

videos.description_hook: The bulk pack was only a saving if you finished it in time. Put an honest maximum on the shelf edge and an arrival month on every pack, with the full six step 6S reset.

rooms.room_note: Shoot the whole room in one day, working top down so falling dust never lands on a surface you have already finished. The hanging fixture over the table is both the light problem and the light opportunity: switch it off for the hero passes so it does not blow out the bare wood, then bring it up lit for the warm evening close. Side light from the window rakes best across bare wood, so book the table and the sideboard surface for the window's brightest hours, and leave the china cabinet interior until later with a white card taped opposite the glass as bounce, since glass fronts throw the room and the tripod straight back at the lens. One tripod, moved, covers everything: chest height and three-quarter for hands work, then the same tripod set on a step stool with the head tilted straight down for the overheads, so nothing has to be boomed over anyone's china. Every frame cuts at the wrists, no exceptions, and no reflection of the operator may sit in the cabinet glass. Clear a working lane on the side of the sideboard nearest the table, because that is the side the drawers open on. On-set safety: the sideboard outlet trace and the china cabinet wall strapping are real work, not staged, so unplug before tracing cords, empty the cabinet and the sideboard drawers before either piece gets pulled out or drilled, and lay the stud finder and the strap kit out before rolling. Never leave the camera running unattended under a loaded tall cabinet. Any chair found with a working joint gets turned to the wall on camera and stays turned, including between takes.

videos.title: Dining Table Reset: Getting the Table Back From Homework and Mail
videos.cold_open_problem: Open overhead on the table as it actually is, homework, unopened post, a craft box and a laptop sharing the surface, then push in on the one chair nobody has pulled out in weeks because a stack of paperwork is sitting on it. Frame it as a conflict rather than a mess: someone in this house has made the dining table their desk, and every polite request has failed to move it. Set up the decision this video has to settle, that an activity landing here more than three evenings in a week is not clutter, it is an activity with nowhere else to live, so it either gets a caddy and a named shelf or the room stops being a dining room.

segments.covers: Everything comes off in one armful, and the sorting rule is by owner, not by type.
beats: The whole tabletop cleared to the floor in one continuous armful rather than item by item, with the reason given: a table sorted one object at a time never actually empties.

Floor piles laid out by person instead of by category, because the homework, the post and the half finished craft project each belong to a human being who can carry them, while a pile called paper belongs to nobody.
One genuinely ambiguous object, a stack of unopened post, walked through the decision and landing on a named pile rather than back on the wood.
The bare tabletop held at the end of the pass, with nothing staged back onto it yet.

Set up the settlement this video owes, that the argument gets decided by measuring the largest dish genuinely served from here, and that a strip of tape takes the place of the good intention.

A cloth that fails the measure held against the edge, with the real reason it never gets used made visible, that it looks wrong the moment it goes on and gets folded away again.
The keepers set aside, the cloths that fit the table you own plus one sized for the table with the leaf in.
The failures retired on the spot: a stain already treated once and not shifted becomes rags today rather than next season, and partial napkin sets travel with the cloth they match or leave with it.

rooms.room_note: One person, one tripod, window light. No crane, no drone, no jib, no second operator, no lighting rig. Shoot the whole room in one daylight block, mid-morning to early afternoon, curtains open and lamps off for wide work so the natural light stays consistent between setups. Group the lamp-on shots for Side Tables and the screen-off shots for Media Center at the end of the day as the room dims, because those two zones need the lamp or the dark screen reading as the light source rather than fighting the window. Every overhead is a locked frame, never a moving one: for the coffee table and side tables, set the tripod high with the head tilted down or use a lateral arm, positioned so only forearms enter the frame and the operator stands outside it. Nothing travels along the floor route on an overhead; the circulation path is covered by a locked high wide from the doorway looking down the route, plus a handheld forward-facing walk held at chest height where only the basket and forearms are in shot. Behind the media unit is the one setup window light cannot reach: pull the unit forward the day before, clamp a single work light to the wall side, and shoot three-quarter from floor level on the tripod. On-set safety: the television must be anchored and the bookcase strapped into studs before any pull test or climbing angle is filmed, and the strap-fitting shots are filmed first so the pull test is genuinely against a finished fix. No candle is ever lit unattended for a shot; the candle beats are filmed unlit. Recliner and sofa bed mechanism shots are filmed slow-close with a hand well clear and nothing and nobody in the closing path. Keep a laundry basket, a dark towel for emptied contents, velcro ties, corner guards, a stud finder, a step, cable clips, a label maker and a microfiber cloth on set for the whole day.

videos.title: Sofa Reset: Seats That Hold People, Not Storage
videos.cold_open_problem: Open on hands lifting three decorative pillows off the sofa onto the floor, then the same three pillows back on the seat, then the same lift again. Name the working definition that settles this zone: something you move every time you sit is not seating, and it is not decor either, because decor stays where it is put. Name the avoided reason directly, that the pillows were a gift from someone, and set up the count the video will make: how many can stay in place while a person actually sits.

segments.covers: Everything comes off the seats and out of the seams, then splits into three destinations, not two.
beats: Hands strip the sofa completely: cushions off, throws off, all seat contents onto a sheet on the floor, so the bare deck is in frame before any decision is made.

Hands work the seams and the back gap, pulling out coins, hair ties, a magazine wedged behind the armrest, a spare remote. Cover why the seams are the part of this zone that never gets sorted, and lay each find on the towel where it can be counted.

Three piles get named as they are built: leaves-the-room, goes-in-the-wash, lives-here. Cover why the middle pile has to exist, because laundry that migrated onto this sofa is a laundry decision and mixing it into a sofa decision is where the sort stalls.
The second and third throw blanket get routed to the wash or the leaves pile, keeping only what the basket holds folded.

short.hook: Hands pulling find after find out of one sofa seam in a single unbroken shot, each one laid on a dark towel beside it
short.standalone_note: Open by naming this as a living room sofa and the seams and deck under the cushions as the part nobody sorts, then close by naming the three destination piles so the Short teaches a method rather than only showing a reveal.

segments.covers: Three homes get chosen by how this sofa is actually sat on: one remote tray, one throw basket, one reading slot.
beats: Hands place the remote tray on the arm someone reaches from while sitting, and the obvious wrong answer gets named, which is the arm nearest the television.
The throw basket goes at one end of the sofa and the throws are folded to one matching size, so the basket reads as a visible limit rather than swallowing an unlimited pile.
Reading matter gets one slot. Cover the shared test all three homes have to pass, that nothing gets lifted off a cushion before a person sits down.
A reach test: a hand and forearm enter from sofa height, take the remote off the tray and return it without the shoulder ever coming into frame.
shots: Locked overhead of the sofa with tray, basket and slot placed, each briefly outlined
Close on hands folding two throws to matching size and dropping them into the basket
Three-quarter from seat height of a hand reaching the tray, forearm only in frame
Macro on both remotes seated in the tray
on_screen_text: One tray, one basket, one slot

short.hook: A hand reaching from sofa height for a remote and closing on nothing, then the tray sliding to the arm the hand was already going to
short.standalone_note: Establish in the first line that this is a sofa remote and throw problem in a living room, and state the rule the three homes exist to serve, that nothing gets lifted off a seat before a person sits.

segments.covers: Clean the upholstery that hands and hair actually touch, and even out where the wear lands.
beats: Upholstery tool along the seams and across the exposed deck. Cover why this only works after Sort, because the tool reaches only what has already been exposed.
Hands wipe the arms and the headrest, the two places where hand oil and hair oil land, and the cloth is held next to a clean one so the difference is in frame rather than described.
Cushions get rotated and flipped so the seat nobody chooses takes a turn at the wear. Cover this as cleaning to inspect, because the flip is when a split seam or a failing zip gets found.
shots: Locked close on one seam with the upholstery tool drawn through frame, tripod fixed
Macro of the used cloth held beside a clean one after the headrest pass
Locked overhead of cushions being lifted, flipped and set back in a new order
Three-quarter of the exposed sofa deck before and after the tool passes

short.hook: An upholstery tool drawn down one sofa seam, then a cloth held up after a single pass across the headrest
short.standalone_note: Say in the first line that this is a sofa with its cushions already removed, since the seam pass makes no sense otherwise, and end on the flip named as the moment you inspect rather than the moment you finish.

segments.covers: The two hazards this seating actually produces: a mechanism that closes on fingers, and a throw trailing onto the night-time walkway.
beats: Hands work the recliner footrest and the sofa bed hinge closed slowly, with a deliberate check of the empty floor in front of the chair first. Frame this as fall, cut, or crush, and name that patch of floor as where a child sits.
Macro on the crush point of the mechanism with nothing in it, and the fix stated as the slow close plus the look, made a household rule rather than a one-time check.

A throw is shown trailing off the sofa onto the floor, then the same spot in low light. Frame this as fall, with the specific event named, standing up from that exact seat in the dark, which is what the basket prevents.
See Chapter 21, the hazard hunt, and the rule of fixing what you find at the moment you find it.
shots: Macro on the recliner hinge closing slowly, hand well clear of the path
Low locked frame of the empty carpet directly in front of the footrest, nobody in shot
Close on a throw hanging from the sofa arm across the walkway
Locked overhead of the same throw folded into the basket, walkway clear
on_screen_text: Find it, and fix it now

short.hook: A low locked shot of the empty carpet in front of a recliner, the footrest coming down toward the lens and stopping
short.standalone_note: Name the room and both hazards explicitly, since a mechanism close-up on its own reads as generic, and deliver both fixes inside the Short: the slow close with a look at the floor, and the throw basket keeping blankets off the walkway.

segments.covers: The rule lives on the throw basket label, where anyone can read it from the seat they are sitting in.
beats: Hands write and fix the label to the throw basket, carrying the rule itself rather than only the word throws.
Cover why the label holds where a spoken rule does not: this room fails by donation, each person leaves one thing and nobody sees a mess they caused, so the standard has to be readable from the sofa.
Quote the frozen line, that a standard is the best way you know today, written down, and note the label gets rewritten when the household finds a better way.
shots: Macro on the label being written, then pressed onto the basket
Three-quarter from sofa seat height showing the label legible at that distance
Locked overhead of the finished seating with tray, basket and label all readable
on_screen_text: Put the rule on the basket

short.hook: Three throw blankets dumped over a sofa arm beside an unlabelled basket, then a label going on that carries a rule rather than a category name
short.standalone_note: Set up in the first line that this is a shared living room sofa where several people each leave one thing behind, because the label only earns its place against that specific failure.

segments.covers: The reset rides on the lamp going off, an action already happening in this room every night.
beats: Hands square the cushions and drop the throws in the basket, then reach for the lamp switch. Cover the trigger as the lamp going off, an event that already happens, not a reminder anyone sets.
Show the whole reset running against the length of turning the lamp off, with no number on screen, so the point lands as short rather than as a measurement.
Cover why the event owns this rather than a named person: whoever is last out does it because the lamp is in their hand, which is what keeps it from becoming anyone's chore.
shots: Locked overhead of hands squaring cushions and dropping two throws into the basket
Close on the hand reaching the lamp switch, room going dim
Three-quarter of the reset room in low light, walkway and seats clear

short.hook: A hand already on a lamp switch, stopping, then going back to square the cushions before the light goes out
short.standalone_note: Re-establish the finished state in the opening seconds, seats clear and throws folded in one basket, so the viewer knows what is being maintained, and name the trigger as the lamp itself rather than a time of night.

close.standard_beat: Return to the finished sofa in the same locked overhead used at the top: every seat sittable without lifting anything, throws folded to one size in the labelled basket, at most one cushion per seat, both remotes in the tray on the arm people reach from. Read the standard off the basket label, seats hold people not storage, then show the trigger once more as the cushions get squared and the lamp goes off.
close.next_zone_teaser: Point at the coffee table just in frame, still carrying four mugs and four books, and name its own hard call, the book you are supposedly in the middle of.

videos.description_hook: If you move the same pillows onto the floor every time you sit down, those pillows are not seating. Here is the full 6S reset for a living room sofa, hands only, in the order that actually works.

videos.title: Coffee Table Reset: The Tray Sets the Limit
videos.cold_open_problem: Open on a locked overhead of four books stacked on a coffee table, with a hand opening each cover in turn to show where the bookmark is sitting. Name the split this video makes: one of these is being read and three are being stored, and putting them away has felt like admitting you stopped. State the consequence for the surface itself, that this table cannot hold a standard while it is quietly acting as storage for decisions nobody has made.

segments.covers: The top clears completely, and only what was genuinely used in the last two days goes back.
beats: Hands sweep the entire top onto the floor in one pass, so the decision starts from an empty surface rather than from what is already sitting there.
Each item comes back only if somebody used it in the last two days. Cover why the empty start makes the test honest, because judging items in place always favours leaving them.
Named departures happen in frame: the candle burned down to the foil, the coasters nobody uses because they live on the far corner, the three-month-old magazines, the takeaway menus.

The bookmark test gets applied to the stack: two weeks without the bookmark moving means storage, and storage happens on a shelf. One book per person stays, and it comes back down the moment it gets opened again.
shots: Locked overhead of the loaded table, then the identical frame emptied
Close on a hand opening a cover to a bookmark sitting near the front
Macro on the candle burned to the foil and the menus going into the leaves pile
Three-quarter of the returning items being set back one at a time
on_screen_text: Used in the last two days

short.hook: Four books on a coffee table, four bookmarks opened in a row, three of them nowhere near the middle
short.standalone_note: Establish in the first line that this is a living room coffee table and that the book stack is the pile that stalls it, then deliver the whole rule inside the Short: two weeks without the bookmark moving means you are storing it, one book per person stays on the table.

segments.covers: The tray becomes the table's entire standing inventory, and the coasters get placed by reach from the sofa.
beats: The tray goes down and gets named as the limit itself, not as decoration: what fits on it is what lives on this table.
Four coasters and the remote in use go on the tray, positioned within arm's reach of whoever sits on the sofa, so a mug lands on a coaster without anyone leaning across the table.
At most one book or one plant is allowed beside the tray, with the rest of the top left showing.
A reach test: a hand and forearm enter from sofa height and set a mug on a coaster without the frame ever showing a lean.
shots: Locked overhead of the tray holding four coasters and one remote, table top visible around it
Three-quarter from sofa seat height of a hand setting a mug on a coaster, forearm only
Close on the single permitted book beside the tray
Macro along the tray edge as the visible boundary

short.hook: A mug travelling toward a coffee table, then a coaster sliding into the exact spot the hand was already heading for
short.standalone_note: State up front that the tray defines everything allowed to stand on this table, because without that framing the coaster placement reads as a small styling tip rather than the rule it is.

segments.covers: Clean under the tray and beneath the table, where this surface quietly fails.
beats: Hands lift the tray and wipe the whole top including the ring marks that were hiding underneath. Cover why a tray without this step only moves the dirt out of sight.
The underside edge and the lower shelf get done, since that is where crumbs and dust collect unseen and where the grime that never shows in a wide shot is actually sitting.
A glass top gets two passes, one for grease and one dry, filmed under raking lamplight so the prints are visible before and gone after.
shots: Locked overhead of the tray lifting to reveal the ring marks underneath
Macro along the underside edge and the lower shelf with the cloth
Close with a table lamp raking across the glass top, prints visible, then the same angle after the dry pass
Three-quarter of the finished top from doorway distance

short.hook: A tray lifting off a coffee table to reveal a perfect ring of marks it had been hiding
short.standalone_note: Name the surface and the fact that a tray had been sitting on it, and close with the two-pass rule for a glass top so the Short teaches a technique that works on its own.

segments.covers: Two real hazards at this table: a hard square corner at a toddler's head height, and an open flame in a paper neighbourhood.
beats: The camera drops to the height of a child learning to walk, so the glass edge and square corner arrive at forehead level in frame. Frame this as fall, cut, or crush, and state the fix plainly as corner guards or a different table, not vigilance.
Hands fit a corner guard in macro as the actual repair, done now rather than planned.

The unlit candle is set back in frame with its neighbours named, throws, magazines and paper. Frame this as burn or fire, and name this as the surface most often left burning when everyone goes to bed.
The candle leaves the table entirely as the decision, rather than being shifted to a different corner of the same top.
shots: Low three-quarter at toddler head height with the square corner and glass edge crossing the lens
Macro on hands fitting a corner guard to the square corner
Close on an unlit candle surrounded by throws and magazines
Locked overhead of the candle being lifted off the table

short.hook: A camera dropping to the height of a toddler until a coffee table corner lines up exactly with the lens
short.standalone_note: Name both hazards as living room coffee table hazards in the first line, and put both fixes in frame inside the Short: the corner guard fitted, and the candle leaving the table rather than moving along it.

segments.covers: A photograph of this table's finished tray settles what clear means here, with nothing left to interpret.
beats: The finished table gets photographed from the sofa seat angle it is actually seen from, framed to show the tray, four coasters, the remote in use and the one permitted book.
Cover what this photo does that a written rule cannot: it settles the argument about what clear means on this specific top, because the count and the layout are visible rather than described.
See Chapter 25, the ideal-state photo, and note the photo gets retaken when the standard genuinely improves.
The phone holding the photo is held up beside the live table in matching framing so the match or the gap is visible in one shot.
shots: Locked overhead of the finished tray serving as the reference image itself
Close on a phone screen holding the photo, the live table behind it in the same framing
Three-quarter of the photo propped where the household passes it

short.hook: A phone held up in front of a loaded coffee table, the photo on its screen showing the same table with a tray, four coasters and one book
short.standalone_note: Say that the photo was taken of this exact table on its best day and now settles what clear means on it, otherwise the shot reads as an ordinary before and after rather than a standard.

segments.covers: The table resets on the trip to the kitchen that is already being made.
beats: Hands gather the last mug of the evening, then sweep everything sitting off the tray into the same load. Cover the trigger as a trip already happening, so the reset costs no extra journey.
The off-tray items get distributed on the way rather than dumped in a heap, which is what stops the mess relocating to another surface.
Cover how the tray makes the trigger workable: overflow is visible from across the room, so whoever picks up the mug can see what has to travel with it without inspecting the table.
shots: Locked overhead of an evening table with mugs and off-tray items
Close on hands loading the last mug plus the strays into one grip
Three-quarter of the table left at tray-only state as the loaded hands leave frame

short.hook: A hand picking up the last mug of the night, stopping, then collecting everything not on the tray into the same grip
short.standalone_note: Re-establish the tray rule in the opening line, because this whole trigger depends on off-tray already being a defined category on this table.

close.standard_beat: Return to the opening locked overhead, now holding one tray with four coasters and the remote in use, at most one book beside it, and wood or glass showing across most of the top. State the standard, if it does not fit on the tray it does not live on the table, then show the evening trigger once: the last mug goes to the kitchen and everything off-tray travels with it.
close.next_zone_teaser: Tilt to the media unit behind the table and the cable tangle visible underneath it, and name the next call, every cable gets its device named out loud or it leaves the house.

Close setup for bookmark checks and single-item decisions

Close on the last-mug pickup with the strays in the same grip

videos.title: Behind the TV: Label Every Cable and Anchor the Screen
videos.cold_open_problem: Open on hands lifting a box of cables out of the media unit and tipping it onto a towel, then picking up one lead and holding it still. Name what is actually in this unit: a working device nobody has switched on in a year, and a box of cables kept in case they fit something. Name the avoided reason directly, that the devices cost real money and letting them go reads as admitting the money is gone, and set the video's answer against it, that the money went when the device stopped being used, not when it leaves the house.

segments.covers: Every cable gets its device named out loud or it leaves, and every dead device gets one power-on test.
beats: Hands unplug and lay out every cable in a row on the floor, so the count is in frame before any decision is made.
Each cable is picked up and the device it serves gets named before the hand finishes lifting it. Cover the rule and its reason, that an unnamed cable will still be unnamed next year.
Named departures happen in frame: the composite leads, the disc player nobody has loaded in a year, the streaming stick from two televisions ago, the charger with the old connector.
Each device gets powered on once. Cover the test: if it does not boot, or it boots and nobody in the house asks for it inside the month, it goes to recycling or resale this week.
Discs and games get one decision each, sell, lend, or recycle, with no undecided pile allowed to form on the floor.
shots: Locked overhead of every cable laid out in a row on the floor
Close on a hand lifting one lead, the other hand pointing to the device it serves
Macro on an old connector held next to the current one
Three-quarter of a device being powered on, indicator light coming up or staying dark
Locked overhead of the sell, lend and recycle groups for discs and games

short.hook: A hand lifting cables one at a time from a tangle, naming a device for each, until one lead gets no name and goes straight into the leaves pile
short.standalone_note: Establish in the first seconds that this is the box of cables from behind a television, and deliver the whole rule inside the Short: name the device out loud before you finish picking the cable up, or it leaves.

segments.covers: Cables get bundled by device path, and controllers get one ventilated bin at the height of whoever plays.
beats: Hands bundle cables with velcro ties by device path, so one console can be pulled forward without disturbing the sound bar. Cover the test, pulling a single device out and watching nothing else move.
The single power strip gets positioned and every bundle routed to it, so there is one path behind the unit rather than four.
Controllers and remotes go into one ventilated bin set at the height of whoever plays, and the reason the top of the unit fails is shown in frame, things slide off the back and rejoin the tangle.
The pull-out test is filmed: one console comes forward while every neighbouring cable stays slack.
shots: Three-quarter from floor level behind the unit showing bundles running to one strip
Close on hands fitting a velcro tie around one device path
Macro on the ventilated bin with controllers seated in it
Close on a console being pulled forward while neighbouring cables stay slack

short.hook: One console pulled forward out of a media unit while every other cable behind it stays completely still
short.standalone_note: Show the tangled before state in the first seconds and name bundling by device path as the reason the pull-out works, otherwise the movement has no visible cause.

segments.covers: Dust is what turns a warm device into a hot one, so the vents and the television back panel come first.
beats: Vacuum across the console and amplifier vents and the whole back panel of the television. Cover the connection: this is a cleaning pass that inspects for a fire risk, because dust is what turns a warm device into a hot one.
Macro on a packed vent before and after, so the blockage is visible in frame rather than described.
The screen gets a dry microfiber cloth only, with the reason spray is never used stated as the cloth crosses.
Hands run along each cable during the pass, checking for a cracked or scorched section, which is the inspection half of this step.
shots: Macro on a vent packed solid with dust, then the same vent after the pass
Three-quarter of the vacuum working across the television back panel
Close on a dry microfiber cloth crossing the screen
Macro on fingers running a cable, stopping on a damaged section

short.hook: Macro on an amplifier vent packed solid with grey dust, then the same vent clear
short.standalone_note: Name the device and the stake in the first line, that packed vents behind a media unit are a fire risk nobody can see, and include the dry-cloth-only rule for the screen so the Short delivers a full technique.

segments.covers: Heat, power and a tipping screen: the three hazards behind and on top of this unit.
beats: A hand's gap of clear air is measured around the amplifier and console vents. Frame this as burn or fire, and name that all three fire risks in this zone sit hidden behind the unit.
One power strip plugged into another is shown, then undone. State the rule plainly, never run one strip into another, with every cable checked for scorching as they are separated.

The television gets anchored to the wall or to the unit, filmed as the actual fix being fitted. Frame this as fall, cut, or crush, and name the specific event, a screen tipping off the front edge when a child pulls the edge or climbs the shelf below it.
A drink on top of the console and another beside the power strip get removed. Frame this as water and electricity, liquid sitting directly over live connections.
shots: Close on a hand measuring the air gap at the amplifier vent
Macro on one power strip plugged into another, then separated
Three-quarter of hands fitting an anchor strap from the television to the wall
Low locked angle at child height on the front edge of the screen and the shelf below it
Close on a glass being lifted off the console and set elsewhere

short.hook: A low locked shot at child height looking up at the unsupported front edge of a television standing on a low unit
short.standalone_note: Name the room and the media unit, show the anchor strap being fitted as the fix inside the Short, and name the two hidden hazards alongside it, blocked vents and a strip plugged into a strip, so the Short covers this zone's real safety picture.

segments.covers: Labels at both ends plus matching outlet labels make an orphan cable obvious without moving the unit.
beats: Hands label both ends of a cable as it goes in, and label the strip's outlets to match.
Cover what this makes visible: a cable that belongs to nothing now stands out at a glance, with no tracing and no pulling the unit out from the wall.
The check gets demonstrated, scanning the strip and stopping on one unlabelled plug immediately.
See Chapter 14, visual controls, as the chapter behind labels, outlines and boundaries.
shots: Macro on a label wrapping one cable end, then the matching end
Close on the power strip with its outlets labelled
Three-quarter scanning the strip, one unlabelled plug standing out
Locked overhead of the finished bundle with labels readable

short.hook: A hand scanning across a labelled power strip behind a television and stopping dead on the one plug with no name on it
short.standalone_note: Establish first that every cable in this unit was labelled at both ends and the outlets labelled to match, since the scan only reads as a system once the viewer knows the labelling rule.

segments.covers: Two rhythms hold this zone: nothing switches on unlabelled, and controllers ride out with the credits.
beats: A new device is brought in and held unpowered while its cable gets labelled at both ends. Cover the rule, that it does not get switched on until the labels are on, which is the only moment anyone is willing to do it.
Hands drop controllers into the bin as the television goes off. Cover the trigger as the credits rolling, an event already happening in this room.
Cover why these two rhythms are enough for this unit: it only degrades when a device arrives unlabelled or a controller ends the night somewhere other than the bin.
shots: Close on a new device held while a label goes onto its cable
Macro on the label going on before the plug goes in
Three-quarter of controllers dropping into the bin as the screen goes dark
Locked overhead of the finished unit with the bin filled and one bundle visible

short.hook: A brand new device sitting unplugged on the floor beside a television while a label goes onto its cable first
short.standalone_note: State the rule as the opening beat, that nothing gets switched on until its cable is labelled at both ends, because the delay is the entire point and looks arbitrary without it.

close.standard_beat: Return behind the unit and hold on the finished state: every cable labelled at both ends running in one bundle to a single labelled strip, nothing plugged in for a device no longer owned, a clear hand's gap of air at the amplifier and console vents, the screen anchored, every controller and remote in one bin. State the standard, every cable is labelled at both ends and every device has clear air on its vents, then show the trigger, credits rolling and the controllers going back on the way out.
close.next_zone_teaser: Pan to the bookcase beside the unit, top shelf loaded and nothing strapped, and name the next reset, every book through your hands one shelf at a time and the unit finally fixed into the studs.

shot_list: Three-quarter floor-level setup behind the pulled-out unit, single clamped work light on the wall side
Locked overhead of the full cable layout on the floor
Close setup for single-cable naming and label application
Macro on vents before and after the dust pass
Low child-height angle on the television front edge and the shelf below
Three-quarter of the anchor strap being fitted
Macro on the power strip outlets and the strip-into-strip hazard
Close on the console pull-out test with neighbouring cables slack
Locked overhead of the ventilated controller bin at play height
Three-quarter of the screen going dark for the sustain trigger
videos.description_hook: Pick up a cable and name the device it serves before you finish lifting it. If you cannot, it leaves. Full 6S reset for the media unit, hands only, including the anchor.

videos.title: Bookshelf Reset: One Shelf at a Time, Strapped to the Wall
videos.cold_open_problem: Open on a hand pulling a book off a shelf, turning it face out, then setting it back without opening it. Name why this shelf is where sorting stalls, because a shelf is partly an argument about who you are. Set up the two questions the video keeps separate: whether you would open this again, and whether you are keeping it so a visitor sees it.

segments.covers: One shelf at a time, every book through your hands, with the identity question split in two.
beats: Hands take one shelf down completely onto the floor, in order. Cover why the whole unit at once fails and one shelf at a time works, because every book has to pass through your hands to get a decision.
Clear departures go first with no debate: duplicates, manuals for appliances you replaced, free paperbacks from a conference, anything water-damaged.
The display objects get the same pass: empty frames, the dead plant, the souvenirs you stopped seeing years ago.

The two questions get asked on separate items. First, would you open it again or press it into a friend's hand, in which case it stays with no further debate. Second, and only if the first is no, are you keeping it so a visitor sees it, which holds for two or three books and does not hold for forty.
Unread books get one shelf, capped between two bookends, with the intake rule stated: a new one arrives, it does not fit, one leaves.
shots: Three-quarter of one shelf being emptied onto the floor in order
Close on hands turning a single book over, cover to spine
Macro on a water-damaged edge and a duplicate pair side by side
Locked overhead of the unread shelf filling between two bookends until they will not close
Close on the dead plant and the empty frames leaving the shelf

short.hook: Two bookends squeezed toward each other along a shelf of unread books until one book has to come out
short.standalone_note: Establish in the first line that this is a living room bookshelf and that this shelf holds the unread books capped between bookends, then state the intake rule inside the Short: a new one arrives, it does not fit, one leaves.

segments.covers: Grouping follows how you hunt for a book, weight goes low, and every shelf keeps slack.
beats: Books go back grouped by subject first and author second. Cover the reason against the popular alternative, that you hunt by subject, so arranging by colour makes the shelf harder to use than it was.
Heavy art and reference volumes go on the bottom shelves. Cover the twin reason, easier to lift from and a fall from there does no harm.
A hand's width of empty space is left at one end of each shelf and named as where the next book lands rather than as a gap.
Frames and objects get gathered into two or three groups instead of spaced evenly along every shelf, with the difference shown in one wide frame.
shots: Three-quarter of a shelf being refilled by subject group
Macro of a hand held sideways against the slack at the shelf end
Close on heavy reference volumes being placed on the bottom shelf
Wide locked frame comparing evenly spaced objects to two gathered groups

short.hook: A hand held sideways against the empty end of a bookshelf, measuring the gap that is not allowed to be filled
short.standalone_note: Name the shelf and say what the slack is for in the first line, that it is where the next book lands, because an empty gap otherwise reads as a styling choice.

segments.covers: Dust the tops of the books and the top of the tallest unit, which is where this room's dust actually settles.
beats: Hands dust the top edges of the books themselves rather than only the shelf boards. Cover why the shelf never stays clean, because the boards get wiped and the books keep the dust.
Shelf fronts get wiped where hands grab to pull a spine out, with the used cloth held in frame.
The very top of the tallest unit gets done from a step. Cover that this is where the room's dust settles and where nobody ever looks.
shots: Macro along the top edges of a row of books with the cloth
Close on the shelf front where hands grip, cloth passing
Locked high frame on the top of the unit, hands arriving into frame from below with the step visible at the base
Macro on the cloth after the top of the unit is wiped
on_screen_text: Dust the books, not just the boards

short.hook: A cloth drawn along the top edges of a row of books, coming away grey

segments.covers: A tall loaded bookcase and how people reach its top shelf: the two ways this zone hurts someone.

videos.description_hook: Measure the narrowest gap on your living room route. If you cannot carry a full basket through without turning sideways, the problem is not the clutter. Full 6S reset, hands only.

rooms.room_note: Shoot the whole room in one day, in this order: Primary Media Zone first, because its cables cross the floor into every other zone and clearing them opens the floor for the tripod everywhere else. Natural light only, so schedule the two floor-level zones (Toy and Play, Blanket and Comfort) for the brightest part of the day, and the two cabinet-interior zones (Media, Charging) for when a clamped white card can bounce window light into the dark cabinet rather than adding a lamp. Access is the constraint behind the television unit, so pull the unit forward yourself before setting up and mark its original floor position with low-tack tape so it goes back square. Tripod placement, single operator throughout: one tripod with a counterweighted horizontal arm parked over the play mat and the craft surface, one tripod at about seat height for the sofa, basket, and shelf work, and a handheld macro setup for cable ends, vent slots, thumbstick collars, and box corners. Nothing above the wrists is ever in frame, so run each reach once and check the framing on the camera screen before rolling, since there is nobody watching a monitor for you. On-set safety: the anti-tip check happens on camera with a real strap, so have a spare strap and the correct bolts on hand before the shoot rather than discovering the mount is loose mid-take. Unplug the glue gun between takes and keep its cooling tile in shot so the cooling spot is established visually. Never film a real swollen battery pack, use a clearly labeled stand-in pack and say on screen that it is a stand-in.

Show the two honest endings being set up at the start, moving the save data or handing over a controller for one real session, and make clear the console is settled inside this session rather than the next one.

Split the pile into what pairs with a device still in this house and what pairs with something already gone, and let the pile of dead remotes build on camera, because that is usually two or three.
Work the call: plug the old console into the television, and show both honest outcomes, the save data moving to a card or the current console, or a controller being handed off for one real session.
Photograph the save screen, then route console, controllers, and cables out together in one trip, since splitting them is how half of it returns to the cabinet.

Hold up a cracked seam, a corroded battery compartment, and a wheel that will not stay on, and apply the today rule, repaired today or gone today, because later is not a real time.
Start the honest week on the gift toy: tape a square on the mat, set it in the square, touch nothing, then show the square still marked and the toy still square-on at the end of it.

Work the call on camera by sorting the gaps into substitutable, a meeple, a token, a die, a bill of play money, and structural, a rules booklet, a board section, a card from a deck that must be complete, a puzzle piece. Show a coin and a printed sheet standing in for the first kind.

videos.title: One Basket, One Rule: Sorting Throw Blankets by Use Instead of Looks

Set out the decision this basket keeps getting backwards, the instinct to keep the wool one because it looks like the room you want and quietly retire the fleece because it looks tired. Establish the test the video runs on, that this basket stores comfort and not decoration, so the measure is reaches rather than looks.

Add the third failure, a smell that survives washing, and rule out washing it again as the next step.
Route the failures honestly on camera, into car blankets, pet bedding, or rags, and out of this room today.

Work the call by reaches rather than looks: the fleece everyone fights over stays, and the untouched wool throw goes to the guest bed where beautiful and unused is actually the job, or it goes out. Apply the same test to the knitted heirloom, into the linen closet or to the relative who will wrap up in it.

videos.title: One Strip, Named Slots: Setting Up a Family Charging Station
videos.cold_open_problem: Open on a drawer being pulled open and a hand lifting a retired phone, screen dark, out of a nest of cables. Set out the contradiction that has kept it there: it is being held as a backup in case something breaks and as an archive because there are photos on it never transferred, and it cannot be both. Make clear it is serving neither right now, and that it gets settled in this session while the device is in hand and the charger is on the table.

segments.covers: Every cable and plug is matched to a device in this house that currently works, and the unmatched go to recycling rather than back in the drawer.
beats: Lay every cable and plug out in one straight line, because a drawer cannot be sorted while it is still a tangle.
Bring the actual devices to the line and set each one at the end of the cable that fits it, rather than working from memory.
Sweep what is left into a recycling bag, since unmatched is not spare, and keep one spare of each connector type in a labeled bag.

Settle the retired phone: a backup is one you have charged and switched on within the last year, so run the photo transfer now on camera, or say plainly it will never happen, then send the handset with its battery to a proper collection point.
