Three-quarter of the vanity door open showing the taped ideal-state photo
Off-axis mirror pass framed to keep the rig out of the reflection
Low wide of the finished bare counter in window light
videos.description_hook: The bathroom counter fills up because one heat tool earned a permanent spot next to the outlet. This is the full 6S pass that gets it back to a single tray you can lift with one hand.

videos.title: Vanity Drawers: Sorting by Routine and Reading Every Date
videos.cold_open_problem: Open overhead on a drawer being pulled, then a hand lifting out one expensive palette or bottle that has been used twice. Hold on it. Name the avoidance directly, that keeping it is not thrift but paying storage on a decision that already went wrong, and that this is the object skipped past on every Sort pass because binning it means admitting the money is gone. Then show the rest of the drawer it has been protecting.

segments.covers: One drawer at a time onto a towel, and every tube, jar, and bottle gets turned over to find a date or an open-jar symbol.
beats: Empty a single drawer onto a towel and explain the one-drawer-at-a-time rule, that the room stays usable and the pass actually finishes.
Demonstrate the turn-and-read action on several items, showing where the printed date and the open-jar symbol sit on different packaging.
Call the usual offenders as they surface, mascara, liquid foundation, and sunscreen, and separate them from the usual volume, dead hair ties and orphan bobby pins.
Show the two outbound piles forming, past-date and simply not used, and the small survivor pile that will go back.
shots: Overhead of the drawer being tipped onto the towel
Macro on a hand rotating a bottle to find the open-jar symbol
Macro on a printed date on a crimped tube end
Overhead of the three piles resolving on the towel
Close on a handful of orphan bobby pins going into a bin

short.hook: Macro on a thumb rotating a jar until the little open-lid symbol appears, a mark most people have never noticed on something they use daily.
short.standalone_note: Explain what the open-jar symbol means and where it is printed, because the Short depends entirely on the viewer reading that mark.

segments.covers: Divide by routine, morning, evening, and weekly, rather than by product type, and stand the long-handled things upright.
beats: Lay dividers into the empty drawer and assign them out loud as morning, evening, and weekly or occasional, explaining why time of day beats product category in a drawer you reach into half awake.
Load each compartment from the survivor pile, narrating the routine question asked of each item rather than what kind of product it is.
Stand combs, brushes, and dental supplies upright in their own section, showing that upright means nothing has to be dug through to reach what is underneath.
shots: Overhead of empty drawer with dividers being placed
Overhead of the three compartments filling one at a time
Close on brushes being stood upright in a section
Three-quarter of the drawer opening to a readable layout in one look

short.hook: Two drawers side by side, one sorted by product type and one sorted by time of day, with a hand finding the same item in each.
short.standalone_note: State the sorting principle explicitly, divide by when you use it rather than what it is, since the comparison carries no meaning without it.

segments.covers: Lift the dividers out and tip the drawer, because loose powder, hair, and grit collect underneath where nobody looks.
beats: Remove the dividers and tip the empty drawer over a bin, showing the amount of loose powder, hair, and grit that comes out.
Wipe the drawer bottom and then the runners, explaining that the runners are what makes a drawer feel cheap when they are gritty.
Wipe each divider separately before it goes back, so the clean drawer does not receive dirty inserts.
shots: Overhead of dividers lifting out to reveal the grit trapped beneath
Three-quarter of the drawer being tipped over a bin
Macro on a cloth running along the drawer runner
Close on dividers being wiped on a towel before reinstallation
on_screen_text: It all lives under the dividers

short.hook: Dividers lift out of a drawer and the camera holds on the layer of powder and hair that was underneath the whole time.
short.standalone_note: Establish that this is a bathroom vanity drawer and that lifting the dividers is the step people skip, since the reveal is the entire payload.

segments.covers: Loose blades in a drawer you reach into blind will find a fingertip, and low drawers hold liquids and pills a child can pull open.
beats: Show the hazard as it actually appears, bare cartridges and blade refills loose among the brushes, and explain that a hand going in for a comb without looking meets the blade first.
Correct it two ways, cap every blade, or give all razors one lidded box in a fixed corner you never grope past, and show the box going into that corner.

Address the low drawer, polish remover, small scissors, and loose vitamins within reach of a child who can pull a drawer open, and show the fix, move liquids and pills to an upper drawer or fit a catch.
shots: Macro on a bare blade cartridge sitting among brush bristles
Close on caps going onto blades one at a time
Three-quarter of the lidded box being set into its fixed corner
Low angle at child height of a bottom drawer sliding open, hands only
Close on a drawer catch being fitted

short.hook: Open at child height on a bottom vanity drawer sliding open to reveal polish remover and loose vitamins at eye level.
short.standalone_note: Frame it as one of the five safety questions, poison, choke, or strangle, and give both fixes, move it up or fit a catch.

segments.covers: Each divider label carries a count, so a new item has to beat something already in the slot.
beats: Write counts onto the divider labels on camera, two lipsticks in rotation, one comb, one brush, and explain that the count is what makes the right state obvious at a glance.
Show the rule in action, a third lipstick arriving and being held against the two already in the slot until one of them leaves.
Explain that a standard is the best way you know today, written down, and that the count can change later as long as it stays written.
shots: Macro on a label being written with a count
Overhead of labeled dividers reading across the open drawer
Close on three lipsticks held over a two-slot compartment
Overhead of the loser leaving the drawer
on_screen_text: Put a number on the label

short.hook: A third lipstick hovering over a compartment labeled for two, and a hand deciding which of the existing two leaves.
short.standalone_note: State the counted-label standard first, because the Short is only a decision if the viewer knows the slot has a written limit.

segments.covers: Laundry day is the trigger, and the top drawer gets one look while the towels are already in your arms.
beats: Show the trigger in its real form, towels being carried into the bathroom on laundry day, then the top drawer being pulled with the load still under one arm.
Do the pass on camera, lifting out anything empty or dried out, and show how short it is, one drawer, one look.
Explain that this catches a week of drift and that attaching it to a trip already being made is what keeps it happening.
shots: Three-quarter of folded towels being carried in, arms only, no face
Overhead of the top drawer opening with one hand
Macro on an empty tube being squeezed and dropped in a bin
Overhead of the drawer closing, contents unchanged otherwise

short.hook: Towels under one arm, the other hand opening a drawer and pulling two dead tubes out of it before the towels are even put away.
short.standalone_note: Name laundry day as the trigger and the top drawer as the scope, so the Short reads as a habit rather than a tidy-up.

close.standard_beat: Open each drawer in turn on camera to show the standard holding, divided by routine, every category carrying a written count on its label, nothing past its date, and then show the laundry day trigger once, towels in one arm, top drawer in the other hand.
close.next_zone_teaser: Everything that left these drawers in bulk went below the basin, and that cabinet is hiding something more expensive than clutter.

shot_list: Overhead side arm above the open drawer for every empty, divide, and reload sequence
Macro rig for dates, open-jar symbols, blades, and labels
Three-quarter tripod at drawer height for tipping and wiping
Low child-height angle for the bottom drawer hazard sequence
Overhead of the towel with one drawer's contents spread out
Close on the wall or drawer front for the catch fitting
Three-quarter of towels being carried in for the trigger beat, arms only
Overhead of all drawers open in sequence for the closing standard
videos.description_hook: Every jar in a vanity drawer has a date on it, and the drawer is sorted by the wrong thing. Here is the full 6S pass, including the palette you have been skipping past.

videos.title: Under the Sink: Storage That Never Hides a Leak
videos.cold_open_problem: Open on the cabinet doors swinging wide to a wall of product, then push in to where the P-trap should be and find paper towels stacked in front of it. State the arithmetic being avoided, that a joint which weeps unnoticed for months turns a cheap washer into a rotted cabinet base and a floor that has to come up. This cabinet is the only storage in the room, which is exactly why it has been packed wall to wall.

segments.covers: Everything comes out and lines up by job, and the duplicates and the unidentifiable bottle reveal themselves.
beats: Empty the cabinet completely onto the floor and line the contents up by job, glass, tub and tile, toilet, drain, polish, explaining that sorting by job is what exposes duplication.
Show the result this room always produces, three half-full bottles of the same thing standing together in one job line.
Handle the bottle nobody can identify, no readable label, unclear contents, and explain plainly that it goes, because an unidentified chemical is not stock.
Separate paper goods and bulk toiletries from the chemistry, since they are going to be treated differently in the next pass.
shots: Three-quarter of the cabinet doors opening on the full state
Overhead of the floor with contents lining up in job columns
Close on three matching half-full bottles standing side by side
Macro on a faded or missing label being turned in the hand
Overhead of the empty cabinet interior, pipework finally visible

short.hook: A cabinet emptied onto the floor and the products lining up by job, with three identical half-full bottles landing in the same column.
short.standalone_note: Say this is the under-sink cabinet and that the sorting rule is by job rather than by brand, which is what makes the duplicates visible.

segments.covers: Build the bins around the P-trap rather than fighting it, and keep the joint and both shut-off valves in the sightline.
beats: Point out the P-trap and both shut-off valves in the empty cabinet, establishing them as the fixed features everything else works around.
Fit two pull-out bins clear of the trap, showing them sliding without touching the pipework, and explain that building around the plumbing is the whole design decision here.
Load paper goods and bulk toiletries on the side with headroom, and place sprays at the front where a label reads without kneeling.
Set the pale tray on the cabinet floor and leave it empty, explaining that a pale surface is what makes a drip visible early.
shots: Three-quarter into the empty cabinet with the trap and valves in frame
Close on a bin sliding out past the trap without contact
Overhead through the open doors of both bins in position
Macro on the pale tray being set on the cabinet floor
Three-quarter of the doors open with valves and trap still clearly visible

short.hook: A bin sliding out from under a sink and passing clean around the P-trap, with the joint staying visible the whole time.
short.standalone_note: Identify the P-trap and the shut-off valves by name and say why they must stay visible, since the Short is otherwise just a bin moving.

segments.covers: Clean to inspect, because the cabinet floor is where a slow leak shows itself before it ever looks like water.
beats: Wipe the cabinet floor and then look hard at it, explaining what to look for, a dark ring or a soft patch in the board, which is what a slow leak looks like before it looks like water.
Press the board with fingertips to test for softness on camera, showing the difference between a stain and a spongy patch.
Wipe the neck of every bottle before it goes back, explaining that this is what keeps the pale tray from turning sticky and unreadable.
Tie the pass back to the principle, that cleaning here is an inspection with a cloth in your hand.
shots: Overhead through the doors of the cabinet floor being wiped
Macro on a dark ring in the board under a low raking light
Close on fingertips pressing the board to test for softness
Macro on a bottle neck being wiped clean before it returns

short.hook: Fingertips pressing a cabinet floor and finding a soft patch in the board, the shape a leak takes before it ever looks wet.
short.standalone_note: Explain that this is the base of an under-sink cabinet and that a soft board means a slow leak, since the visual alone reads as nothing.

segments.covers: This cabinet holds the harshest chemistry in the house at toddler height, and two of these products must never meet.
beats: State the two absolute rules plainly, never store bleach where it can tip into an ammonia-based cleaner, and never decant anything into a drink bottle, and show a drink bottle being removed from the cabinet as the example.
Show the separation being built, the two products physically placed so a tip cannot land one into the other.

Address the height, filming at a crawling child's eye level to show bleach, drain opener, and bowl cleaner behind one unlatched door, then fit a magnetic catch or move the chemistry above the sink line.
Handle the crush hazard, a heavy bulk jug stacked on a pull-out bin ready to come down on your hand, and move heavy goods to the cabinet floor beside the tray.
Cover the water and electricity question, a drip at the trap creeping toward a socket or a plugged-in nightlight behind the cabinet, framed as find it, and fix it now.
shots: Low angle at crawling height of the cabinet door opening
Close on a drink bottle being lifted out and set aside
Three-quarter of a magnetic catch being fitted to the door
Close on a heavy jug moving from atop a bin down to the cabinet floor
Macro on the trap joint with a socket visible on the wall beyond
on_screen_text: Find it, and fix it now.

short.hook: Camera on the floor at crawling height as a cabinet door swings open onto drain opener and bowl cleaner at eye level.
short.standalone_note: Name the hazard as poison, choke, or strangle, and give both remedies, a magnetic catch or moving the chemistry above the sink line.

segments.covers: One open container per job, backstock capped at two, and bins labeled by job rather than by brand.
beats: Write bin labels by job, glass, tub and tile, toilet, and explain why labeling by job rather than brand stops bowl cleaner quietly ending up among the glass sprays.
Apply the one-open-per-job rule on camera, consolidating or removing the second open bottle in a job line.
Set the backstock cap at two and show what exceeds it leaving the room rather than being squeezed in.
Restate the sightline standard as part of the written standard, that the trap joint and both valves stay visible whenever the doors are open.
shots: Macro on a label being written with a job name
Close on the label going onto the front edge of a bin
Overhead of a job column reduced to one open bottle plus backstock
Three-quarter of the finished cabinet, doors open, trap and valves in clear view
on_screen_text: Label the job, not the brand

short.hook: Two bins side by side, one labeled with a brand name and one labeled with a job, and a hand reaching correctly first time for only one of them.
short.standalone_note: State the label-by-job rule outright and give the one-open-per-job cap, since the comparison is the whole lesson.

segments.covers: The hand soap refill is the trigger, and the entire leak check is a low look before the doors close.
beats: Show the trigger as it already happens, the hand soap at the basin being refilled from the bottle stored below.
Drop to a low look over the cabinet floor and the trap joint, and state that this is the entire leak check, nothing more.
Close the doors and explain why attaching the check to a refill already being made is what stops it becoming a chore that gets skipped.
shots: Close on hand soap being topped up at the basin, hands only
Low three-quarter from a crouch height, cabinet floor and trap joint in frame, no body shown
Macro on the trap joint, dry and clean
Three-quarter of the doors closing on the finished cabinet
on_screen_text: Refill the soap, check the trap

short.hook: A hand soap bottle topped up, then a low look along the cabinet floor and the pipe joint before the doors shut.
short.standalone_note: Say the refill is the trigger and that the look at the trap joint and cabinet floor is the complete check, so it does not read as an incomplete inspection.

close.standard_beat: Swing the doors open on the finished cabinet and state the standard against what is in frame, the P-trap and both shut-off valves in plain sight, one open bottle per job, backstock capped at two, then run the trigger, a soap refill followed by a low look along the cabinet floor.
close.next_zone_teaser: The medicines that came out of this cabinet do not belong down here at all, and the cabinet they do belong in needs a session with the small print.

shot_list: Three-quarter tripod square to the open cabinet doors for all before and after states
Low crawling-height angle for the child reach and hazard sequence
Overhead of the bathroom floor with the full cabinet contents in job columns
Macro rig on the P-trap, the shut-off valves, and the cabinet base board
A single low side light raking across the cabinet board to reveal a dark ring or soft patch
Close on bin runners and the pale tray at cabinet floor level
Macro on labels being written and applied to bin front edges
Close at basin height on the hand soap refill trigger
Three-quarter of the magnetic catch being fitted to the door frame
videos.description_hook: The cabinet under the bathroom sink is usually packed to the wall, which means the pipe joint is buried. Here is how to store everything you need and still see a leak on day one.

videos.title: The Medicine Cabinet: In Date, Labeled, Actually Needed
videos.cold_open_problem: Open on a hand lifting a half-course of antibiotics or a bottle of strong painkillers from a procedure two years ago out of the cabinet. Hold on the label. Name what is being avoided, that it is kept because it might come in useful and because handing it back feels like waste, and state the reality plainly, that leftover painkillers sitting behind a mirror are the most likely thing in this room to seriously hurt a visitor.

segments.covers: Read every label and every date, and route expired, unlabeled, and no longer needed medicine into a take-back bag.
beats: Clear the cabinet shelf by shelf and read every label and every date on camera, including the small print on boxes kept because the box was still good.
Show the three disqualifiers being applied one item at a time, expired, unlabeled, and prescribed for a condition nobody here has now.
Show the take-back bag filling and state where it goes, a pharmacy take-back, and that nothing goes down the toilet.
Set the survivors aside as the only stock that will be reloaded.
shots: Overhead of a shelf's contents laid out on a towel
Macro on a printed expiry date on a blister foil
Macro on a prescription label with the patient name masked
Close on boxes going into the take-back bag one by one
Three-quarter of the empty cabinet with shelves bare

short.hook: Macro on the small print of a box someone kept because the box still looked fine, with the date landing well in the past.
short.standalone_note: Establish that this is a medicine cabinet Sort and name the three disqualifiers, since the Short turns on the rule rather than the single box.

segments.covers: Group by the reason you come to this cabinet, and put the two-in-the-morning items where you can find them without the light on.
beats: Sort the survivors into groups by reason rather than by brand or by box size, headache, stomach, cut, cold, eyes.
Load the groups into three bins, pain relief, stomach and cold, first aid, and show the first aid bin being lifted one-handed to prove it can be carried to whoever is bleeding.
Place the two things you reach for at two in the morning on the shelf you can find without turning the light on, and demonstrate that reach in low light.
shots: Overhead of survivors grouping into reason piles on a towel
Close on three bins being loaded through the open cabinet
Three-quarter of the first aid bin lifted out with one hand
Low-light close on a hand finding the front shelf item without looking
on_screen_text: Group by the reason you came

short.hook: A first aid bin lifted out of a cabinet with one hand and carried away, the test that decides how big it is allowed to be.
short.standalone_note: Say the bin has to be carryable one-handed to whoever is bleeding, which is the reason for the size limit.

segments.covers: Shelves come out and get washed, and they go back completely dry, because a damp shelf is what turns tablets chalky.
beats: Take the shelves out and wash off the sticky rings left by cough syrup and the dust of old blister foil.
Dry them all the way through before they go back and explain the reason specific to this room, that a damp shelf turns tablets chalky in here.
Wipe the cabinet body and the mirror door hinge line while the shelves dry.
shots: Macro on a sticky syrup ring on a glass shelf
Three-quarter of shelves being lifted out of the cabinet body
Close on shelves being dried on a towel, both faces
Macro on blister foil dust in a shelf corner being wiped out

short.hook: Macro on the sticky ring a cough syrup bottle has left welded to a glass shelf, then the shelf coming out of the cabinet entirely.
short.standalone_note: Note that the shelf has to go back fully dry because damp turns tablets chalky, which is the point the Short exists to make.

segments.covers: Bathroom humidity breaks tablets down, this cabinet must stay above real child reach, and nothing ever goes down the toilet.
beats: Explain that bathroom humidity breaks tablets and capsules down faster than a bedroom shelf does, and move anything taken daily out of this room entirely, showing it leave.

Measure child reach the honest way, from the height of the closed toilet lid a child can climb onto rather than from the floor, shown as a hand rising into frame to that height with the closed lid in shot below as the reference.
Fit a child-secure catch to whatever stays, and show it engaging.
Move a glass peroxide bottle or a heavy first aid tin down from the top shelf above a hard basin, since heavy and breakable belongs at eye level, not overhead.
shots: Close on a hand carrying daily medication out through the bathroom doorway
Three-quarter of a hand and forearm rising into frame to the reach height, the closed toilet lid in shot below as the climb reference, no body shown
Macro on a child-secure catch engaging on the cabinet door
Close on a glass bottle moving from top shelf down to eye level
on_screen_text: Measure from what they can climb
Heavy and breakable at eye level

short.hook: A hand rising to the height of a closed toilet lid and landing easily on the cabinet shelf everyone assumed was out of reach.
short.standalone_note: State the rule that reach is measured from what a child can climb onto, not from the floor, because the shot is meaningless without it.

segments.covers: Bins are labeled by symptom rather than brand, and the first aid bin holds a fixed kit that never becomes a home for spare vitamins.
beats: Write bin labels by symptom and explain the test, that a guest or a sitter should find what they need without asking which box the cold tablets are in.
Lay out the fixed first aid contents on camera, plasters, tape, gauze, and one pair of scissors, and load them.
Show the drift being refused, spare vitamins being offered to the first aid bin and going elsewhere instead.
Restate the standard as the best way you know today, written down, and put the labels where they read from outside the closed door.
shots: Macro on symptom labels being written
Overhead of the fixed first aid contents laid out before loading
Close on a vitamin bottle being turned away from the first aid bin
Three-quarter of the cabinet open with all three labels readable

short.hook: Three labeled bins in a medicine cabinet and a hand going straight to the right one without hesitating or reading a brand name.
short.standalone_note: Give the sitter test in full, that someone who does not live here should find it without asking, since that is what justifies symptom labels.

segments.covers: The pharmacy trip is the trigger, and the new box does not go in until the dates in that bin have been read.
beats: Show the trigger as it already happens, a pharmacy bag coming through the bathroom door and being set down.
Put the new box into its bin and read the dates of everything already in that bin before the door shuts, showing the read happen rather than describing it.
Show the take-back bag being placed where it will ride back on the next trip, closing the loop without a reminder or an app.
shots: Close on a pharmacy bag being set on the counter, hands only
Overhead of one bin lifted out and its contents date-checked
Macro on a date being read on an item already in stock
Three-quarter of the take-back bag hung ready by the door

short.hook: A pharmacy bag lands on the counter and the new box is held back while every date already in that bin gets read first.
short.standalone_note: Name the pharmacy trip as the trigger and the one-bin scope, so the Short does not read as a full cabinet clear-out.

close.standard_beat: Open the finished cabinet and state the standard against what is visible, only in-date, correctly labeled, currently needed medicine, grouped by symptom and kept above child reach, then show the trigger, a pharmacy bag arriving, a box going in, and the dates in that bin being read before the door closes.
close.next_zone_teaser: The room's other daily surface is the one you stand in wet with your eyes half shut, so the shower and tub are next.

videos.title: Shower and Tub: Four Bottles, One Squeegee, Real Grip

Name the reason they stay, some cost too much to admit, some were gifts, and some hold an inch that cannot be poured away, and name what that costs, a caddy that never dries out.

beats: Line every bottle along the tub edge and shake each one, showing how much is actually left and how many are near empty.

short.standalone_note: Give the in-use test explicitly, touched in the last two weeks of showers, since the line-up alone does not carry a decision rule.

segments.covers: Each person gets their own shelf or corner rather than one mixed crowd, and the squeegee hangs where a wet hand meets it.
beats: Assign each person a shelf or a corner of the caddy and load them separately, explaining why one mixed crowd is what makes people shift bottles instead of reaching.

segments.covers: Spray, leave the room to work another zone, come back and wipe, then squeegee from the top down and leave the door open.
beats: Spray the walls and the tray, then step out, explaining that chemistry needs time rather than scrubbing and that this is where the counter or the toilet gets done instead of waiting.
Return, wipe, and rinse, then squeegee glass and tile from the top down, showing why top down means you never re-wet a finished surface.
Work the dark line where the wall meets the tray specifically, since that is the join this zone is judged on.

videos.title: Bathroom Linen: Three Towels Per Person, Ranked Honestly

Name it as a shelf running backwards, and note that it has been running backwards for years.

segments.covers: Every towel comes out and gets ranked by which one your hand actually goes to after a shower.
beats: Empty the shelf completely and rank every towel by hand, explaining that ranking beats sorting into keep and toss because it forces a comparison.
Show the four categories that always fail, the thin, the stiff, the shedders, and the odd single from a lost set.
Split the rejects on camera, the best of them becoming cleaning rags and the rest going to a shelter that takes textiles.
Count the survivors against three bath towels per person, one in use, one in the wash, one folded on the shelf.

videos.description_hook: Most households dry themselves on their worst towels and save the good ones for visitors twice a year. Here is the full 6S pass that puts the shelf back the right way round.

rooms.room_note: Small, hard surfaced and reflective, which makes it the trickiest headless room in the series. The mirror and any glass screen will show the camera and the tripod, so set the tripod off the mirror axis, shoot the mirror from a low three quarter angle, and check every frame for a reflected camera before rolling. This is a one person shoot: tripod, window light or the open door, a white bounce card on the floor to lift shadows inside the vanity cabinet and behind the pedestal, and one small battery light panel gelled to daylight for interiors and for raking light on the tile. Tape or clamp the panel, never rest it on a wet surface. The overhead needs a horizontal arm because the counter sits tight to the wall and a standard tripod cannot centre over it. Floor is tile, so pad the tripod feet and lay a towel for kneeling shots. Shoot the whole room in one day and follow the manual's own start order: put the stored guest towels in the wash before the first frame, shoot the vanity counter first, and shoot the linen shelf last when the wash is done. On set safety: shoot the chemical handling beats with capped bottles only, and open the door and window for any sequence involving bowl cleaner. Never film bleach and an acid cleaner open in the same frame, even as a demonstration.

videos.title: Guest Bathroom Vanity Counter: The Three Item Reset
videos.cold_open_problem: Open overhead on a vanity holding two lives at once: a soap pump and a tissue box on one side, a family toothbrush cup, hair clips behind the tap and a razor on the other. Pose the fork this household has been dodging, whether this is a guest bathroom or a bathroom somebody actually lives in, and set up that the video settles that question out loud instead of resetting the same counter twice a week forever.

Settle the fork before anything goes back. If nobody actually brushes their teeth at this basin, the toothbrush cup leaves today and nothing personal returns. If a child or a housemate genuinely uses it, that one named person gets a labeled caddy or drawer holding their two items, alongside the guest three.
Make the reasoning visible: a hotel counter standard aimed at a room somebody lives in fails twice a week, which is a standard pointed at the wrong room rather than anybody being careless.
Put back only the answer you picked, soap, tissues and hand towel, plus the named caddy if that was the call.
Cover the demotion trap for this counter, that half used products on their way out of the house do not get parked here, they leave.

short.standalone_note: Name the room and the floor material inside the Short, since the whole point is glass meeting tile with a barefoot visitor standing over it.

segments.covers: The answer you picked becomes a picture anyone in the house can reset the counter against.
beats: Read the standard against the finished counter: three things live here permanently, soap, tissues and hand towel, plus the named caddy if that was the call.
Photograph that exact arrangement from the doorway angle, pointing to Chapter 25, the ideal-state photo, and make the case that a picture of the right answer beats a description of it.
Tape the print inside the vanity door and show it being found by someone opening the cabinet.
Make the placement point: the picture lives where the person resetting the counter is already standing.
shots: Overhead of the finished counter, held clean and still.
Close on a printed photo being taped to the inside of the vanity door.
Three quarter of the cabinet door swinging open to reveal the photo.
Split framing of the printed photo held against the real counter behind it.

short.hook: A printed photo of a finished vanity is held up in front of the real vanity, and the two frames line up item for item.
short.standalone_note: Say inside the Short that the photo is the standard for this counter and that it lives taped inside the cabinet door where the next person will already be standing.

segments.covers: Both triggers hang off trips that already happen, so the counter never waits on somebody remembering.
beats: Give the guest arrival trigger: the moment someone confirms they are coming, walk in, top up the soap and hang a fresh hand towel, since soap level and towel are the two things a visitor registers.
Give the standing household trigger from the standard: when fresh towels go away after laundry, the guest hand towel gets swapped in the same motion.

Shoot both as single unbroken trips, hands only, so it is visible that the soap top up happens on a walk through you were making anyway and the towel swap happens with the laundry already in your arms.
shots: Close on a soap bottle being topped up beside a phone lying face down, no screen content in frame.
Three quarter of a folded stack of laundered towels being carried in and one peeled off for the ring.
Overhead of the fresh towel squared on the ring, the rest of the counter unchanged.
on_screen_text: Attach it to a trip you already make

short.hook: A stack of clean laundry comes through the door and one towel peels off the top straight onto the guest ring without a second trip being made.
short.standalone_note: Name the trigger plainly inside the Short, that putting laundry away is when the guest hand towel gets swapped, and say which room the ring is in.

close.standard_beat: Land on the finished counter from the doorway and read the standard off what is in frame: soap, tissues and hand towel, plus the one named caddy if that was the answer, and anything a visitor brings leaves with them. Then run the trigger once more, the laundry stack coming in and one towel going onto the ring in the same motion, so the standard and the thing that holds it are seen back to back.
close.next_zone_teaser: The counter is clear because everything that did not belong went somewhere. Next we open the door underneath it, where the hotel miniatures have been collecting for years.

shot_list: Overhead arm rig locked over the counter for the before, the clearing, the sorted groups and the finished state.
Three quarter tripod at counter height for hand work at the basin, tap and soap pump.
Doorway wide at standing height for the visitor's view, used for before, after and the ideal-state photo match.
Macro on a tabletop tripod, repositioned between takes, for the tap collar, drain lip and the label of a discarded travel bottle.
Low macro across the wet counter for the glass slide hazard beat.
Floor level three quarter on the towel with the sorted groups laid out.
Cabinet door interior close for taping and revealing the standard photo, small panel taped under the counter.
Mirror pass from an off axis three quarter position, frame checked for a reflected camera before every take.
videos.description_hook: A guest vanity counter holds three things: soap, tissues and a hand towel. The harder question is whether this is really a guest bathroom at all.

videos.title: Under the Guest Sink: Two Bins and a Toilet Paper Line
videos.cold_open_problem: Open on a hand pulling a bag of hotel miniatures out from under the guest sink and tipping it onto a towel: shampoos from three different trips, a lotion nobody opened, conditioner samples with battered labels. Name the deadlock exactly, that throwing out free soap feels like waste and keeping it feels like hospitality, so the bag has sat under this sink for years doing neither, and set up that the video settles it with arithmetic rather than feeling.

segments.covers: The cabinet comes out entirely and the miniature question gets settled with a number.
beats: Pull everything out onto a towel on the floor and show the true volume, which is always more than the cabinet suggested.
Work the miniatures honestly: keep the unopened ones a guest would actually use, throw out the started ones, and make the point that a half used bottle is not an offering.
Do the arithmetic on camera. A guest staying two nights uses one shampoo, one conditioner, one soap and one lotion, so four unopened bottles with the least battered labels stay and the rest go today.
Separate the household backstock that drifted in here and show it going back to the bathroom it came from.
Close the escape route: if binning them is genuinely beyond you, they go into a shelter donation box this week and into the car, not back onto the shelf.
shots: Three quarter, low, of the cabinet door opening on the loaded state.
Overhead of everything spread across a towel on the tile floor.
Macro on hands turning bottles to check seals, one clearly opened and one clearly sealed.
Overhead of the four chosen bottles set well apart from a much larger discard pile.
Close on the discard pile going into a bag and the bag being carried out of frame.
on_screen_text: Started bottles are not an offering

short.hook: A bag of hotel miniatures tips out onto the floor, four bottles get picked out of the spread, and everything else goes into a bin bag.
short.standalone_note: Give the arithmetic before the picking starts, one guest, two nights, one of each, so the number four is earned and the viewer can run it on their own cabinet.

segments.covers: Two lift out bins and a toilet paper stack a guest sees without asking.
beats: Set the rule at two bins rather than five, and show that more containers in a cabinet this size only hide things at a higher resolution.
Load one bin with guest supplies, a new toothbrush, a wrapped bar of soap and the four travel bottles in a small dish. Load the other with the cleaning kit standing upright on a shallow tray.
Test both by lifting each with one hand, and make the reason explicit, that the cabinet base has to stay visible.
Stack the toilet paper on its own where it is seen the second the door opens, on the plain fact that a guest hunting for a roll will not come and ask you.
shots: Overhead of two empty bins side by side before loading.
Close on the four travel bottles being arranged in a small dish so they read as an offering.
Three quarter of one hand lifting a loaded bin clear of the cabinet.
Low three quarter from seated height showing what is visible the instant the cabinet door opens.

short.hook: A cabinet door swings open and the toilet paper stack is the first thing in frame, before anything else in there registers.
short.standalone_note: Say inside the Short that this is the guest bathroom cabinet and that a visitor hunting for a roll will not knock on your door to ask.

segments.covers: The cabinet base gets cleaned to inspect it, because it is the only place a slow leak can announce itself.
beats: Empty the cabinet completely and wipe the base, describing what you are looking for rather than only cleaning: dark rings, staining, or softened board that mean the trap has been weeping.
Get a light in and inspect the trap and the joint above the base.
Wipe the neck and cap of every bottle before it goes back, showing the cause and effect, that dried cleaner running down the outside of a bottle is what makes a whole cabinet sticky.
shots: Close, small panel taped under the counter, on the bare cabinet base being wiped.
Macro on a dark ring in the board with the panel set low for raking light.
Macro up at the trap joint from floor level.
Close on a cloth wiping the neck and cap of a cleaner bottle.

short.hook: A cloth wipes a cabinet base clean and a dark ring stays behind in the board, unmoved by any amount of scrubbing.
short.standalone_note: Explain inside the Short that this is the base under a bathroom sink and that the ring is not dirt, it is the trap above it telling you something.

segments.covers: Poison, choke or strangle in the one bathroom a visiting child gets sent into alone.
beats: Show the height problem directly: bowl cleaner and bleach under this sink sit at exactly the height of a visiting toddler who has been sent in to wash their hands without an adult.
Give the two acceptable fixes and no third one, lift the cleaning bin to a high shelf elsewhere or fit the cabinet with a latch, and fit the latch on camera.
State the storage rule hard, that bleach never shares a bin with an acid limescale or bowl cleaner, because a loose cap on both is all it takes for them to meet. Handle only capped bottles in frame.

Cover the second hazard, fall: a slow weep from a trap nobody sees, because nobody opens this cabinet, reaches the tile as a thin invisible film long before it shows as a puddle, which is why the base stays bare.
shots: Low three quarter with the camera set at a small child's eye height, on the open cabinet full of chemicals.
Close on hands fitting a cabinet latch, screwdriver in frame.
Close on the cleaning bin being lifted out of the room entirely.
Macro on two capped bottles being separated into different containers.
Close on a flat hand sweeping the tile in front of the cabinet, checking for film.

short.hook: The camera drops to a small child's eye height in front of an open cabinet under a sink, and the whole shelf of chemicals sits level with the lens.
short.standalone_note: Establish that this is the bathroom visiting children get sent to on their own, which is what makes this cabinet different from the one in your own bathroom, and end on the latch going on.

segments.covers: Labels a guest can read, and a line on the shelf that counts the toilet paper for you.
beats: Write the two bin labels by hand in plain words, Guest Supplies and Cleaning, and make the point that these are written to be read by a visitor rather than by you.
Draw a line on the shelf at the toilet paper minimum, then show the stack sitting above it and below it.
Explain the mechanism, pointing to Chapter 14, visual controls: when the stack falls below the line it goes on the shopping list and nobody counts anything.
Point out that the bare cabinet base is itself a visual control, since a leak now has somewhere obvious to show.
shots: Close on a marker writing a bin label by hand.
Close on a line being drawn along the shelf edge at the minimum height.
Overhead of the stack above the line, then a matched frame with it below.
Wide of the finished cabinet from the doorway with both labels legible.
on_screen_text: Plain words a guest can read
Below the line, on the list

short.hook: A line gets drawn along a shelf edge behind a stack of toilet paper, then rolls come off one at a time until the line is showing.
short.standalone_note: Say what the line means and where this shelf is before the stack starts dropping, otherwise the reveal has nothing to land on.

segments.covers: Restocking hangs off a shop you already do, inspection hangs off a chore you already do.
beats: Give the restock trigger: when you restock your own bathroom after a shop, open this cabinet on the same trip and build the toilet paper stack back up to the line.
Give the inspection trigger from the standard: you already open this cabinet for the brush before the weekly bowl clean, so a hand runs across the base while you are down there.
Make the point that neither one is a reminder or an app, both hang off something that already happens in the house.
shots: Three quarter of shopping bags set down and rolls carried straight through to the guest cabinet.
Overhead of the stack being rebuilt up to the line.
Close on a hand reaching in for the brush and sweeping flat across the base on the way out.
on_screen_text: Same trip, not a new one

short.hook: A hand reaches into a cabinet for the toilet brush and, on the way back out, sweeps flat across the bare cabinet base without breaking rhythm.
short.standalone_note: Name the weekly bowl clean as the thing that already happens and say what the hand is feeling for, damp on a base that should be dry.

close.standard_beat: Open the cabinet door on the finished state and read the standard against what is in frame: two labeled lift out bins, a visible toilet paper stack sitting above its line, and nothing loose on the base so a leak has somewhere obvious to show. Then run the trigger once, a hand going in for the brush and coming back out across the bare base.
close.next_zone_teaser: The cleaning kit now lifts out with one hand. Next we carry it to the tub and deal with the grout line you have scrubbed three times and quietly started calling clean.

shot_list: Low three quarter tripod at open cabinet height, the primary setup for before, loading and the finished reveal.
Camera resting on the tile at a small child's eye height for the chemical height hazard beat.
Overhead arm rig over a towel on the bathroom floor for the full unload and the sorting of miniatures.
Macro on a tabletop tripod for bottle seals, labels, the cabinet base ring and the trap joint.
Small battery panel taped under the counter for all interior cabinet work.
Close setup on the shelf edge for drawing the minimum line and for writing the labels.
Doorway wide for the visitor's eye view of the open cabinet.
Hallway pickup of shopping bags coming in for the restock trigger.
videos.description_hook: The bag of hotel miniatures under the guest sink is not hospitality and it is not thrift. Here is the arithmetic that finally settles it.

videos.title: Guest Shower Reset: Three Bottles and the Grout You Cannot Clean
videos.cold_open_problem: Open macro on one grout line being scrubbed hard, rinsed, and still coming up gray. Name the thing this household has quietly agreed to accept, that the line has been scrubbed three times and started getting called clean anyway. Set out what it actually is, mold grown into porous grout or a silicone bead that has failed underneath, and that part of every week's clean is being spent on a job that cannot succeed.

segments.covers: Every bottle in this caddy comes out and gets turned over, because this is where the household's rejected products retire.
beats: Take every bottle out of the caddy, line them up along the tub rim, and turn each one over, reading weight and label as the two tests.
Name what this particular zone collects: the shampoo nobody liked, the body wash that smells wrong, the conditioner welded to the shelf by its own dried drip.
Set the keep rule and apply it in frame, one shampoo, one conditioner, one body wash, all readable and all more than a third full.
Bin the old razor and the disintegrating loofah without ceremony, and make the point that a guest reading a stranger's rejected products is the impression actually being left.
shots: Three quarter into the tub, tripod outside on the tile, of the loaded caddy before anything moves.
Overhead of every bottle lined up on a towel laid across the tub rim.
Macro of a hand lifting a conditioner bottle and the ring of dried product welding it to the shelf.
Macro on a faded, unreadable label.
Overhead of the three survivors beside a full discard pile.
on_screen_text: One shampoo, one conditioner, one wash

short.hook: A hand lifts a conditioner bottle out of a shower caddy and the shelf lifts with it, welded on by its own dried drip.
short.standalone_note: State the keep rule in the same breath, one shampoo, one conditioner, one body wash, readable and above a third full, and say this is a guest shower nobody has used since spring.

segments.covers: Nothing stands on the tub floor, and a wet guest without glasses can reach everything.
beats: Hang the caddy or fit a corner shelf, on the single reason that anything standing on the tub floor collects water underneath itself.
Move a bar of soap into a draining dish and show the puddle ring it had been sitting in.
Fit a hook inside the door at a height reachable with wet hands and no glasses on, and demonstrate that reach from inside the tub with hands only.
Make the placement principle explicit for this zone, that a guest is operating this room half blind and half wet, and every decision here answers to that.
shots: Three quarter of the caddy being hung, water clearly not pooling beneath it.
Macro of the puddle ring under a soap bar, then the same soap in a draining dish.
Close on the hook being set at reach height inside the door.
Tripod low inside the tub, framed so only a forearm and hand enter the shot as it reaches for the hook.
on_screen_text: Nothing stands on the tub floor

short.hook: A bar of soap lifts off a tub ledge and leaves a grey puddle ring in exactly its own shape.
short.standalone_note: Name the fix inside the Short, that soap in a shower gets a draining dish and never a flat ledge, and show the dish going in.

segments.covers: Mold gets treated first so its dwell time runs while you work elsewhere.
beats: Spray the grout lines and the bottom band of the curtain liner first, on the reasoning that this needs time and time is not something to spend standing there watching.
Show the dwell as an actual absence: hands leave frame, the locked shot holds on the empty tub, the work moves to the rest of the room, then the same locked frame comes back for the rinse.
Take a fabric liner off the rings and put it into the washing machine instead of scrubbing it by hand.
Rinse and show the result on the grout lines that do respond, which sets up the harder question about the ones that do not.
shots: Macro on grout lines being sprayed along their length.
Close on the pink film band at the bottom of a liner being treated.
Locked wide of the empty tub held through the dwell, hands out of frame.
Three quarter of hands unhooking a fabric liner and carrying it out of the room.
Macro on a rinsed grout line in matched framing with the earlier shot.

short.hook: Grout in a shower gets sprayed, the hands leave the frame completely, and the shot just holds on an empty tub while the cleaner does the work.
short.standalone_note: Explain inside the Short that dwell time is the active ingredient and that standing there scrubbing it early is the wasted part.

segments.covers: Fall, and fall, cut or crush, for someone stepping into a tub they have never used before.
beats: Set the scene precisely, that the person using this tub is stepping into an unfamiliar one, probably at night, onto a surface they cannot judge the grip of.
Fit a non slip mat or adhesive strips on the tub floor, testing the grip on the bare glaze first and on the fitted strips after.
Fall, cut or crush: show what a towel bar screwed into drywall actually is, and that it tears straight out the moment it takes a person's weight, with the tub rim in the way on the fall.
Show what a real grab point looks like, one thing solidly anchored, and be plain that a suction rail is not it.
Land the principle behind both, pointing to Chapter 21, the hazard hunt: a non slip surface is a fix, and a warning is not.
shots: Low three quarter into the tub showing the bare glazed floor with the panel set low for raking light.
Macro of a flat hand pressing and sliding on the wet glaze, then the same press on the fitted strips.
Close on adhesive strips being laid and pressed down.
Macro on a towel bar mount and the drywall behind it, then on a suction rail cup lifting at one edge.
Close on a hand gripping a properly anchored rail and pulling against it.
on_screen_text: Towel bars are not grab handles

short.hook: A flat wet hand presses down onto the glazed floor of a tub and slides away under barely any pressure at all.
short.standalone_note: Establish that this is a guest tub and the person standing in it has never used it before and cannot judge the grip, which is the entire hazard.

segments.covers: A short checkable list for a shower that stands unused for months, and the point where cleaning becomes repair.
beats: Read the standard against the finished tub: three bottles, one soap, one mat, one anchored grab point, and no personal items.
Add the unused shower clause and explain why it exists in this zone and nowhere else in the house, that a shower standing a month gets run hot for a minute before a guest arrives.
Show that run and say what it proves, that it clears the stale water sitting in the line and confirms the drain is still moving freely.

Settle the call as the hardest clause in this standard: one proper treatment with full dwell time and a stiff brush, and if the line darkens again inside two weeks it stops being a cleaning job and moves to the repair list, meaning raking out and regrouting or cutting the old silicone and running a fresh bead. Make clear that naming it a repair is the decision, and that it buys one Saturday instead of a chore with no end.
shots: Wide of the finished tub from outside with everything in the standard visible in one frame.
Close on the tap running hot, steam rising, water going down freely.
Macro on a treated grout line, then a matched frame of the same line darkened again.
Close on that line being marked and written onto a repair list on paper.
on_screen_text: Run it hot before they arrive
Two weeks, then it is a repair

short.hook: A grout line gets one proper treatment and comes up clean, then a matched shot of the same line two weeks later shows it dark again.
short.standalone_note: Deliver the whole rule inside the Short, one treatment with full dwell time and a stiff brush, and if it comes back within two weeks it goes on the repair list instead of the cleaning list.

segments.covers: Whoever used this tub last leaves it in a state that stops the film coming back.
beats: Set the rule for the last person out, squeegee the glass or shake out the liner, and drape the bath mat over the tub rim rather than leaving it flat on the floor.
Show the failure mode specifically, a liner left bunched against the tile, and that this fold is exactly where the pink film starts again.
Give the standing trigger from the standard: when you strip the guest bed after a visit, whatever the guest left in the shower goes out on the same trip to the laundry.
shots: Close on a squeegee crossing a glass screen in one pass.
Three quarter of a liner being shaken out and spread flat rather than bunched.
Macro on a bunched liner pressed to tile, then on the pink film sitting only in that fold.
Overhead of a bath mat being folded over the tub rim.
Three quarter of hands carrying stripped bedding through with the shower items balanced on top.
on_screen_text: Strip the bed, clear the shower

short.hook: A curtain liner is pulled away from the tile where it had been bunched, and the pink film is sitting only inside the fold.
short.standalone_note: Say who the rule belongs to, whoever used the shower last, and give the three actions, squeegee or shake out, spread the liner flat, mat over the rim.

close.standard_beat: Hold on the finished tub and read the standard as the frame shows it: one shampoo, one conditioner, one body wash, all readable and above a third full, over a non slip tub floor with one anchored grab point. Then run the trigger, stripped bedding going out with the guest's leftovers carried on the same trip, and point at which grout line now sits on the repair list rather than the cleaning list.
close.next_zone_teaser: One thing in this room belongs on a list too, and it is not grout. Next we deal with the object this household has silently agreed not to look at.

shot_list: Three quarter tripod set outside the tub at rim height, the primary setup for caddy work, hanging and the finished wide.
Low in tub angle with the small panel set low for raking light across the glaze, for the bare floor and the non slip fitting.
Macro on a tabletop tripod for grout lines, liner film, bottle labels and the puddle ring under the soap.
Overhead arm rig over a towel laid across the tub rim for the bottle lineup and sort.
Low in tub position framed to hold everything above the wrist out of shot, for the wet hand reach demonstrations.
Matched framing pairs, locked and marked with tape, for every before and after on grout and glaze.
Hallway pickup for carrying the liner and the bedding out to the laundry.
Flat surface setup with paper and pen for writing the repair list.
videos.description_hook: You have scrubbed that grout line three times and quietly started calling it clean. It is not dirt, and no product is going to fix it.

videos.title: The Guest Toilet Area: The Brush Is a Consumable
videos.cold_open_problem: Open close on a toilet brush being lifted out of its holder: splayed bristles, and an inch of gray water in the bottom of the holder coming up with it. Name what this object is, the thing the household has silently agreed not to look at, and that it has stood there for years spreading more than it removes. Put the avoided decision on the table, that a brush is a consumable and not a fixture.

segments.covers: The tank top and the floor behind the bowl get cleared down to one reserve roll.
beats: Clear everything off the top of the tank and out from behind the bowl, naming the usual population as it comes off: the collection of air fresheners, the second brush, the magazines, the box of something nobody has identified in years.
Give the reason this particular zone accumulates, that these surfaces are flat, hidden from the doorway, and never inspected because nobody in the house uses this room.
Set the keep rule and apply it, one reserve roll stays in the open and nothing else.
shots: Three quarter of the loaded tank top and the gap behind the pedestal before anything moves.
Overhead of everything cleared onto a towel on the floor.
Macro on the dust outline left behind an object that had not been lifted in years.
Close on the single reserve roll being set back.
on_screen_text: Tank top and behind the bowl

short.hook: Objects come off a toilet tank one at a time and each one leaves a clean rectangle behind it in the dust.
short.standalone_note: Name the zone as the guest toilet area and give the keep rule, one visible reserve roll on the tank and nothing else, so the clearing has a destination.

segments.covers: Placement here is decided by a seated guest and by the door swing.
beats: Put the reserve roll where a seated person reaches it without standing, and demonstrate that reach from seated height, since a roll a seated person cannot reach is not a reserve roll.
Set the brush and the trash can on the side away from the door swing, and show the door opening into where they used to stand.
Give the standard behind both placements, that a guest should never have to stand, reach across, or move something to use this room.
shots: Camera at seated height beside the bowl, a hand reaching to the roll in its old position and then its new one.
Three quarter of the door swinging open and just clearing the relocated can and brush.
Overhead of the finished floor layout around the pedestal.

short.hook: Camera sits at seated height beside a toilet and a hand reaches for the spare roll, comes up short, then the roll moves and the same reach lands.
short.standalone_note: State the rule inside the Short, that a reserve roll a seated person cannot reach without standing is not doing its job.

segments.covers: Treat the bowl first and work outward, because the smell is not coming from where people scrub.
beats: Treat the bowl first, under the rim and at the water line, then leave it, so dwell time runs while the rest of the work happens.
Work outward in order while it dwells: seat hinges, then the base of the pedestal, then the floor behind it.
Show the finding plainly, that the floor behind the pedestal is where splash and dust collect and where the smell in a guest bathroom actually comes from.
Introduce the color coded cloth, a color used nowhere else in the house, so it cannot travel to a kitchen surface by accident.
shots: Macro under the rim as cleaner is run along it.
Close on the water line ring before treatment, matched framing for after.
Macro on seat hinges opened and cleaned.
Low close on the floor behind the pedestal with the panel set low for raking light across the dust and splash line.
Close on a distinctly colored cloth being taken from the bin and held clear of everything else.
on_screen_text: Under the rim first, then leave it
The smell is behind the pedestal

short.hook: A low camera slides in behind a toilet pedestal under raking light, into the strip of floor that has never once been cleaned.
short.standalone_note: Say up front that this strip is where a guest bathroom smell actually comes from, otherwise the shot is just a dirty floor with no argument attached.

segments.covers: Poison, choke or strangle, twice over: what gets stored in this corner and what gets mixed in it.
beats: Show the bowl cleaner parked behind the pedestal and give the geometry, that it stands at a crawling child's eye level and usually with the cap loose.
Fix it on camera, cap tight and back into the cleaning bin every time, and make clear this is a placement rule rather than an intention.

State the mixing hazard without softening it: bleach and an acid bowl cleaner used one after the other in a small room with the door shut and no fan running produce a gas that will drop a healthy adult.
Give the rule as three plain instructions, use one product, ventilate, never store the two together, shown with capped bottles only and the door and window open in frame.
shots: Camera resting flat on the tile behind the pedestal, on a cleaner bottle with a loose cap.
Macro on the cap being tightened fully.
Close on the bottle going back into the labeled cleaning bin.
Three quarter of the door and window being opened, air visibly moving a light curtain.
Overhead of two capped bottles being placed into separate containers, well apart.

short.hook: The camera lies flat on the tile behind a toilet pedestal, at a crawling child's eye height, staring straight at a bowl cleaner bottle with the cap sitting loose on it.
short.standalone_note: Name the room and finish on the fix, cap tight and straight back into the cleaning bin every time, so the Short ends on an action rather than a warning.

segments.covers: Five checkable lines, put where the person holding the brush will read them.
beats: Read the five lines against the finished zone: one visible reserve roll, backstock in the cabinet, brush dry in its holder, liner in the can, and no ring at the water line.
Write those five lines by hand on a card and stand the card upright in the cleaning bin.
Make the placement argument, that the person holding the brush reads the standard at the exact moment they can meet it, rather than on a fridge or in a folder.

Settle the call as part of the standard: splayed bristles or liquid in the holder means both go out today and a fresh set comes in, and from then on the brush gets rinsed in the flush and propped under the closed seat to drip before it goes back. Offer the honest alternative, that a disposable head version ends the argument for anyone who will not realistically do that handling.
shots: Close on a hand writing five short lines on a card.
Three quarter of the card standing upright in the cleaning bin.
Close on a splayed brush and its holder of gray water going into a bag together.
Macro on a fresh brush propped under a closed seat, dripping.
Wide of the finished zone with all five standard items visible in one frame.
on_screen_text: Read it while holding the brush

short.hook: A splayed toilet brush and its holder of gray water both go into a bin bag in a single movement.
short.standalone_note: Give the two part test before the disposal, splayed bristles or liquid standing in the holder, so a viewer can walk off and check their own.

segments.covers: The trigger is a trip already being made on a fixed night, plus the monthly habit a room nobody uses still needs.
beats: Give the trigger from the standard: carrying the trash out on collection night already puts you standing here, so a new liner drops in and the reserve roll gets checked while the bag is in your hand.
Shoot it as one continuous motion, bag out, liner in, roll straightened, so it is visible that nothing was added to the evening.
Close the loop on the monthly habit for a room nobody uses, a mug of water down the traps and a bowl treatment with full dwell time whether or not anybody has been in here.
shots: Three quarter of a bag being lifted out of the can.
Close on a fresh liner being snapped into the empty can.
Close on a hand straightening the reserve roll upright.
Overhead of a mug of water going down the sink and then the floor drain.
on_screen_text: Bag out, liner in, roll upright

short.hook: One unbroken take from beside the bin: bag out, fresh liner snapped in, a hand straightens the spare roll, done.
short.standalone_note: Name the trigger, trash collection night, and say which room this is, since the whole idea is attaching the task to a trip already being made.

close.standard_beat: Hold the finished zone wide and read the standard off what is in frame: one reserve roll visible from the seat, a dry brush in a dry holder, a lined can, and no ring at the water line. Then show the card standing in the cleaning bin and run the trigger, bag out and liner in on collection night.
close.next_zone_teaser: The room is clean and stocked. The last thing a guest touches is a towel, so next we deal with the good ones you have never let anybody use.

videos.title: Guest Towels: One Bundle Per Guest, Built From Your Best
videos.cold_open_problem: Open on two towel stacks side by side, one plush and untouched, one thin and gray, and a hand reaching past the good one for the worn one. Name the arrangement nobody in this house says out loud, that guests are not quite allowed to use the nice towels. Then set out the fact that breaks it, that towels thin whether they are used or not, so the good set is aging untouched on a shelf while visitors dry off on something gray.

segments.covers: Every towel is unfolded and judged in daylight, not in closet light.
beats: Carry the stack out to daylight and unfold every towel fully, on the point that closet light hides exactly the things you are looking for.
Name the four disqualifiers and show each one in frame: thin along the fold line, permanently gray, stiff from too much softener, or carrying a hair dye or nosebleed stain.
Anything disqualified leaves the guest stack and becomes a rag or a car towel today, shown being cut or bagged so it cannot come back.
Close the loophole out loud, that a disqualified towel does not go back on the shelf just in case.
shots: Three quarter of the stack being carried out of the closet into window light.
Overhead of a towel unfolded flat and backlit, light coming through along the fold line.
Macro on a stain, then on a stiff, matted pile surface.
Close on a rejected towel being cut into rags on a hard surface.
Overhead of the survivors set against the discard pile.
on_screen_text: Rag today, not just in case

short.hook: A towel is held flat against a window and the light comes straight through along the fold line.
short.standalone_note: List all four disqualifiers inside the Short, since the backlight only demonstrates one of them, and say these are guest towels being judged.

segments.covers: Towels are stored as complete sets, so hosting is one lift instead of three searches.
beats: Reject the usual method on camera, stacking like with like, and show its cost, that setting up for a visitor becomes three separate searches.
Build a bundle instead, bath towel, hand towel and washcloth folded together into one unit, with the fold sequence shown in full so it is repeatable.
Set the quantity honestly, two bundles ready covers most households, matched to the number of guests actually expected.
Give the bath mat its place flat underneath the bundles, and finish with a hand's width of air above the stack.
Name the shelf disqualifier, that no thin gray towel kept for the dog shares this shelf.
shots: Overhead of three separate like with like stacks, then hands breaking them apart.
Overhead, locked and continuous, of the full bundle fold sequence.
Three quarter of one finished bundle lifted off the shelf in a single hand.
Close on the bath mat sliding in flat beneath the bundles.
Wide of the finished shelf with clear air above the stack.

short.hook: Overhead and unbroken, three towels fold down into one bundle that then lifts off the shelf in a single hand.
short.standalone_note: Say what goes into the bundle before the fold starts and why it exists, so that setting up for a visitor is one lift rather than three searches.

segments.covers: The stored set gets washed although nobody used it, and the closet gets checked for what it has been doing to them.
beats: Give the reason the stored set goes in hot even though it looks clean, that a towel folded in a closed closet all season carries a musty note that appears the instant it gets wet.
Connect it to the shoot order and the working order, that the wash goes in before anything else in the room is touched and this shelf finishes last because the cycle sets the pace.
Wipe the empty shelf, then run a flat hand along the back wall of the closet, saying what the hand is checking for, damp, which is what the towels have been drinking.
Show what that damp looks like on the back wall, so a viewer can recognise it in their own closet.
shots: Three quarter of the stored set going into the machine untouched and unused.
Close on the empty shelf being wiped end to end.
Macro of a flat hand moving along the closet back wall under the small panel.
Macro on a damp patch or bloom on that back wall, panel set low for raking light.

short.standalone_note: Explain that this is stored guest linen nobody has touched, and that the wash and the wall check are one job, since the closet is why the towels smell of the closet.

segments.covers: Burn or fire, and fall, both specific to a linen shelf in a shared closet.
beats: Burn or fire: if this closet also holds the water heater, show towels pressed against the tank, a hot pipe, or the heater's cable, and be plain that no amount of neat folding fixes a scorch and fire risk.
Set the clearance rule and measure it on camera, a hand's width of clear air around anything that gets hot, with no stack leaning on the unit and no cable trapped behind one.
Free the cable from behind the stack and route it clear.

Fall: bring the bath mat back in for the second hazard, a curled or hardened rubber backing. Flex it so the cracks open on camera, and give the failure, that it stops gripping tile and slides out from under someone stepping off wet.
shots: Three quarter of the shared closet showing textiles pressed against a water heater or hot pipe.
Close on a flat hand held against the tank to measure clearance, then the stack pulled back to that line.
Macro on a cable trapped behind a stack, then freed and routed clear.
Macro on a bath mat backing being flexed, cracks opening across the rubber.
Low close of that mat sliding on tile under a light push.
on_screen_text: A hand's width of clear air

short.hook: A bath mat is turned over and the rubber backing gets flexed until cracks open right across it.
short.standalone_note: Say what the backing is for and what the cracks mean, that it stops gripping tile and slides out from under a wet foot stepping off a tub.

segments.covers: The shelf is marked so a missing bundle reads as a gap without anyone counting, and the good towels go into service.
beats: State the shelf standard, two complete bundles on the marked shelf with the bath mat flat beneath them.
Mark the shelf edge where the second bundle ends, and give what the mark does, it turns a count into a look.
Demonstrate it by lifting one bundle away so the exposed mark reads as an obvious gap, then putting it back.
Name the standard as Chapter 24 teaches, so the shelf, the mark and the name all agree and the household calls it the same thing every time.

Settle the call as the hardest clause here: the guest bundle is built from the best towels in the house, put into service today, and the ones they replace get demoted to rags on the same trip so they cannot creep back. Handle the exception too, that a towel genuinely too good for a guest is not linen at all, it is a keepsake, and it belongs anywhere except this shelf.
shots: Close on a mark being made along the shelf edge.
Overhead of two bundles sitting flush to the mark.
Matched overhead with one bundle lifted away and the mark exposed.
Close on the old set going into the rag bag on the same trip.
Close on a keepsake towel being carried out of the linen closet entirely.
on_screen_text: Mark where the second bundle ends
A gap you see, not count

short.hook: One towel bundle lifts off a shelf and the mark drawn underneath it suddenly reads as an obvious gap.
short.standalone_note: Explain the mark and the shelf standard, two bundles with the mark at the end of the second, before the bundle is lifted, or the reveal has nothing to land on.

segments.covers: The guest leaving is the trigger, and the whole loop closes before you sit down.
beats: Give the trigger exactly as the standard states it: the guest's departure starts it, bed and bathroom get stripped together, washed together, and the shelf restocked before you sit down.
Show the used bathroom set going into the same load as the bed linen, one wash and one trip.
Show the shelf restocked before the sheets are dry, on the point that this shelf is never left part stocked waiting on somebody's memory.
Close the room out by noting that a full marked shelf is what makes the next arrival a single walk through rather than a search.
shots: Three quarter of bedding gathered and carried through with the bathroom set balanced on top.
Close on both going into the machine together.
Overhead of fresh bundles going back onto the marked shelf.
Wide of the finished closet, a hand's width of air above a full stack.

short.hook: Stripped bed linen and used bathroom towels get carried through in one armful and go into the same machine together.
short.standalone_note: Name the trigger, a guest leaving, and finish on the shelf restocked before the sheets are dry so the loop closes inside the Short.

close.standard_beat: Hold the finished shelf and read the standard against it: two complete bundles, a bath towel plus a hand towel plus a washcloth in each, the bath mat folded flat beneath, and the mark showing where the second bundle ends. Then run the trigger in full, the guest leaves, bed and bathroom get stripped and washed together, and the bundles go back before the sheets are dry.
close.next_zone_teaser: That wash is running now, and it has to come out right. Next we follow it into the room where every standard in this house either holds or quietly falls apart, the laundry room.

Hallway carry through position for the departure trigger sequence.
videos.description_hook: Your guests dry off on the worn towels while the good ones age untouched on a shelf. Towels thin whether anyone uses them or not.

rooms.room_note: Most laundry rooms are interior and narrow, lit by one overhead bulb, so the working light is that fixture plus whatever spills through the open door from the nearest window. Lift the shadow under the machine lids with a white bounce card or a folded sheet angled off the ceiling rather than adding a second source, and shoot the machines with the tripod set low and tight against the opposite wall for three-quarter angles, since there is rarely room to stand back. For tops of machines and the folding counter, reverse the centre column or stand the tripod on the counter itself and angle down; there is no space for an overhead rig and no second pair of hands on this shoot. Record all voiceover separately, because a running drum, a spin cycle and an extractor fan will bury a live track. On set safety, and this is not optional because the camera does not care: unplug the dryer at the wall and shut off both taps before any shot that involves pulling a machine out, tilting it back, or disconnecting a duct or a fill hose. Sheet metal under a tilted machine is sharp, so gloves on the hands in frame for those setups. Bleach and any ammonia based cleaner stay capped in every shot and are never opened in the same take, even for illustration. Keep the walking line between door and machines clear of cable at all times, and tape down anything crossing the floor near the drying rack, since that floor gets wet on purpose in one of these shoots.

videos.title: Washer and Dryer Reset: Lint Screen, Door Gasket, and the Dryer Duct
videos.cold_open_problem: Open on towels going round for a second tumble while a hand rests on a warm dryer casing, the household's standing excuse in one image, that the machine just runs a bit slow these days. Then narrow the whole video to the single question this zone turns on, the month the dryer was last pulled out and the duct cleared, and frame what follows as what happens when nobody in the house can name it.

segments.covers: Both machine tops and both drums come clear in one pass, and what comes off leaves the room instead of moving sideways.
beats: Both machine tops shown as found, then hands sweeping the whole surface into one holding basket, so nothing gets sorted while it is still standing on a lid.
A hand reaching into the washer drum and behind the agitator for the single sock, which goes to the folding zone basket rather than back onto a machine.
The three usual survivors handled one at a time, a hardened box of dryer sheets, a bottle of softener that stopped being used, a cap with no bottle, each routed out of the room rather than shelved.
The rule that governs this pass made visible: nothing coming off one machine is allowed to land on the other.
shots: Overhead of both machine tops as found, one continuous take of hands clearing them into a basket
Three-quarter of a hand reaching behind the agitator and coming out with a sock
Tripod close, macro framing on the crusted neck of a softener bottle
Overhead of the emptied lids, bare metal, held for a beat
