Close on the step stool being carried in and set in the corner of the room
Three-quarter of heavy ream boxes coming down from the high shelf to the bottom shelf
Upward angle at the finished top shelf, light items only

short.hook: A hand presses down on an empty office chair seat and the castors turn under the weight, before anyone tries to stand on it.
short.standalone_note: Show the step stool arriving and staying in the room as the resolution, and name the falling box hazard too, since the clip should end with both fixes rather than one warning.

segments.covers: Min and max written on a card at the front edge of every shelf, readable from the doorway.
beats: Write min and max on a card for each shelf and clip it to the front edge.
Read the cabinet from the doorway, where one shelf is visibly below its line without anyone stepping in or counting.
Show the cabinet being read and the last pack taken by a hand that never had to ask you, since the card removes you as the gatekeeper.
Point to Chapter 14, visual controls.
shots: Macro on a min and max card being written
Close on the card clipping to the front edge of a shelf
Three-quarter from the doorway with one shelf visibly below its min
Close on a hand reading a shelf card and taking the last pack without counting

short.hook: A supply cabinet seen from a doorway, and one shelf is obviously below its line without anyone counting anything.
short.standalone_note: Show the card being written and clipped to the shelf edge before the doorway reveal, because the payoff shot only works once the viewer knows what the card says.

segments.covers: The shopping list gets written when you open the last pack, before you break the seal.
beats: Open on a hand lifting the last pack of something off the shelf with the gap behind it, which is the trigger.
Carry it still sealed to the household shopping list on the fridge and write it on, since the seal is the deadline and the moment passes once it opens.
Cut that against adding it after it runs out, which is always the day you need it.
Restate the standard, one open plus one spare of anything used monthly, with min and max at the front of every shelf.

Three-quarter of the sealed pack being carried out of the room

short.standalone_note: State that the seal is the deadline and name the trigger as opening the last pack, because the walk to the fridge is meaningless without knowing the pack is deliberately still sealed.

close.next_zone_teaser: That is all six zones of the home office, so the room now runs on six standards and six triggers, and the next room in the series starts at the door you came in through.

videos.description_hook: You were not wrong about the price, and that is exactly why the surplus is still on the shelf. Count it against a year of honest use, cap it, and write min and max where you can read them from the doorway.

rooms.room_note: Shoot with the main door rolled up for light, and plan the day so the slab sits in open shade rather than half sun and half shadow, because a hard light line across concrete wrecks continuity between setups. Light is door light and window light only. The one addition is a bounce board and a small battery LED clamped to a shelf edge, no stands and no second head, used to lift the insides of cabinets, bins, and the underside of the overhead racks, which go black on camera even when the eye reads them as fine. Park the car outside for the whole shoot so the tripod can sit centre slab and the parking bay reads as clear floor. This is a one person shoot. Tripod work is three positions and no more: a horizontal arm over the bench top and over the floor sheet for overheads, a three quarter position at chest height on sticks for wall, shelf, and rack work, and a macro setup on a short focus rail for date marks, labels, contacts, and blade edges. The camera never rides a ladder, and it never leaves the tripod while hands are in frame, so any sense of movement is built from locked frames that hands enter and leave. Nothing above the wrists enters frame at any point, so mark hand entry and exit lines on the floor with tape before rolling. On set safety: real hazards are demonstrated in their safe state only. Fuel cans stay sealed and stay outside the house envelope, garden chemicals stay capped and stay in their own labelled containers, no vehicle is ever raised on a jack for a shot, oily rags used in any frame go into the closed metal can at the end of the take, and battery packs shown on chargers come off the charger the moment the shot ends. Sound is voiceover only, so record wild room tone plus close foley of clamps racking, a bin lid, a spade scrape, and a broom on concrete.

videos.title: Garage Workbench Reset: Clearing the Bench Down to Bare Wood
videos.cold_open_problem: Open overhead on the half finished project that has held the bench since spring, framed so the timber, the loose hinges, and the drift of other rooms' clutter around it read as one mass. A hand arrives with a small repair job, finds nowhere to set it down, and takes it away again. The problem is specific: this is the only surface in the house where things get fixed, it has been unavailable for months, and the cause is one object nobody has given a verdict to. Name the three verdicts waiting on it, a named weekend written on it, a breakdown that returns the timber and hinges to stock, or the skip.

segments.covers: The bench top comes down to bare wood, and nothing goes back up without a verdict, including the stalled project itself.
beats: Time condensed overhead of the whole bench top being cleared onto the floor sheet, so the volume that was living on one working surface reads in a single frame.

Hands sort the three things that only ever collect on a bench top, screws living in jar lids, glue bottles with nozzles set solid, and offcuts saved because the grain looked too good to bin, with the point made that each was kept without a verdict, which is why they multiply.

Work the hard one. Hands set the stalled project on bare concrete and place three markers beside it for the three verdicts, and the settling rule is explained, that anything untouched through one full season is not a project any more, it is furniture with your intentions stacked on it.

Show the tempting wrong move, hands lifting the project towards a shelf and then stopping, with the reason given, that shelving it moves the decision somewhere darker and costs you the bench in the meantime.
shots: Locked overhead of the full bench top, wide enough to hold both ends, for the clear down sequence.
Close on hands at floor level tipping a jar lid of mixed screws onto the sheet and spreading them flat.
Macro on a glue nozzle set solid, hands squeezing and nothing moving.
Three quarter on the stalled project alone on bare concrete as the three verdict markers are placed beside it.

short.hook: A hand stopping mid lift as a half finished project is about to go onto a shelf, and the reason it never gets to go there.
short.standalone_note: Open by saying this is a garage workbench and the object is a project that has sat on it since spring, then give the one season rule and the three verdicts in full, since nothing in the Short can lean on the parent video.

segments.covers: Homes on the bench are chosen by how the bench is actually used, with the vise given its swing room and the non bench items sent out.
beats: Hands set the vise corner, then sweep an arm's length of open top in front of it, with the reason given, that this space is not spare, it is the arc a long board swings through.
Clamps go onto the rail within reach and fasteners into the drawer directly beneath, chosen by reach distance during a job rather than by tidiness.

Name the impostors and remove them one at a time, the post that came in, the half tin of paint, the parcel waiting to go back, with the point that these never were bench items, and that a bench is the easiest surface in the house to lose to other rooms.
shots: Overhead of a long board being swung through the space in front of the vise, hands only at each end.
Three quarter on clamps going back onto the rail one at a time.
Close on the fastener drawer opening directly beneath the working position.
Close on the post, the paint tin, and the parcel being lifted off the top and carried out of frame.
on_screen_text: Arm's length in front of the vise

short.hook: A long board swinging through an empty stretch of workbench, showing what the empty stretch is actually for.
short.standalone_note: State in the opening seconds that this is a workbench vise corner and that the clear space in front of it is deliberate, then land the three impostor items so the Short carries the whole idea.

segments.covers: Cleaning the bench is inspection work, and the dog holes, the back seam, and the vise screw are where it pays.
beats: Vacuum sawdust and metal filings out of the bench dog holes and out of the seam where the top meets the back wall, with the point that this is the debris a cloth only pushes further in.
Wipe the vise screw down and put a single drop of oil on it, with the reason given, that a vise which turns easily is a vise you use rather than work around.

Sweep the concrete under the bench until the slab reads pale again, and explain what that buys, a dropped chisel or a stray blade showing up instead of living in the sawdust where a hand goes looking.
shots: Macro on a vacuum nozzle drawing filings out of a bench dog hole.
Close raking light shot along the seam between bench top and back wall, before and after.
Macro on one drop of oil landing on the vise screw, then hands turning the handle.
Low three quarter of the broom clearing concrete under the bench until the slab reads clean.

short.hook: Macro on a vacuum pulling a surprising weight of metal filings out of a single bench dog hole.
short.standalone_note: Establish that this is a workbench top and that dog holes and the back seam hold what wiping never removes, then close on the vise screw and the drop of oil so the Short ends on a fix.

segments.covers: The bench has four real hazards, and each one is fixed on camera rather than noted for later.
beats: Water and electricity. Hands inspect the bench outlet and the task light cord for nicks, then plug in a sander to show whether the lead crosses the strip of floor you stand on, and the routing is fixed so it does not.
Fall, cut, or crush. Show a chisel and a utility blade lying edge up on the top, then the sweep of a bare hand clearing sawdust without looking, staged and stopped short, then the edges are put away.

Burn or fire. Show the balled rags in an open bin under the bench, with the point that oil, stain, and solvent rags can heat on their own with no flame near them, then move them into a closed metal can.
Water and electricity again, at floor level. Show the power strip sitting low on a slab that runs wet when a car comes in from the rain, then get it up off the floor.
shots: Macro travelling along the task light cord over a nicked section.
Overhead of the sander lead crossing the standing strip, then the rerouted version.
Close on a bare hand sweeping sawdust across a top with a blade edge up in its path, staged and stopped short.
Three quarter of oily rags going from an open bin into a metal can, lid closing.
Low angle on the power strip on wet looking slab, then mounted clear of the floor.
on_screen_text: Find it, and fix it now

short.hook: A balled oily rag lifted out of an open bin under a workbench, and the fact that it can heat on its own with no flame anywhere near it.
short.standalone_note: Re establish the under bench bin and what the rags have on them, and end with the metal can and the lid closing so the fix is complete inside the Short.

segments.covers: A photo of the cleared bench taped on the wall behind it makes the right state obvious without anyone remembering a rule.
beats: Hands photograph the cleared bench holding only the vise and the task light, then tape the print on the wall directly behind it at eye height.
Demonstrate how it works. A paint tin and a coil of wire go onto the top, then cut to the photo, with the conclusion drawn, that anything the photo does not show is the next thing to leave.
Explain that this standard is a picture rather than a written rule, and quote the line, "A standard is the best way you know today, written down."
Point to Chapter 25, the ideal state photo, for how to shoot one for any zone.
shots: Overhead of the cleared bench framed as the reference photo itself.
Close on hands taping the print to the wall at eye height behind the bench.
Two part close comparison, the real top with a paint tin on it, then the photo with nothing.
Macro on the photo edge with the bench in soft focus behind.
on_screen_text: Vise and task light, nothing else

short.hook: A paint tin sitting on a workbench, and a photo taped on the wall behind it that does not contain a paint tin.
short.standalone_note: Show the photo being taken and taped up first so the viewer knows what they are comparing against, then run the comparison and state the rule in one line.

segments.covers: The end of a project is defined by the bench, and the trigger is the last plug leaving the bench outlet.
beats: Redefine finished. Show glue setting, then show what still has to happen, clamps back on the rail, offcuts into the scrap bin, top swept, all before the task light goes off.
Run the trigger in sequence. Hands pull the last plug from the bench outlet, and that is the cue to pick up the broom, with the emphasis that the signal is the plug rather than a time.
Close the loop back to the photo, hands holding the wall print up against the finished top.
shots: Close on clamps coming off the work and going back onto the rail.
Macro on the plug being pulled from the bench outlet.
Overhead of the sweep, ending on the bare top with vise and task light only.
Close on the task light switch going off last.

short.hook: A plug coming out of a workbench outlet, used as the start of the clean up rather than the end of the job.
short.standalone_note: Establish that the project is done and the glue is setting, then show the plug as the trigger and the three actions it starts, ending on the bare top.

close.standard_beat: Hold on the finished bench, bare except the vise and the task light, with the wall photo in frame behind it, and state the standard, that the bench ends every session bare except those two things. Then replay the trigger in one cut, the plug leaving the outlet followed by the broom, so the viewer leaves with the signal rather than the intention.
close.next_zone_teaser: The bench is clear, but every tool you just put down came off a wall that cannot tell you what is missing, so next we hang the hand tool wall and draw the outlines.

shot_list: Overhead arm locked over the full bench top for clear down, board swing, sweep, and the ideal state photo.
Three quarter chest height on sticks at the vise corner and clamp rail.
Floor level sorting setup on the sheet with the three verdict markers.
Macro focus rail for dog holes, the vise screw and oil drop, cord nicks, and the plug pull.
Low angle at slab level for the power strip and the under bench sweep.
Static on the back wall at eye height for taping and comparing the photo.
Metal rag can setup with room for lid open and lid closed.
Task light switch close for the final beat.
videos.description_hook: The garage workbench is the one surface in the house where things actually get fixed, and it is usually the one surface you cannot use. This is a full 6S reset of a bench top, hands only, including the verdict on the project that has been sitting there since spring.

videos.title: Hand Tool Wall Reset: Duplicates, Outlines, and the Third Hammer
videos.cold_open_problem: Open overhead on a sheet spread across the garage floor as three claw hammers, four adjustable wrenches, and a fistful of Phillips drivers are laid out in rows. The problem is that none of it has ever been thinned, because each tool, held on its own, still works. Show a hand reaching past two hammers to take the third, the one it always takes. Name the real test, which is not whether a tool works but which one your hand actually goes to, and name the cost, that a hammer you never choose is holding the hook that would have made the one you love findable in a single glance from the door.

segments.covers: Every hand tool comes off the wall and out of the cabinet onto one sheet, the duplicates get counted honestly, and dead tools leave as scrap rather than spares.
beats: Time condensed overhead of the wall and the cabinet emptying onto a single sheet, grouped into hammers, drivers, pliers, and wrenches so the duplicate count is undeniable on screen.

Sort the genuinely dead. Hands work a plier rusted shut, a wrench with rounded jaws, and a driver with a chewed tip, with the point that these are scrap metal rather than spares, and that keeping them means hunting past them forever.

Make the third hammer call. Line the hammers up, show the hand choosing, keep that one, then place exactly one deliberate spare where a second person would need it, the kitchen drawer or the boot of the car.
Send the rest out with named destinations rather than a vague pile, a friend, a tool library, or the metal skip.
shots: Locked overhead of the full sheet with tools laid in family rows.
Close on hands trying to open a plier rusted solid.
Macro on a rounded wrench jaw and a chewed driver tip side by side.
Three quarter on the hammer line up with one hand hovering, then taking one.
Close on the deliberate spare being set into a kitchen drawer or a car boot.
on_screen_text: Which one does your hand take

short.hook: Three claw hammers laid out in a row, and a hand going straight past two of them without hesitating.
short.standalone_note: Establish that all three hammers are yours and all three work, then land the test and the one deliberate spare, since the point collapses unless the duplicates are visible first.

segments.covers: The wall is hung by how often your hand reaches, not by tool family, with the sub minute tools at chest height nearest the door.
beats: Show the intuitive wrong version first, tools grouped neatly by family, then explain why that arrangement ignores how the wall is actually used.
Hang the three that come off the wall for jobs taking under a minute at chest height nearest the door, tape measure, utility knife, and the number two driver.
Place pipe wrenches and socket sets lower and further along, with the reason given, that heavier and rarer earns a worse position rather than a better one.
Walk the reach test as a series of locked frames from the doorway inwards, hands entering and leaving at each position so the path reads without the camera moving.
shots: Three quarter of the whole board mid rehang, wide enough to read zones of reach.
Close on tape measure, utility knife, and number two driver going up at chest height with the doorway visible behind.
Low three quarter on pipe wrenches and sockets going to the lower far end.
Locked frame at the doorway looking along the wall, hands entering and leaving at each reach position.
on_screen_text: Under a minute, nearest the door

short.hook: A pegboard arranged perfectly by tool family, then the tape measure you touch every day found hanging at the far end from the door.
short.standalone_note: Say plainly that this is a garage pegboard and that the door is at one end, then give the reach rule and name the three tools that earn the nearest hooks.

segments.covers: Each tool is wiped as it goes back up, and so is the board behind it, because rust starts where hands leave salt.
beats: Hands wipe a tool with an oiled rag as part of hanging it, so the cleaning happens inside the rehang rather than as a separate job.
Wipe the pegboard behind the tool and reveal the tool shaped outline of grime that was hiding under it.
Show on macro where rust actually starts, at the handle end where hands sit, and why that end earns the attention.
shots: Close on an oiled rag drawn along a wrench, then the wrench going onto its hook.
Macro on the handle end of a tool showing early rust freckles.
Close on the pegboard being wiped with the tool shaped clean patch appearing.
on_screen_text: Wipe it as it goes back

short.hook: Macro on a freckle of rust at the handle end of a wrench, the exact place a hand leaves salt.
short.standalone_note: Say that this is a hand tool going back onto a garage wall, and pair the rust detail with the oiled rag wipe so the Short contains the fix as well as the problem.

segments.covers: Edges get sheathed before they touch the wall, hooks get seated properly, and the low cabinet gets a latch.
beats: Fall, cut, or crush, first. Show a handsaw and a chisel hung bare at hand height, then sheath and guard both before they go back up.

Demonstrate the shallow hook problem. A heavy wrench sits on a poorly seated hook and is knocked off deliberately onto a taped floor mark, then the hook is seated properly and the same knock does nothing.
Poison, choke, or strangle. Open the low cabinet on loose box cutter blades, screws, and drill bits at toddler height, then fit a latch and close it.
State the working rule, that the fix happens now rather than getting written down for later.
shots: Close on a saw sliding into a sheath and a chisel guard clipping on.
Three quarter on the heavy wrench falling from a shallow hook onto a taped floor mark, no feet in frame.
Macro on a pegboard hook being seated correctly.
Low overhead into the open low cabinet on loose blades and bits, then the latch closing.

short.hook: A heavy wrench knocked off a shallow pegboard hook, landing on the taped mark where a foot would be.
short.standalone_note: Establish the pegboard and how shallow the hook is before the drop, then show the seated hook version immediately so the Short ends on the fix rather than the scare.

segments.covers: Traced outlines turn the wall into something that reports its own missing tools.
beats: Hands trace the silhouette of a tool onto the board in marker or paint, working through several so the pace of the job is honest.
Demonstrate the payoff. The tenon saw comes off and the frame holds on the empty outline, with the point that the wall tells you it is missing without you having to remember that you own one.
Note that tracing is the slow part of the day and where the time actually goes, and point to Chapter 14, visual controls, for outlines and boundaries.
shots: Flat on close of a tool being traced, marker tip in macro.
Wide three quarter of the board part traced and part bare, showing progress.
Static on a single blank outline where the tenon saw should be.
on_screen_text: A blank outline is a question

short.hook: A tool shaped outline on a pegboard with nothing hanging in it, held long enough for the viewer to work out what is gone.
short.standalone_note: Show a traced tool going up and coming back down first, so the meaning of a blank silhouette is established inside the Short rather than assumed.

segments.covers: Tools return to their outlines inside the job, and the toolbox empties before it touches the floor.
beats: Show the failure mode, a driver left on the bench top overnight, with the point that a tool sleeping off the wall is one the wall has already started to lose.
Run the correct sequence, the driver back on its outline before the step ladder is folded away rather than at the weekend.
Run the trigger. Hands carry the toolbox in from a job and empty it onto the wall before the box is set down, and the frame holds on the box only touching the floor once it is empty.
Close on the whole board with no blank outlines.
shots: Close on a lone driver on the bench in low evening light.
Three quarter of the step ladder being folded with the driver already back on its outline in frame.
Close on hands lifting tools out of a carried toolbox straight onto hooks.
Wide of the complete board, every outline filled.
on_screen_text: Empty the box before it lands

short.hook: A toolbox carried in from a job that does not get set down on the floor until it is empty.
short.standalone_note: Name the trigger at the top, coming back in from a job, and show the pegboard receiving the tools, so the habit reads without the parent video explaining the wall.

close.standard_beat: Hold wide on the finished board with every tool on its own outline and no blank silhouettes, then push in on the chest height cluster nearest the door and state the standard, that a blank outline means you find that tool before you close up. Replay the toolbox trigger in a single cut.
close.next_zone_teaser: Hand tools tell you what is missing at a glance, but the powered shelf hides its problem inside a pack that no longer holds a charge, so next we take on batteries and chargers.

shot_list: Locked overhead over the floor sheet for the full tool lay out and duplicate rows.
Wide three quarter on the pegboard covering the door end and the far end in one frame.
Chest height static on the near board for the sub minute tool cluster.
Macro focus rail for rust freckles, hook seating, marker tracing, and rounded jaws.
Floor mark setup for the controlled wrench drop, taped and cleared.
Low overhead into the open low cabinet with room for the latch fit.
Doorway locked frame for the reach test, hands entering and leaving.
Step ladder and toolbox setup for the Sustain sequence.
videos.description_hook: You probably own three hammers and four adjustable wrenches, and every one of them still works, which is exactly why the wall never gets thinned. This is a hands only 6S reset of a hand tool wall, ending with traced outlines that tell you what is missing.

videos.title: Power Tool and Battery Shelf Reset: One Shelf Per System, Nothing Left on a Charger
videos.cold_open_problem: Open on a good drill sitting beside one tired pack and a charger nobody makes any more. The problem is that the tool itself is genuinely fine, which is why it has survived every previous clear out, and it is on a platform that no longer exists. Show a hand picking it up, turning it over, and setting it back down unused. Name the way the decision gets made, with money rather than loyalty, and name the shelf level cost, that running three battery systems means a hunt through three shelves every time you want to put a hole in a wall.

segments.covers: Every pack is tested in the tool it belongs to, and dead packs, orphan chargers, and damaged tools leave the same day.
beats: Line every pack up on the bench and run each one in its own tool until the shelf splits into packs that hold a charge and packs that do not, with the point that guessing does not work here, which is why the session is mostly Sort.
Show a pack dying inside a minute under load and going into the leaving pile with its recycling destination named.
Pull the chargers for tools you no longer own, and the sander with the taped cord, with the point stated plainly, that a taped cord is not a repair.

Make the dead platform call. Price one replacement pack against a current equivalent tool, and apply the rule, that more than half the price of a new tool, or no pack available at all, means the tool is finished, so it is sold with its charger while it still means something to somebody, or taken to electrical recycling.
shots: Overhead of every pack lined up in rows by system on the bench top.
Close on a pack seating into a drill, trigger pull, and the tool slowing to a stop.
Macro on a taped power cord.
Close on hands setting the orphan drill and its charger together into a labelled box for recycling.
on_screen_text: Test every pack in its own tool

short.hook: A battery pack that reads as full going into a drill and dying inside a minute under load.
short.standalone_note: Establish that these are garage battery packs being tested one at a time in their own tools, then give the rule for what a dead platform costs you before the Short ends.

segments.covers: The shelf is grouped by battery system rather than by task, with consumables directly beneath the tools that take them.
beats: Show the failure this fixes, a hand carrying a green pack across to a red tool, then rebuild so one shelf carries the tools, packs, and charger of a single platform.
Mount each charger at the front edge of its own shelf, setting up the visual signal that pays off in Standardize.
Load the shallow drawer directly beneath with blades, drill bits, and sanding discs, pairing each consumable to the tool that takes it.
Show every tool going back in its case or onto a labelled hook with guards down.
shots: Three quarter wide of the shelf bay mid rebuild, one system per shelf becoming readable.
Close on a charger being mounted at the front edge of a shelf.
Overhead into the open shallow drawer as blades and discs are laid in.
Close on a drill going back into its case, latches closing.

short.hook: A green battery pack being carried across a garage to a red tool, then the shelf layout that makes that walk impossible.
short.standalone_note: Name the mismatch in the first line and show both shelves rebuilt, since the grouping rule only reads if the viewer sees the two systems separated on camera.

segments.covers: Cleaning here is vents and contacts, because packed dust and dirty terminals shorten the life of the tool.
beats: Brush or blow the motor vents of a drill and a saw clear of packed dust, showing what comes out, with the reason given, that a vent clogged with plaster dust runs a motor hot enough to shorten its life.
Clean the battery contacts and the charger terminals, with the before state held on macro long enough to read.
Make the inspection point, that while the tool is in your hands and clean you can see a cracked case or a frayed cord you would otherwise never notice.
shots: Macro on drill motor vents packed with pale dust, then clear.
Close on the dust leaving a saw housing, backlit against the open garage door.
Macro on battery contacts being cleaned, then on the charger terminals.

short.hook: The plaster dust that comes out of one drill's motor vents, backlit in an open garage doorway.
short.standalone_note: Say what the tool is and that the dust has packed into the vents, then give the reason plainly so the Short teaches something rather than just being satisfying to watch.

segments.covers: This is the highest fire risk shelf in the garage, and guards and cracked cases get checked one tool at a time.
beats: Burn or fire. Packs come off the charger once full and sit at partial charge on a shelf well clear of the fuel can and the rag bin, with the separation shown as a real distance on camera.
Fall, cut, or crush. Check that every blade guard springs back freely on its own, including the one that has been sticking, shown on a circular saw guard released and repeated.
Retire a tool with a cracked case rather than pushing it behind the others, with the wrong move shown first, the hand sliding it to the back of the shelf.
Water and electricity. Charger bases sitting on the slab where meltwater runs off the car, and leads daisy chained to feed the whole shelf, get the bases up and the leads sorted.
shots: Wide three quarter showing the pack shelf and the fuel can with clear distance between them.
Macro on a saw guard swinging closed under its own spring, repeated.
Close on a cracked tool housing, then hands sliding it to the back, then pulling it out again.
Low angle on charger bases sitting on damp slab, then relocated.

short.hook: A lithium pack charging on a wooden shelf next to a petrol can, held long enough to be uncomfortable, then separated.
short.standalone_note: Establish that this is a garage charging shelf and name what is sitting beside it, then land the storage rule, that packs come off when full and sit at partial charge well clear of fuel.

segments.covers: One label per system and a front edge charger make a pack left charging visible from the doorway.
beats: Apply one shelf label per battery system so the shelf states which platform it is without anyone opening a case.
Show the doorway view. With the charger at the front edge, a pack left charging reads as a lump on the shelf edge from the door without walking in, cut between empty and occupied.
Explain that the shelf edge is doing the checking rather than anyone remembering, and quote the line, "A standard is the best way you know today, written down."
shots: Close on labels going onto shelf edges, one per system.
Matched pair from the doorway, no pack on the charger and then a pack on the charger.
Macro on the pack overhanging the front edge, showing the silhouette that gives it away.

short.hook: The view from a garage doorway of a shelf edge, clean, then the same view with a battery pack sitting proud of it.
short.standalone_note: Explain in the first line that the charger is mounted at the front edge on purpose, otherwise the comparison reads as a tidiness point rather than a signal you can see from the door.

segments.covers: Pulling a full pack is part of finishing the job, and the nightly door lock is the backstop.
beats: Redefine finishing the job to include pulling the full pack off the charger, shown in the same sequence as putting the drill back in its case.
State the rule on screen, that nothing sleeps on a charger, whatever the manual claims about smart cut off.
Run the trigger as two locked frames, a hand entering at the charger shelf edge to lift a pack off in passing, then the side door lock turning in the same evening light.
Point to Chapter 22, prevent and prepare, for why this one is written as a route rather than a reminder.
shots: Close on a full pack coming off the charger and going onto the shelf beside the case.
Locked frame at the charger shelf edge, a hand entering and lifting a pack off without pausing.
Macro on the side door lock turning.
Final wide of the shelf bay with no pack on any charger.

short.hook: The last walk of the night past a charging shelf, and a hand lifting a pack off it without breaking stride.
short.standalone_note: Name the trigger as locking the side door for the night and state the rule about packs and chargers, since the lifted pack does not explain itself on its own.

close.standard_beat: Hold on the finished bay, one shelf per system, chargers at the front edges with nothing on them, tools cased or hooked with guards down, and state the standard, that no battery sleeps on a charger and no tool goes back with its guard held open. Then replay the side door route in one cut so the trigger is the last thing seen.
close.next_zone_teaser: Powered tools are handled, and the next shelf is the one nobody reads, bottles of fluid for cars, some of which are not on this driveway any more.

shot_list: Bench top overhead for the pack line up and the testing sequence.
Wide three quarter on the full shelf bay covering all systems in one frame.
Doorway position static, locked, for the matched charger edge pair.
Macro focus rail for contacts, terminals, vents, cracked cases, and taped cords.
Backlit setup in the open garage doorway for the vent dust shot.
Low angle at slab level for charger bases and leads.
Separation wide showing pack shelf and fuel can distance.
Locked frames along the nightly route, shelf edge and side door lock.
videos.description_hook: A good tool on a dead battery platform is the hardest thing on this shelf, because there is nothing wrong with the tool. This is a hands only 6S reset of the power tool and battery zone, including the storage rules for the highest fire risk shelf in the garage.

videos.title: Car Care Shelf Reset: Upright Fluids, Opened Dates, and Bottles for Cars You Sold
videos.cold_open_problem: Open on a deep row of fluid bottles and pull out the two thirds full ones. The problem is that these cost real money, they have not gone off, and they fit nothing on your driveway. Show a hand turning a bottle to find a label soaked away to unreadable grey. Name the rule that settles the shelf, that every bottle must match a vehicle parked at this address, and name why the row grew this deep, that nobody could tell which bottles were still good, so nothing was ever thrown out.

segments.covers: Every bottle is read label by label, and anything that does not match a car on this driveway leaves with a named destination.
beats: Line every bottle up on the bench and work the row one at a time, reading each label properly rather than by shape and colour, which is why this pass is slow.
Pull the three failure types, oil in a weight your current engine does not take, coolant for the van you sold, and the half bottle whose label has soaked away to grey.
Apply the matching rule, no vehicle at this address means no keep, and split the leaving pile into the neighbour who drives that model and the council's household hazardous waste collection.
State the disposal rule and show it being respected, that nothing goes down a drain.
shots: Overhead of the full bottle row on the bench, deep enough to read as a problem.
Macro on a label soaked to unreadable grey, hands turning the bottle.
Close on hands comparing an oil weight on a bottle against the figure in the handbook.
Three quarter of the leaving crate being loaded, marked for hazardous waste.

short.hook: A two thirds full bottle of coolant for a van that was sold two years ago, still standing in the front row.
short.standalone_note: Establish the fluid shelf and the matching rule in the first line, and finish with the disposal route, since this Short lives or dies on giving the viewer somewhere to take the bottle.

segments.covers: Fluids stand upright on a drip tray at waist height, and the dead engine kit lives together by the door.
beats: Set the shallow drip tray at waist height and stand every bottle upright on it, with the reason given, that a weeping cap shows as a ring on the tray rather than soaking into a shelf you never look at.
Build the emergency bag, jumper cables, tyre gauge, and lug wrench together in one bag right by the door.
Give the placement reason plainly, that you go for those three with a dead engine, in the dark, in a hurry, and that this is the only condition the position has to serve.
Show the reach test from the doorway, the bag lifted in one movement, hands only.
Show the bottles facing out so a label can be read without lifting anything off the tray.
shots: Three quarter of the tray at waist height with bottles being stood upright in a row.
Overhead into the tray showing the flat clean surface.
Close on cables, gauge, and wrench going into one bag.
Hands only lift of the bag from its spot beside the door in a single motion.
on_screen_text: Dead engine, dark, in a hurry

short.hook: Everything you actually grab when a car will not start, going into one bag that lives by the garage door.
short.standalone_note: Name the three items and the condition they get used in, since the point is placement under pressure rather than tidiness, and show the one motion lift.

segments.covers: Wiping the shoulders and reading the tray is how a slow leak becomes visible early.
beats: Wipe every bottle shoulder as it goes back onto the tray, and check the tray itself for the ring that says something is seeping.
Explain what the ring gives you, information about a weeping cap the week it starts rather than a soaked shelf found much later.
Handle the cloth question, wash mitts and microfibre towels washed on their own and never with house laundry, so grit and old wax stay out of the good towels.
shots: Macro on a bottle shoulder being wiped, residue visible on the cloth.
Overhead of the tray with a faint ring on it, then the clean tray.
Close on wash mitts and microfibre towels going into their own wash bag.

short.hook: A faint ring on a drip tray under a row of car fluids, and how it names the bottle whose cap is weeping.
short.standalone_note: Show the tray and the bottles standing on it first so the ring has a visible source, then say what the ring is telling you and what you do about it.

segments.covers: Petrol, rags, antifreeze, and how a car is supported are the four that genuinely matter here.
beats: Burn or fire. Any can that has ever held petrol stays out of the house envelope, capped tight, and never on a shelf near the water heater's pilot flame, shown as the pilot and the distance, with the can sealed throughout.
Burn or fire again. Polish and oil rags go into a metal can with a lid rather than the plastic bin, shown as a swap on camera.

Poison, choke, or strangle. Show a decanted unlabelled bottle being taken out of use and a spill absorbed and lifted properly, with the reason stated plainly, that antifreeze tastes sweet and a dog or a curious child will drink it.
Fall, cut, or crush. The trolley jack is stored wound fully down, and axle stands are shown standing ready under the sills as the standard, with no vehicle raised for the shot.
shots: Wide showing the sealed fuel can and the water heater with clear separation, no vapour work of any kind.
Close on rags moving from a plastic bin into a metal can, lid closing.
Macro on a spilled puddle being absorbed and lifted, then the floor clean.
Close on a trolley jack fully wound down for storage, and on axle stands standing ready beside it.

short.hook: A puddle of antifreeze on a garage floor, and the plain fact that it tastes sweet to a dog.
short.standalone_note: Name antifreeze immediately, then show the clean up and the never decant rule inside the Short so it ends on an action rather than a warning.

segments.covers: The shelf gets labelled for exactly what belongs on it, and every bottle wears the month it was opened.
beats: Label the tray shelf with the exact list that belongs on it, engine oil, coolant, screenwash, brake fluid, so a tin of deck stain that wanders in from the garden shelf has nowhere to stand.
Mark the month opened on the shoulder of every bottle, working through several so the habit reads as quick.
Explain why the date is the whole point here, that brake fluid pulls water out of the air and coolant goes off once the seal is broken, and the date is the only way you will ever tell which is which.
shots: Close on a shelf edge label going on with the list readable.
Macro on a marker writing a month and year onto a bottle shoulder.
Overhead of the finished tray, every shoulder dated and facing out.
on_screen_text: The date is the only test

short.hook: A marker writing the opened month onto the shoulder of a brake fluid bottle, and why a sealed looking bottle can already be past it.
short.standalone_note: State that brake fluid pulls water from the air and coolant goes off once opened before the marker appears, or the dating looks like decoration.

segments.covers: The tray gets its look while the bonnet is already up, and empties never go back into the row.
beats: Run the trigger, the bonnet already up for the oil check, and the same trip taking in a look along the tray for a fresh ring.
Show the small rule that keeps the row honest, an empty bottle going straight into the bin rather than back onto the shelf.
Point to Chapter 21, the hazard hunt, for working the five safety questions across the rest of the garage.
shots: Hands on the bonnet catch and the dipstick, bonnet up, no person visible.
Cut to hands scanning along the tray, pausing on a clean tray.
Close on an empty bottle going straight into a bin rather than back onto the shelf.
Final wide of the tray, upright and dated.

short.hook: The oil check you already do, extended by one glance along the fluid shelf that catches a weeping cap in the week it starts.
short.standalone_note: Establish that the bonnet is up for a routine oil check and that the fluid tray is a few steps away, then show the scan and the empty bottle rule.

close.standard_beat: Hold on the finished shelf, every bottle upright on a clean tray with an opened date on the shoulder, the emergency bag by the door, and the rags in the closed metal can, then state the standard, that every fluid stands upright, wears an opened date, and belongs to a car on this driveway. Replay the bonnet up trigger in one cut.
close.next_zone_teaser: The car shelf is honest now, and the next one is the slowest in the garage, because it holds the gear from the sports you have quietly stopped playing.

shot_list: Bench overhead for the bottle line up and the label reading pass.
Waist height three quarter on the drip tray shelf, matched for before and after.
Macro focus rail for labels, dates, tray rings, and bottle shoulders.
Doorway setup for the jumper cable bag and the one motion lift.
Separation wide covering the sealed fuel can and the water heater.
Metal rag can setup with lid open and lid closed.
Floor level macro for the antifreeze spill clean up.
Bonnet up setup at the car for the Sustain trigger, hands only.
videos.description_hook: The hardest bottles on a car care shelf are the two thirds full ones, because they cost real money and fit nothing you own any more. This is a hands only 6S reset of the automotive zone, including how to date a bottle so the row never builds up again.

videos.title: Sports Gear Reset: Bikes Off the Floor and the Kit From the Sport You Stopped Playing
videos.cold_open_problem: Open on the skis, the golf clubs, the good tent, and the road bike, each still in perfect order under a layer of dust. The problem is that every one of these was expensive, every one still works, and every one stands for a version of your week that has not actually happened in years. Show a hand lifting a dust sheet and setting it straight back down. Name the rule that settles it, that two full seasons of the right weather with no use means you have not paused, you have stopped, and name the one exception, a date you can genuinely finish the sentence with.

segments.covers: Everything goes out onto the driveway in daylight and gets matched to a person who plays that sport now.
beats: Carry every helmet, ball, racket, and pair of cleats out onto the driveway and lay them out in the open where nothing can hide behind anything else.
Match each item to a named person who plays that sport now, and show what fails the match, cleats a size too small and the paddle from that one river trip.
Work the hard shelf. Apply the two seasons rule to the skis and the clubs, with the point that restacking has never settled either of them and will not this time.

Show the exception used honestly, hands writing a real date onto a bin for the one thing that passes, and the rest going to sale or to someone just starting out while the bindings and the groupset are still current.
shots: Tripod at full extension on the driveway, locked and angled down over the lay out, no people in frame.
Close on hands holding a pair of cleats against a larger shoe for size.
Three quarter of the dust sheet coming off the skis in daylight.
Macro on a date being written onto a bin end.
on_screen_text: Match it to a person who plays
Finish the sentence or it goes

short.hook: A dust sheet pulled off a road bike that has not moved in two years, and the bike underneath is perfect.
short.standalone_note: Establish that the gear is expensive and undamaged before the rule lands, then give the two seasons test and the named date exception in full, since that argument is the entire Short.

segments.covers: Bikes go on wall hooks nearest the door, balls get contained, and this season sits at the front of the shelf.
beats: Hang the bikes on wall hooks nearest the door and give the Saturday morning test, that nobody should have to unhook three bikes to get one out.
Get the balls off the floor into a tall bin or a bungee front rack, with the failure it fixes shown first, balls rolling under the parked car.
Set this season's kit at the front of the shelf with the off season behind it, and show the depth difference so front and back read clearly on camera.
Hold on the bare floor beneath the hanging bikes as the result worth aiming at.
shots: Three quarter of a bike being lifted onto a wall hook, hands and frame only.
Low overhead of a ball rolling under a car, then the same ball dropping into a tall bin.
Straight on close of the shelf showing front and back rows.
Wide of bare floor under the hanging bikes.

short.hook: A football rolling under a parked car in a garage, then the tall bin that ends it happening again.
short.standalone_note: Show the floor problem and the container fix inside the Short, and add the bikes nearest the door rule so it carries more than one usable idea.

segments.covers: Gear put away damp or muddy is gear you will not want to touch next season.
beats: Air out and wipe down helmet liners and shin pads, with the liner shown coming out and going back.
Hose the mud off cleats and dry them right through before they go back, with the emphasis on right through rather than surface dry.
Leave the cooler propped open with a rag of baking soda inside, with the reason given, that a cooler closed on a damp summer is how it comes out smelling of one.
shots: Close on a helmet liner being lifted out and set to air.
Three quarter on cleats being hosed on the driveway, water and mud running off.
Close on the cooler propped open with the rag inside.

short.hook: The camping cooler that always smells of last summer, and the fix that is just leaving the lid propped open.
short.standalone_note: Name the cooler and the smell problem immediately, then show the propped lid and the baking soda rag as the whole answer inside the Short.

segments.covers: Helmets have an end of life, and overhead bike hooks have to land in structure rather than plasterboard.
beats: Fall, cut, or crush. Hands tilt a helmet to the light to find the date moulded inside, then retire it, with both retirement conditions given, one real impact even when the shell looks perfect, or a moulded date already passed.
Check the bike hooks, which must be rated and driven into studs rather than drywall anchors, shown with a stud finder and the fixing point marked.
Run the swing test, a car door opening into the space where a hanging wheel would be, then move the hook so it does not.

Cover the two smaller ones, skis stored edge out at head height turned in, and camp stove canisters and lantern fuel lifted out of the sports bins to live with the other flammables, plus the reminder that a cooler is not a ladder.
shots: Macro on the moulded date inside a helmet, hands tilting it to the light.
Close on a stud finder against the wall and a pencil mark going on.
Three quarter of a car door swinging open beneath a bike hook position.
Close on ski edges turned away from head height, and a canister being lifted out of a sports bin.
on_screen_text: A cooler is not a ladder

short.hook: The manufacture date moulded inside a bike helmet, in the place almost nobody has ever looked.
short.standalone_note: Show where the date is and state both retirement conditions, one impact or a date already passed, so a viewer can go and check their own helmet the moment it ends.

segments.covers: One labelled bin per activity, and the label carries a person's name as well as the sport.
beats: Label one bin per activity, then add the name of the person it belongs to, with the point that the name is doing the real work rather than the sport.
Show the test in action, a piece of gear held over each bin in turn and matching none, and draw the conclusion plainly, that it has no owner in this house and does not stay in it.
Set the finished shelf so the bin carrying a child's name sits where that child can lift it down unaided, which is what turns the name on the label into something that holds.
shots: Close on a label being written with a sport and a name.
Three quarter of a stray item being held over each bin in turn and matching none.
Wide of the finished shelf with the named bins at the heights their owners can reach.

short.hook: A piece of sports kit held over every bin on a garage shelf in turn, and it matches none of them.
short.standalone_note: Establish that each bin carries a sport and a person's name before the matching test runs, since the whole point is the name rather than the category.

segments.covers: The shelf turns twice a year on weather, not on a date.
beats: Run the swap, front and back of the shelf trading places the first weekend you turn the heating on, and again the first weekend you leave the windows open all day.
Give the reason the trigger is weather rather than a calendar month, that the house already tells you and nobody has to remember.
Show the swap done quickly so it reads as a short job rather than a project.
shots: Close on a thermostat being turned up, hands only.
Time condensed three quarter of front and back rows trading places.
Close on a window being opened wide, matched to the thermostat shot.
Final straight on of the shelf with the new season at the front.

short.hook: A thermostat going up for the first time in autumn, used as the cue to turn a whole garage shelf around.
short.standalone_note: Pair the thermostat and the open window as the two triggers and show one complete swap, so the rhythm reads without the parent video.

close.standard_beat: Hold on bikes hanging over bare floor, one labelled bin per activity carrying a sport and a name, and this season's kit at the front, then state the standard. Replay the two triggers back to back, the heating going on and the windows going open, so the swap reads as something the house tells you to do.
close.next_zone_teaser: The play gear is settled, and the next zone holds the one shelf in the garage that has to be latched, because what is on it is meant to kill something.

shot_list: Tripod at full extension on the driveway, angled down, for the full gear lay out in daylight.
Three quarter on the bike wall covering hooks and the door in one frame.
Straight on locked shelf frame, matched for front and back row swaps.
Macro focus rail for helmet dates, labels, and moulded markings.
Driveway hose setup for cleats, with drainage clear of the tripod feet.
Car door swing setup beneath the hook position.
Stud finder and fixing setup at hook height.
Thermostat and window setups indoors for the Sustain triggers.
videos.description_hook: Skis, golf clubs, a good tent, a road bike. All expensive, all still working, none used in years, and that is why this is the slowest shelf in the garage. This is a hands only 6S reset of the sports zone, with a rule that actually settles it.

videos.title: Garden Tool Zone Reset: Handles Off the Floor and the Latched Chemical Shelf
videos.cold_open_problem: Open on the garden chemical shelf, a bag of feed with the top rolled over, a jug of concentrate that moved here from your last house, and something in an unlabelled sprayer that you are fairly confident is weed killer. The problem is that the unlabelled one is the easy call, because you cannot safely use what you cannot name, and the rest are being stored above head height for a growing season nobody has committed to. Show a hand picking up the sprayer, turning it all the way round, and finding nothing written anywhere on it.

segments.covers: Broken yard tools and hopeful spares leave, and the chemical shelf gets its own honest count.
beats: Work the obvious failures first, the rake with three tines left, the hose with the split you have meant to patch for two summers, and the cracked nursery pots kept for seedlings you never started.
Count the spades honestly, laid side by side on the slab, and make the point that a garage that holds four of them digs with one.
Make the chemical call. Start with the unlabelled sprayer, which goes to hazardous waste this month without being opened again, and give the reason that makes it the easy decision.

Apply one season of intent to the rest, with the stake named plainly, that anything you will not genuinely use before the next growing season ends is a poison being stored above your children's heads for nothing. Show the leaving containers going out capped and upright with destinations named, a hazardous waste day or a neighbour in its own labelled container, never a drain, a gutter, or the ground behind the shed.
shots: Overhead of four spades laid side by side on the slab.
Macro on a rake missing tines and on the split in the hose.
Close on the unlabelled sprayer being turned in gloved hands, nothing written on any face.
Three quarter of the hazardous waste crate being loaded, each container upright and capped.
on_screen_text: If you cannot name it, it goes

short.hook: An unlabelled sprayer turned all the way around with nothing written on it anywhere, and nobody in the house remembers what is inside.
short.standalone_note: Establish that this came off a garden chemical shelf and that its contents are unknown, then give the disposal route by name so the Short ends with an action the viewer can take.

segments.covers: Long handles hang head up on a rail, the hose lives on a reel beside the door it goes out of, and chemicals get their own shelf with a lip.
beats: Hang every long handle head up on the rail, with the failure it fixes shown first, a fork standing loose in a corner.
Mount the hose on a reel beside the door it actually goes out of, with the reason given, that the door matters more than wherever there happened to be free wall.
Give fertiliser, weed killer, and seed one shelf with a lip on it, placed well away from the cooler and anything else that touches food or skin.
Hold the whole aisle from standing height with nothing leaning in any corner.
shots: Three quarter of long handles going onto the rail one after another.
Close on a fork standing loose in a corner, then the corner empty.
Close on the hose reel mounted beside the door, hose winding on.
Straight on of the lipped chemical shelf with the cooler visibly elsewhere in the frame.
on_screen_text: Handles head up on the rail
Hose by the door it uses

short.hook: A garden fork standing loose in a garage corner, tines up, and the several ways that ends badly.
short.standalone_note: Show the corner and the rail inside the same Short so the fix is visible, and state the head up rule explicitly rather than implying it.

segments.covers: Cleaning garden tools is maintenance, and the spreader hopper is the one everybody misses.
beats: Scrape caked soil off the spade and hoe blades and wipe them with an oily rag, showing how much comes off a blade that looked fine.
Run a file along the spade edge so it bites next time, framed as the difference between a tool that works and one you fight.
Empty and rinse the spreader hopper, with the reason given, that leftover fertiliser eats the metal from the inside out over a winter.
shots: Macro on caked soil being scraped off a spade blade.
Close travelling shot of a file running along the spade edge.
Overhead into the spreader hopper showing caked residue, then rinsed clean.

short.hook: Inside a fertiliser spreader that was put away with the hopper still loaded, and what one winter did to the metal.
short.standalone_note: Name the spreader and what was left in it, then show the rinse, since the lesson here is a habit at the end of a job rather than a repair.

segments.covers: This is the latched shelf, and every cutting end points away from the aisle you walk down.
beats: Poison, choke, or strangle, first. Chemicals stay in their original labelled containers on a latched shelf above child and pet height, never decanted, shown as a decant being refused and a latch being fitted.
Cover slug pellets and granular feed specifically as things a dog can reach and will eat, and get them behind the latch.
Fall, cut, or crush. Hedge shears go up with guards fitted and string trimmers with cutting ends pointing away from the aisle.
Burn or fire. Separate the mower's petrol can from the fertiliser, with the reason given, that fertiliser is an oxidiser and should never sit next to fuel, and the can sealed for the shot.
shots: Three quarter of the chemical shelf above head height with a latch being fitted.
Close on a drink bottle being set beside a concentrate jug, then taken away.
Close on hedge shear guards going on and trimmer heads turned away from the aisle.
Wide showing the sealed petrol can and the fertiliser bag now well apart.

short.hook: A drink bottle set down beside a jug of weed killer concentrate, held just long enough for the reason it never happens to land.
short.standalone_note: State the never decant rule and the latched shelf inside the same Short, and end on the latch closing so it is a fix rather than a warning.

segments.covers: A taped strip behind every handle and one sign on the chemical shelf make both halves of this zone self reporting.
beats: Paint or tape a strip on the wall behind each long handle, then lift a tool off and hold on the bare strip, with the point that a bare strip is a question you answer before you close the door.
Put one sign on the chemical shelf saying garden chemicals only and nothing else, then show something plausible being turned away from that shelf because of it.
Note that the rail and the shelf each get their own visual control, a strip for one and a sign for the other, and see Chapter 14, visual controls.
shots: Close on tape being laid as a strip behind a handle position.
Static on one bare strip in a rail of filled ones.
Close on the chemical shelf sign going up, then a non chemical item being carried away from it.
on_screen_text: A bare strip is a question

short.hook: One bare taped strip in a rail of hanging garden tools, and the question that gap asks before you close the garage door.
short.standalone_note: Show a tool being lifted off its strip so the viewer sees what the strip means, then state the rule in one line so nothing depends on the parent video.

segments.covers: The mower cooling down is the window where the blades get cleaned and hung.
beats: Run the trigger. The mower has to cool before it goes away anyway, and that wait is when the spade gets scraped, wiped, and hung back on its strip.
Show the alternative honestly, a spade found rusted solid the following spring, so the cost of skipping the cooling window is visible rather than asserted.
Close the loop on the strips, hands checking the rail for bare ones before the garage door comes down.
Point to Chapter 21, the hazard hunt, for repeating the chemical shelf pass properly.
shots: Close on a warm mower deck with a spade set down beside it to be worked on.
Macro on a rusted solid spade edge as the counter example.
Three quarter of the spade going back onto its taped strip.
Final wide down the aisle, nothing leaning, every strip filled.
on_screen_text: Clean it while the mower cools

short.hook: The wait you already have while a mower cools down, turned into the reason your spade is not rusted solid next spring.
short.standalone_note: Name the cooling window as the trigger at the top and show both outcomes inside the Short, the cleaned blade and the rusted one, so the payoff is on screen.

close.standard_beat: Hold down the aisle with every long tool hanging head up on its taped strip, nothing leaning in any corner, the hose on its reel by the door, and the latched chemical shelf above head height with its one sign. State the standard, then replay the mower cooling trigger in one cut.
close.next_zone_teaser: The floor and the walls are done, which leaves the part of the garage nobody has looked at in years, the bins overhead.

shot_list: Aisle length wide from standing height, matched before and after.
Rail height three quarter for handles going up and for the bare strip.
Overhead on the slab for the spade count and the tool lay out.
Macro focus rail for blade scraping, filing, hopper residue, and label text.
Above head height setup on the chemical shelf with the latch fit in frame.
Door side setup for the hose reel mount.
Separation wide covering the sealed petrol can and the fertiliser.
Mower cool down setup with room for the spade to be worked beside it.
videos.description_hook: Most garden shelves hold four spades and dig with one, and at least one sprayer nobody can identify. This is a hands only 6S reset of the lawn and garden zone, including the latched chemical shelf and how to get rid of what is on it safely.

videos.title: Overhead Garage Storage Reset: Every Bin Down, Judged, and Labelled
videos.cold_open_problem: Open low, looking up at the overhead racks, then cut to the one box up there that moved in with you and has not been opened since. The problem is that opening it costs an afternoon and might cost more than that, so it has been renewing its own lease for years. Show a hand reaching up, touching the lid, and coming back down without it. Name what settles it, that the box comes down and gets opened on the floor with a rubbish sack, a donation box, and one empty container beside it, and that whatever you keep has to fit that one container and carry a living person's name.

segments.covers: Nothing gets judged from a ladder, so every bin comes down to the floor first.
beats: State the working rule before anything moves, that nobody sorts honestly from the third step of a ladder with one arm through a lid, then show the bins coming down and being set out on the slab.
Start with the two that always exist, the holiday bin that has not come down in three Decembers and the box marked misc.
Open the never opened box with the three things beside it, a rubbish sack, a donation box, and one empty container, and work it all the way through.

Show the wrong move refused, hands starting to tape the box shut to send it back up, then setting the tape down, with the reason given, that a box which goes back unopened has bought itself another five years and taught the rack that this is allowed.
shots: Low wide looking up at the loaded rack, then the same frame empty.
Three quarter of bins being handed down and set out in rows on the slab.
Overhead of the never opened box being cut open, with sack, donation box, and empty container in frame.
Close on hands starting to tape a lid shut, then setting the tape down.
on_screen_text: Do not send it back sealed

short.hook: A box that moved house with you and has never once been opened, cut open on a garage floor with a sack and a donation box already waiting beside it.
short.standalone_note: Establish that it came off an overhead rack and has never been opened, then give the one container and living owner rule so the Short hands over a usable method.

segments.covers: Weight goes low, bulk goes high, and bins are grouped by the time of year they come down.
beats: Put the heavy bins on the lowest rack and the light bulky things, folding chairs and the artificial tree, highest, with the lift you are designing for made explicit.
Group by the time of year they come down rather than by category, so one December trip up the ladder brings the lights, the tree, and the wrapping bin down together.
Show the payoff as one trip, hands and bins only, with the December group coming down together instead of a separate climb for the lights, one for the tree, and one for the wrapping bin.
shots: Three quarter of the rack loading sequence, heavy low and bulky high.
Close on the December group being set together on one bay.
Time condensed of the single trip retrieval, hands only on the bins.
on_screen_text: Grouped by when it comes down

short.hook: One trip up a ladder that brings the lights, the tree, and the wrapping bin down together.
short.standalone_note: Explain that the bins were grouped by the time of year they come down rather than by category, otherwise the single trip reads as luck instead of design.

segments.covers: Wiping the lids is inspection, and so is looking at the ceiling while you are up there.
beats: Wipe the lids and read the dust, with the point made that the depth of dust on an overhead lid is a rough record of how long it has been since anything came out of that bin.
Turn the attention upward. While you are up there, check the rack underside and the ceiling above it for the brown stain that means the roof is letting water in.
Show what to do with a stain if you find one, outlined and dated so you can tell later whether it is growing.
shots: Macro raking light shot of dust depth on a lid, then a wiped stripe through it.
Upward close on the ceiling above the rack, panning slowly.
Close on a brown stain being outlined in pencil with a date beside it.
on_screen_text: Look up while you are up there

short.hook: A finger stripe drawn through the dust on an overhead storage lid, and what that depth actually tells you.
short.standalone_note: Say that this is an overhead garage bin and that nothing has come out of it, then add the ceiling stain check so the Short teaches the inspection idea rather than just the wipe.

segments.covers: What goes overhead is limited by what you can get down safely, and the rack itself has to land in structure.
beats: Fall. Set the two limits before anything goes back up, that nothing goes overhead you cannot bring down one handed on a stable ladder with the other hand on the stile, and nothing you might need in the dark or in a hurry.
Show the fall risk directly, a ladder rocking on a sloped slab, then the corrected version, ladder levelled and the bin handled so a hand stays free.
Check the rack bolts land in joists rather than only in plasterboard, shown with the fixing points found and marked.
Fall, cut, or crush. Check that loaded bins sit fully inside the rails rather than overhanging the parking bay, shot from below where a car door opens.
shots: Low close on a ladder foot rocking on a sloped slab, then levelled.
Three quarter of a bin being brought down with a hand staying on the stile.
Macro on a fixing point being marked at a joist.
Low angle from the parking bay looking up at bins overhanging the rails, then fully inside them.
on_screen_text: If you cannot get it down, it does not go up

short.hook: Looking straight up from the spot where a car door opens, at storage bins hanging out over the edge of the rack.
short.standalone_note: Frame the shot from the parking position and say what is above it, then state the rule about bins sitting fully inside the rails and show the corrected rack.

segments.covers: Big labels, a last opened date, and a map by the light switch mean nobody climbs a ladder to find out.
beats: Put a large label on every bin, sized to be read standing on the slab, and test it by shooting from floor level.
Add the month and year it was last opened to the end of each bin, and say what that date will be used for later.
Tape a small map beside the light switch saying which bay holds what, with the point stated plainly, that nobody climbs a ladder simply to find out.
Point to Chapter 24, the checklist, schedule, and name.
shots: Close on a large label being written and applied to a bin end.
Floor level static reading the labels on the loaded rack, proving legibility.
Close on the map going up beside the light switch, hands smoothing the tape.

short.hook: The label test, stand on the garage floor and try to read your own overhead bins from there.
short.standalone_note: Show the failing small label first and the large one after, both shot from floor level, so the Short proves the point on camera instead of asserting it.

segments.covers: The date gets rewritten the moment a bin is open, and stale dates trigger the next clear out.
beats: Run the trigger. The moment a bin is on the floor with its lid off, the new month and year goes on the end before it goes back up.
Show how the dates get used, a bin whose newest date is two Decembers old coming down and being opened at the next clear out rather than lifted straight back.
Close on the rack reading as a set of dates, with the point that the rack now tells you what to look at next without anyone remembering.
shots: Close on a lid off on the floor and a marker updating the date on the end.
Floor level pan across the rack with the dates legible.
Close on one stale date being spotted and that bin being brought down.
on_screen_text: You do not finish 6S. You keep it.

short.hook: A storage bin lid coming off, and a marker going straight to the end of the bin before anything is taken out.
short.standalone_note: Explain that the date is what stops a bin renewing its own lease overhead, then show a stale dated bin being pulled down so the Short shows the date being used.

close.standard_beat: Hold from floor level on the finished rack, every bin labelled in letters readable from the slab, a last opened month and year on each end, heaviest bins lowest, nothing overhanging the parking bay, and the map taped beside the light switch. State the standard, then replay the lid off date trigger in one cut.
close.next_zone_teaser: That closes the garage, seven zones from the bench to the rack, and the room that used to take everything the house evicted now gives every arrival a verdict the same day.

shot_list: Low floor level wide of the full rack, matched before and after, doubling as the label legibility test.
Tripod at full extension for bins coming down and going up, camera never on the ladder, hands only.
Slab lay out overhead for the bins set out in rows.
Macro focus rail for dust depth, dates, labels, and fixing marks.
Upward setup on the ceiling and rack underside with the clamped LED.
Parking bay low angle for the overhang check.
Light switch setup for the map.
Ladder foot close on the sloped section of slab.
videos.description_hook: There is at least one box on your overhead rack that moved in with you and has never been opened, and it has renewed its own lease every year since. This is a hands only 6S reset of bulk and overhead storage, including the labelling that stops it happening again.

rooms.room_note: Shoot the whole room in one continuous daylight block, ideally an overcast morning through the shop window or open roller door, so the bench top does not blow out and blade steel does not flare. No lighting kit, no second pair of hands. Two core camera positions carry most of it: a tripod with a horizontal arm set over the bench centre for drawer dumps and tray sorts, and a three quarter position at shoulder height on the vise side for hands at work. Reposition that second tripod for the door board, the charger shelf, the rack, the sink, and the floor level angles rather than adding gear. Framing rule for the whole series: nothing above the wrists ever appears, so set the camera low or tight enough that forearms leave frame at the edge, and never stage a shot that needs one person to carry something while another operates the camera. If hands must travel, lock the camera off and let the hands pass through the frame. Practical safety on set: film every cutting and finishing sequence dry, tools unplugged and batteries out, and lay saw sound in afterwards. The finishing zone gets no hot lights, and the solvent cabinet stays open only as long as a shot needs, with the door opened for ventilation between takes. Oil finish rags used as props go into the lidded metal can the moment the shot ends, on camera when it serves the segment. Sawdust ruins both the lens and the audio, so vacuum before each setup rather than between takes, and put a wind sock on the mic because the extractor and the shop fan otherwise sit under every take.

videos.title: Workshop PPE Station: Glasses at the Door, Extinguisher Check, Visitor Set
videos.cold_open_problem: Open tight on the doorway of the shop: one scratched pair of glasses hanging on a nail, an empty unmarked hook beside it, and beyond them the bench with an unplugged saw sitting on it. Establish that the awkward decision in this zone is not your own gear at all, it is what happens when a brother in law or a fourteen year old wanders in and wants to help. Show the current answer, which is no answer, an unlabeled hook and a spare pair nobody has claimed. Make the cost plain: that decision currently gets made in the moment, differently every time, by someone holding something sharp.

segments.covers: Scratched and expired protective gear is worse than none here, because it is the reason people stop wearing gear at all.
beats: Every piece of protective gear in the shop comes out onto a clean towel on the bench, glasses, muffs, dust masks, gloves, and the full contents of the first aid kit.

A hazed pair held into window light, with the chain that makes it dangerous spelled out: scratched lenses mean you lift them off to see the cut line, and that is the moment the chip flies. Verdict is the bin.
The same verdict applied down the towel, perished gloves, respirator cartridges past their printed date, and a first aid kit quietly raided for household plasters with no burn dressing left in it.
The distinction that governs this whole pass, that this gear gets replaced rather than rearranged, because rearranging expired protection only hides it better.
shots: Overhead of the towel filling with gear, one item at a time entering frame from the side.
Macro on a scratched lens tilted into window light until the haze reads.
Close on a thumb finding the printed date on a respirator cartridge.
Close on the first aid kit lid opening to reveal three loose plasters and no burn dressing.

short.hook: A hand tilts a hazed safety lens into the window light until you cannot see through it, then drops it straight in the bin.
short.standalone_note: Name the room and the zone in the first few seconds and say these are workshop safety glasses off the door hook, or nobody knows whose lens this is or why it matters.

segments.covers: The gear hangs on the path you already walk, at the door you come in through, not on the far wall past the bench.
beats: The current arrangement shown honestly in one frame, the gear rack on the far wall past the bench and the bare door frame in the foreground, with the walk between them being exactly the walk people skip.
Hooks going into the door frame stud, glasses and hearing protection paired on one hook so a set never gets split.
Sets sized and labeled to the actual people who work in this shop rather than one generic set for whoever shows up.
A silhouette traced behind each item, and what the silhouette buys, a missing pair reading at a glance instead of after a search.
shots: Locked off wide down the entry path, far wall rack at the end of it, bare door frame in the foreground.
Close on a hand driving a hook screw into the door frame stud.
Overhead of a pencil tracing around a pair of muffs laid flat on the board.
Wide of the finished board with every silhouette filled but one.

short.hook: A pencil traces the outline of a pair of ear muffs on a board, the muffs lift away, and the empty shape reads as missing.
short.standalone_note: Establish that this is a workshop door board with one labeled set per person, or the tracing looks decorative rather than functional.

segments.covers: How you clean this gear is what keeps it wearable, and the shop rag is the thing destroying it.
beats: The habitual wrong move shown first, a dusty shop rag dragged across a lens, identified as where the scratches actually come from.
Lenses washed in soap and water at the shop sink and left to air dry, with the clarity difference held against the window.
Sweat and sawdust wiped off the earmuff cushions, and what a stiff crusted cushion does, which is stop sealing while still sitting on your head, so the protection quietly stops working.
shots: Macro on a dusty rag dragging across a lens with grit visible in the weave.
Close on hands lathering lenses under a running tap.
Macro on a cloth wiping a compressed earmuff cushion, dust lifting away.
Two lenses held side by side against the window, one washed and one not.
on_screen_text: Soap and water, not the shop rag

short.hook: Two safety lenses fill the frame against a bright window, one washed and one wiped on a shop rag, and the difference lands before a word is said.
