short.standalone_note: Say plainly that this rag lives in a sawdust shop, so the viewer understands why it is loaded with grit rather than just dirty.

segments.covers: Two physical checks this zone exists to guarantee, the extinguisher and the power cutoff.
beats: The extinguisher lifted off its bracket, weight felt, gauge read on camera, with the needle needing to sit inside the green band.
The floor in front of the bracket shown as it actually is, a stack of timber leaning against the wall, then cleared, framed as the burn or fire question.

A hand flat on the shop power cutoff, then the real test run, the same reach repeated with eyes shut and hands only, because sawdust in your eyes and the lights off is the condition you will actually need it in.
A boundary taped on the floor in front of the bracket so the timber has a visible edge to stop at rather than creeping back over the next month.
shots: Close on hands lifting the extinguisher clear of its bracket.
Macro on the pressure gauge needle sitting in the green band.
Three quarter of hands sliding leaning timber away from the wall below the bracket.
Close on a hand travelling the wall and landing on the cutoff switch, then the same travel repeated slower.
Overhead of tape being pressed onto the concrete to mark the clear floor boundary.

short.hook: A hand travels along a workshop wall in near darkness, searching, and lands flat on the power cutoff.
short.standalone_note: State that this is the shop power cutoff and that blind reach is the standard, since out of context the gesture just reads as fumbling.

segments.covers: Two dates written where you will actually read them, plus one placement trick that makes the glasses unskippable.
beats: Masking tape torn, an inspection date written on it, and pressed onto the extinguisher bracket, then the same again on the first aid kit lid, because the date belongs on the thing rather than in a list somewhere else.
The safety glasses hung over the plug of the saw, with the consequence demonstrated, no powering up without handling the glasses first.
Both dates read from standing height without lifting or opening anything, which is the actual test of whether a date is written where it will be read. Point to Chapter 24, the checklist.
shots: Macro on a marker writing a date onto masking tape.
Close on the tape being pressed onto the extinguisher bracket.
Three quarter of a hand reaching for the saw plug and having to lift the glasses off it first.
Wide of the finished board and extinguisher with both dates legible in frame.

short.hook: A hand reaches for a saw plug and finds a pair of safety glasses hanging on it, blocking the grab.
short.standalone_note: Explain in the first beat that the glasses were deliberately hung on the plug of the saw, otherwise it reads as clutter rather than a designed obstacle.

segments.covers: The trigger that refills the board, tied to switching off the shop light, and the visitor rule made permanent.
beats: The failure path first, glasses set down on the bench and slid into a jacket pocket, then the jacket lifted off its hook and out of frame with them still in it.
The trigger in its place, gear going back onto its silhouettes as the hand reaches the shop light switch, so whoever opens the door next finds a full board.

The visitor rule from the cold open closed out physically, the spare set hung on a hook marked for visitors and the rule written on a card pinned beside it, decided in advance rather than while holding a running grinder.
The reason this holds without willpower, that it is one rule on a wall, and the reminder that you do not finish 6S, you keep it.
shots: Close on glasses going into a jacket pocket, then the jacket lifting off its hook and leaving frame.
Three quarter of hands hanging glasses onto their silhouette.
Close on a hand at the light switch with the full board visible behind it.
Macro on a marker writing the visitor rule onto a card pinned by the spare hook.

short.hook: Safety glasses go into a jacket pocket, the jacket lifts off its hook and leaves, and the next hand through the door lands on an empty board.
short.standalone_note: Set up that this is a shared workshop door board meant to be full for whoever arrives next, which is the entire reason the pocket is a failure.

close.standard_beat: Hold a slow wide of the finished board at the door, one labeled set per user plus the marked visitor set, silhouettes filled, dated extinguisher and dated first aid kit in the same frame, and state the standard as it now stands. Then show the trigger once in real motion, glasses coming off and going straight onto their hook rather than into a pocket or a drawer.
close.next_zone_teaser: With the glasses findable and the gauge in the green, the next zone is the surface everything else in this room happens on, the main workbench, and the half assembled project that has been sitting on it since spring.

shot_list: Overhead bench setup for the gear laid out on a towel.
Macro setup with window backlight for lenses, gauges, and printed dates.
Three quarter at the shop door covering the hook board and hook fitting.
Locked off wide down the entry path from the door toward the far wall rack.
Close on the extinguisher bracket and the floor space in front of it.
Wall travel shot ending on the power cutoff, shot twice at different speeds.
Macro marker and masking tape writing setup on the bench.
Close on the saw plug with glasses hanging over it.
Light switch shot with the finished board in the background.
videos.description_hook: Start the workshop here, at its smallest zone, because everything else in the room involves a blade, a solvent, or a cloud of dust. Glasses at the door, muffs beside them, gauge in the green, and one visitor rule you decide before you need it.

videos.title: Workshop Bench Reset: Clear the Top, Trace the Tools, Keep It Bare
videos.cold_open_problem: Open on the half assembled something occupying the best surface in the shop, dust settled evenly across the top of it, its hardware waiting in a jar alongside. Establish how long it has sat there by running a finger through the dust on a joint. Name the real reason it has not moved, which is that the next step is one you are not sure how to do, so the bench pays for that hesitation every single session. Set the stakes in the room's own terms: this is the only surface where a project actually gets built, and while that thing sits there you do not have one.

segments.covers: Every half finished project on this bench gets a verdict, and the test is a spoken next action plus a date.
beats: The bench top and the shelf beneath it cleared completely onto a sheet on the floor, with the reason stated, that partial clearing is how the same pile survives every reset.
The call introduced as a test rather than a mood: name the next physical action and name a date this month, both in one breath, or the project is finished.

The failed verdict carried out in full on camera, the assembly coming apart, hardware back to the fastener drawers, stock back onto the rack, with the point made that keeping it assembled was never keeping the project alive, only keeping the surface unusable.
The fast throwaways run separately and quickly, snapped blades, glue bottles gone solid, brackets you cannot identify, all leaving now.
The holding decision for anything that genuinely earns its way back, which is a date written onto it in marker rather than a good intention.
shots: Overhead of the bench top emptying, objects leaving frame in sequence.
Three quarter of hands lifting a dusty half built assembly clear of the bench.
Close on a screwdriver backing hardware out of the assembly into a tray.
Macro on a glue bottle being squeezed with no give at all.
Overhead of the bare bench top and the empty shelf beneath.
on_screen_text: Cannot name both, it is finished

short.hook: A dusty half built project gets lifted off a workbench and immediately taken apart on camera, screw by screw.
short.standalone_note: Give the one breath rule up front, next physical action and a date this month, or the disassembly reads as giving up rather than deciding.

segments.covers: Reach decides placement at this bench, and the tools your hand wants mid cut live inside the arc you can cover from the vise.
beats: The arc marked in chalk from the standing position at the vise, covering only what a hand reaches without stepping, so the rule is drawn rather than argued.
The mid cut tools placed inside that arc, marking knife, combination square, and block plane, with the reason those three and nothing else.
Everything used once a project moved to the wall behind, sorted as two piles rather than a fine ranking.
Traced silhouettes introduced as the mechanism that makes a missing chisel show up before you finish vacuuming.
A run of bench in front of the vise cleared long enough to lay a board across, proved by laying a board across it.
shots: Overhead of a hand sweeping an arc from the vise position with chalk marking the reach limit.
Close on the marking knife, square, and block plane landing inside the chalk arc.
Three quarter of tools going up onto the wall rack behind the bench.
Wide of a board laid across the cleared run in front of the vise.
on_screen_text: Mid cut tools inside the arc
Once a project goes on the wall

short.hook: A hand sweeps a chalk arc across a workbench from the vise, and everything left outside the line gets picked up and moved.
short.standalone_note: Establish that the arc is the reach you have while a workpiece is clamped in the vise, since the chalk line means nothing without that condition.

segments.covers: Clean this bench to inspect it, not to impress, and the method matters more than the effort.
beats: The bench top vacuumed in strips and the nozzle taken down into the dog holes, with the reason given plainly, that a broom launches the finest sawdust back into the air where it settles on wet finish and into your lungs.
Dried glue drips scraped off with a chisel laid flat, and why a proud glue bead matters, because it telegraphs straight into the next workpiece clamped over it.
The vise screw wiped clean and given a drop of oil, then the handle turned so the change is both audible and visible.
What the cleaning exposed named as the actual purpose of the pass, cracks, scoring, and wear along the front edge that dust was hiding.
shots: Overhead of a vacuum nozzle travelling the bench top in strips.
Macro of the nozzle entering a dog hole and the dust disappearing.
Macro of a chisel laid flat lifting a glue drip in one curl.
Close on an oil drop landing on the vise screw, then the handle turning.

short.hook: A chisel laid flat pops a hardened glue drip off a bench top in one clean curl, macro and slow.
short.standalone_note: Say why the drip matters, that it prints itself into the next workpiece clamped over it, or this is a satisfying scrape with no lesson attached.

segments.covers: Two failures this bench produces on its own, a vise that lets go and an edge lying up in an open tray.
beats: A test piece clamped and then twisted by hand, with jaws worn smooth releasing a workpiece mid cut named as the fall, cut, or crush question here.
The verdict on worn jaws given as fresh faces or a rebuild, not a mental note to be careful with an unreliable vise.
The lamp cord moved off the run of bench a handsaw crosses, with the conflict made obvious by laying the saw along its cut path first.
The tray hazard taken head on, a hand reaching across the bench without looking and stopping above a chisel lying edge up, then the corrected storage with edges down or sheathed.
The damp concrete underfoot shown as the reason cord routing and standing position matter at this bench, framed as the water and electricity question.
shots: Close on hands twisting a test piece in the vise jaws with movement visible.
Macro on jaw faces worn smooth and shiny.
Overhead of a lamp cord lying across the bench with a handsaw laid along its cut path.
Close on a hand reaching across an open tray and stopping a finger's width above an upturned chisel edge.
Low angle on a cord running off the bench down onto bare concrete.
on_screen_text: Jaws that slip let go mid cut
Nothing edge up in a tray

short.hook: A hand reaches across a workbench without looking and stops a finger's width above a chisel lying edge up in an open tray.
short.standalone_note: Frame it as the fall, cut, or crush question and show the corrected tray in the same clip, so the Short delivers a fix rather than just a scare.

segments.covers: Two visual controls make the right state obvious at this bench, traced outlines and one photo of the cleared top.
beats: Every chisel and square traced onto the tool wall in permanent marker, so a gap reads as a missing tool rather than as empty space.

One photo taken of the fully cleared bench and taped at eye level where you actually stand, with the point stated directly, that the photo is what bare means here so bare stops being a matter of opinion.
The connection made to Chapter 25, the ideal state photo, and to the line that a standard is the best way you know today, written down.
The standard written in plain words on a card beside the photo, one project on the bench at a time, and the bench ending every session bare except the vise and the lamp.
shots: Macro on a marker tracing the outline of a chisel on the tool wall.
Close on a chisel lifting away to leave a filled outline and an empty one side by side.
Overhead of a phone photographing the cleared bench, hands only on the phone.
Close on the printed photo being taped at eye level above the bench.
on_screen_text: This photo is what bare means

short.hook: A printed photo of an empty workbench gets taped to the wall directly above the actual bench, and both end up in the same frame.
short.standalone_note: Explain that the photo settles what finished looks like at this bench, otherwise taping up a picture of your own bench looks strange.

segments.covers: The clear down is the last part of the session, and it is bolted to the task lamp switch.
beats: The trigger in real motion, a hand rising to the task lamp switch over a bench that is already clear, because the clear down happens before the light goes out.
Why this trigger and not a time of day, which is that once the safety glasses come off you are finished and you know it, so the clear down has to land earlier than that.
The failure version for contrast, the same lamp going off over a loaded bench, and the state that leaves you to inherit next session.
The loop closed on the standard, one project on the bench at a time, held by a designed habit rather than by willpower.
shots: Three quarter of a hand rising to the lamp switch with a bare bench beneath it.
Overhead of the last few items leaving the bench in one sweep into the project tray.
Close on the same lamp switch with a cluttered bench beneath, lit then dark.
Wide of the finished bench in low light, vise and lamp only.
on_screen_text: Clear down before the light goes out

short.hook: A hand reaches for a task lamp switch above a cluttered workbench, stops, and pulls back to clear the last items off first.
short.standalone_note: State the trigger explicitly, that the bench must be clear before the lamp goes off, since the hesitation carries no meaning on its own.

close.standard_beat: Hold a wide of the bench in its finished state, bare except the vise and the task lamp, one project tray holding the current job's parts, every chisel and square sitting on its traced outline, dog holes empty and nothing underneath. Restate the standard as one project on the bench at a time, then show the trigger once, the hand reaching for the lamp switch over an already clear bench.
close.next_zone_teaser: The tools that just went back on the wall are the hand tools. Next is the zone where the guards, the cords, and the batteries live, and the expensive tool inside it that has not cut anything in two years.

shot_list: Overhead bench setup for clearing, sorting, vacuuming, and tracing.
Three quarter at the vise side for clamping, reaching, and lamp switch work.
Macro setup for glue drips, jaw faces, vise screw oil, and marker tracing.
Low angle at floor level for cords running down onto concrete.
Chalk arc reach sequence framed directly overhead.
Board laid across the cleared bench run to prove the clearance.
Phone photographing the cleared bench, hands only on the phone.
Tool wall shot covering filled and empty outlines together.
Low light finish shot of the bare bench with lamp and vise.
videos.description_hook: The workbench is the only surface in the shop where a project actually gets built, which is why the half finished one sitting on it costs you every session. Here is the test that settles it, plus the outlines and the one photo that keep the top bare.

videos.title: Power Tool Storage: Guard Tests, Cord Tests, and the Tool You Never Use
videos.cold_open_problem: Open on the case in this zone that cost real money and has not cut anything in two years, dust lying flat across the lid, latches stiff when a thumb works them. Open it and show the battery inside sitting at nothing. Name why it is still here, which is that selling it would mean admitting the purchase was wrong, so instead it quietly loses value on a shelf while the packs in it age out. Set the wider stakes of the zone in the same breath: every object on these shelves has a guard, a cord, or a battery, and each of those is a way this zone can hurt you.

segments.covers: Duplicates and dead packs judged honestly, with the expensive tool call as the centrepiece.
beats: The duplicates lined up in matched pairs on the bench, the second drill and the sander you replaced but kept, so the doubling is visible rather than theoretical.
Questionable battery packs put on a tester, with the standard set plainly, that a pack which will not hold a charge through one job is recycling, not a spare.
Every cord repaired with electrical tape cut out of the zone, with the tape unwound on camera to show the damage underneath.
The expensive tool call run on camera against its two questions, work done in the last twenty four months, and whether you would happily hire one for a day if the job came up tomorrow.

The reframe that makes the verdict stick, that a tool losing value on your shelf is a decision you are storing rather than an asset you are holding, and that selling now is what keeps its packs worth having.
shots: Overhead of two drills and two sanders laid out in matched pairs on the bench.
Close on a battery pack clicking into a tester with the charge reading visible.
Macro on electrical tape being unwound from a cord to show the split sheath beneath.
Three quarter of the dusty tool case being lifted out of the zone and set down by the door.
on_screen_text: Taped cord is not a tool

short.hook: Two nearly identical cordless drills get set side by side on a bench, and one of them is picked up and carried out of frame.
short.standalone_note: Give both questions in full, twenty four months of work and whether you would hire one instead, since the pickup means nothing without the test attached.

segments.covers: A tool is stored with the parts that make it usable, or it is not really stored at all.
beats: One complete home built on camera, the circular saw with its rip fence and its blade wrench joined to the tool itself instead of floating in a drawer.
The same done for the router, collet spanners and the bits it actually takes, with the failure this prevents named, that hunting for a collet spanner is how a router ends up used without one.
The attachment method shown up close, a clip, a small pouch, or a magnet on the tool body, so the accessory travels with the tool rather than back to a drawer.
Hooks chosen and set for the weight they actually carry, one labeled home per tool, with the saw resting on its shoe rather than hanging by its cord.
shots: Overhead of a circular saw with its rip fence and blade wrench laid beside it, then joined to it.
Macro on a blade wrench clipping into its holder on the saw body.
Close on router collet spanners going into a pouch that hangs with the router.
Three quarter of tools landing on labeled hooks along the wall, saw resting on its shoe.

short.hook: A blade wrench gets clipped onto the body of a circular saw instead of dropped into a drawer.
short.standalone_note: Name the consequence out loud, that a missing spanner is how a router gets used without one, so the clip reads as a safety move rather than tidiness.

segments.covers: Cleaning here restores how the tool actually cuts, because packed dust and pitch change its behaviour.
beats: Motor vents brushed and blown clear of packed sawdust, with what packed vents do to a motor trying to cool itself explained as it happens.
Pitch taken off saw blade teeth with resin remover, before and after held in the same frame, with pitch named as the reason cuts started burning.
Clogged sanding pads pulled and compared against a fresh one under raking light.

The parts nobody cleans in this zone done last, the saw shoe and router base scraped free of gum so they slide true, and dust wiped off battery terminals and charger contacts so a pack seats properly.
shots: Macro on a brush clearing packed dust from motor vents, dust falling away.
Macro on saw blade teeth before and after resin remover.
Close on a loaded sanding pad peeling off under raking light beside a fresh one.
Macro on a cloth clearing dust from battery terminals and charger contacts.
on_screen_text: Clean the shoe and the contacts

short.hook: Macro on circular saw teeth going from black pitch to bare steel as resin remover does its work.
short.standalone_note: Explain that the pitch is why the saw started burning its cuts, or this is a cleaning shot with no reason behind it.

segments.covers: The guard test, the cord test, and the storage rules that separate this zone from a shelf full of hazards.
beats: The retracting guard on every saw worked with a thumb and confirmed to snap back on its own, with a sticky guard named as the injury waiting in this zone.
A guard that hesitates shown against one that does not, and the verdict given as service or retire, rather than a note to be careful with it.
Each cord flexed at the strain relief where the sheath cracks first, with cracked sheathing framed as the water and electricity question on bare damp concrete.
Loose blades stored flat in a drawer where your hand goes in first, then the corrected storage, sleeved or racked on edge.
The plugged in rule set and demonstrated, no corded tool ever stored plugged in, with the unplug happening as part of putting the tool away rather than as a separate task.
shots: Macro on a thumb pushing a saw guard open and the guard snapping shut on its own.
Close on a guard that hangs open a beat too long before dropping, played back slowed.
Macro on fingers flexing a cord at the strain relief with the sheath cracking open.
Close on a hand entering a drawer of loose flat blades, then the same drawer with blades sleeved.
Close on a plug leaving the socket as the tool goes onto its hook.

short.hook: A thumb pushes a circular saw guard fully open and lets go, and the guard hangs there instead of snapping shut.
short.standalone_note: State that a guard must return on its own and that a sticky one is the injury waiting in a workshop, since the hesitation is subtle on a phone screen.

segments.covers: Labeled homes on the wall and one written charge rule at the chargers.
beats: Each tool's home labeled on the wall or the shelf edge, so an empty space names what is missing instead of just sitting empty.
The charge rule written on a card at the charger shelf itself, partial charge, off the charger when the job ends, resting on a shelf that is not wood.
The reason behind the shelf material given in this zone's own terms, packs left on chargers indefinitely on a wooden shelf under a bench full of sawdust, framed as the burn or fire question.
The readable end state demonstrated, empty charger cradles and packs sitting on bare metal, so a glance at the shelf tells you whether the rule was followed.
shots: Macro on a label being pressed onto a shelf edge beneath a hook.
Overhead of battery packs resting on a metal shelf with the charger cradles empty beside them.
Close on a marker writing the three part charge rule onto a card at the charger shelf.
Wide of the labeled wall with one empty labeled space clearly visible.
on_screen_text: Off the charger at job end

short.hook: Battery packs come off their chargers one after another onto a bare metal shelf, and the charger lights go dark behind them.
short.standalone_note: Say why the shelf is metal and why the packs come off at job end, since the move looks arbitrary without the fire reason.

segments.covers: Battery onto the charger and tool onto its hook, travelling as one motion.
beats: The paired motion filmed at the end of a job, the pack coming off and going onto the charger while the tool continues onto its hook, hands never stopping in between.
The rule that holds it stated, the two actions travel together or neither happens, with the failure version shown, a pack on charge and the bare tool abandoned on the bench.
The door check added, a hand pausing on the latch and turning back to confirm no charger is left running behind a locked shop door.
The state this produces held for a beat, every tool guarded, unplugged, and stored with the accessories it needs to work.
shots: Continuous three quarter following hands from tool to charger to hook without a cut.
Close on a bare tool left on the bench with a charger light glowing behind it.
Close on a hand on the door latch, turning back toward the charger shelf.
Wide of the finished zone with every charger light dark.
on_screen_text: No charger running behind the door

short.hook: One unbroken shot follows a pair of hands pulling a battery, seating it on the charger, and hanging the tool, without a single pause between.
short.standalone_note: Name the rule that the two actions travel together or neither happens, otherwise this is just someone putting a tool away.

close.standard_beat: Wide of the finished zone with every tool in a labeled home, guards closed, blade wrench and chuck key attached to their own tools, batteries resting on bare metal off the chargers, no loose blade in a drawer, and no taped cord anywhere on the shelves. State the standard as it now reads, every tool rests guarded, unplugged, and stored with the accessories it needs to work, then show the door check with all charger lights dark.
close.next_zone_teaser: The tools are complete, but a project still stops the moment you cannot find the right screw. Next is the fastener wall, and the inherited jar of mixed hardware that has followed you through two houses.

shot_list: Overhead bench setup for duplicate line ups and accessory pairing.
Macro setup for guard snap tests and cord flexing, shot at high frame rate on the phone.
Close setup on the charger shelf for battery, label, and card work.
Three quarter along the tool wall for hooks and labeled homes.
Raking light setup for sanding pads and blade pitch.
Continuous follow from tool to charger to hook with no cut.
Close on saw shoe and router base cleaning at the bench.
Door latch shot looking back into the zone with charger lights out.
videos.description_hook: Every object in this zone has a guard, a cord, or a battery, and each one is a way it can hurt you. Guard tests, cord tests, a written charge rule, and the two questions that settle the expensive tool you never use.

videos.title: Fastener Wall: One Size Per Compartment, Sample Screw on the Front
videos.cold_open_problem: Open on the jar, a tin from a relative's garage holding a few kilograms of unsorted screws, nuts, and washers, tipping slowly onto a tray until it stops being a jar and starts being a heap. Establish the argument that has kept it alive through two houses, that there is obviously good hardware in there, and grant that the argument is true. Then name the trap this zone actually runs on, that tipping out a jar of screws feels like progress, which is exactly why this jar keeps getting relocated instead of decided.

segments.covers: Keep only hardware you can name confidently, and give the inherited jar exactly one sitting.
beats: The mixed jars emptied onto a tray in one motion and spread flat, so the actual content is visible rather than imagined.
The keep test set out loud, only what you can name confidently by size and type, with the failure case demonstrated, an unnameable fastener going straight to the scrap tin.
Rusted screws, bent nails, and the anchors that came free with a shelf you no longer own swept out, named as clutter rather than as a stock of hardware.

The inherited jar call run by pricing the alternative first, a full box of the screws you actually drive against the evening you would otherwise spend sorting, then one sitting only, picking out just the sizes that already have a compartment.
The ending that decides it, the remainder going to metal recycling that same day, and the warning attached, that tipping it into a smaller jar is exactly how it survived the last two moves.

short.hook: A heavy jar of mixed hardware tips onto a tray, and only a small handful of screws gets picked back out of the heap.
short.standalone_note: State the pricing test up front, that a box of the screws you actually drive costs less than an evening of sorting, or the small keep pile looks lazy rather than deliberate.

segments.covers: Type first, size second, with the sizes you drive weekly at hand height.
beats: The kept hardware sorted by type first and then by size, with the two step logic laid out on the tray before anything enters a drawer.
Height bands walked by hand, the sizes you drive weekly at hand height, the specialty hinges and threaded rod up high.

The pairs that get confused deliberately separated, deck screws away from drywall screws, with what that particular mix up costs you in a joint. Point to Chapter 14, visual controls.

segments.covers: Cleaning these drawers is really an inspection, and the corners tell you where the cabinet is standing.
beats: The drawers vacuumed of metal filings and grit, with the nozzle taken into the corners rather than wiped across the middle.
The bottom corners checked for rust bloom, and the bloom shown up close when it turns up.
The diagnosis that follows given immediately, that bloom means this cabinet is sitting against a cold outside wall and needs moving before it gets refilled.
The principle behind the whole pass restated in this zone's terms, that you clean to inspect, and corner bloom is exactly the kind of thing a layer of filings hides.

segments.covers: A loaded fastener cabinet is far heavier than it looks, and spilled hardware is a floor hazard for more than you.
beats: The weight shown honestly by lifting one loaded drawer and then the whole empty carcass, so the difference is felt rather than claimed.
The cabinet fixed into studs rather than plasterboard anchors, with the stud found and the fixing driven on camera, and the timing stated, before it gets loaded rather than after.
The tipping failure demonstrated safely, a lightly loaded unit tethered from behind out of shot, rocking forward as the highest drawer of bolts opens, then the fix, load low and secure the top.

The floor hazard split into its two real questions, spilled screws on concrete putting you on your back holding something sharp, and loose screws, washers, and wall anchors sitting at exactly the height where a toddler or a dog finds them first.
A deliberate spill swept and vacuumed on camera as the closing action of the pass.

segments.covers: One compartment per size, no shared drawers, and a minimum line that announces a low bin.
beats: The rule stated with no softening, one compartment per size, no exceptions and no shared drawers, then a shared drawer emptied and split into two on camera.
A minimum line marked inside the compartments you empty most, drawn on the inner wall so it is visible the moment the drawer slides open.
The effect demonstrated, a drawer opening with its contents sitting below the line, which is a reorder signal rather than a discovery made halfway through a project.
The purpose of the whole zone tied back to the mark, that a project never stops for a hardware run.

segments.covers: Pocket hardware goes home before the tools do.
beats: The end of job pocket emptied onto the bench, which is where this zone quietly refills itself with mixed hardware.
The trigger given its motion, the handful of leftover fasteners returned to their compartments before a single tool goes back on the wall.
The unnameable leftovers handled on the spot, into the scrap metal tin rather than into a holding jar to be dealt with later.
The loop closed on the cold open, that a holding jar is precisely how the inherited jar was born in the first place.

close.standard_beat: Slow pan across the finished wall, one fastener type and size per compartment, a sample screw glued to each drawer face, deck screws separate from drywall screws, no tin of mixed hardware anywhere on the shelf, and a marked minimum line inside the compartments you empty most. videos.title: Material Rack: Store Wood Flat, and Set a Size Floor for Offcuts
videos.cold_open_problem: Open on the offcut bin, overfull, with hands pulling out one short piece after another and standing them on the floor until the row runs out of frame. Grant the hard part immediately by turning a few of them over, clean grain, no nails, genuinely usable wood, every one. Then name the asymmetry that keeps the pile growing: the cost of keeping an offcut is invisible and the cost of tossing one feels sharp, so the decision goes the same way every single time and the bin only ever gets fuller.

segments.covers: The offcut bin comes apart piece by piece against a written size floor, and some stock leaves for reasons other than size.
beats: The size floor written on the bin face before anything is touched, shorter than your forearm or narrower than your palm, with the forearm and palm used on camera as the measure.
The bin taken apart piece by piece, each held against the floor, with the rule doing the deciding instead of the piece making its case.
The bin cap introduced as the second limit, one bin and no overflow, so when it is full the shortest piece in it leaves to make room for the newest.
The reframe that makes it workable, that you are judging whether a piece is better than the worst piece already in the bin, not whether it is good wood.

The stock that leaves for other reasons pulled separately, twisted or badly cupped boards, anything with hidden nails or an unknown coating, and pressure treated scrap, with the coated stock stated plainly as never going on the fire.

short.standalone_note: Give both limits, the size floor and the one bin cap, or the forearm measure looks like a gimmick rather than a decision rule you can copy.

The route from the bench to the door cleared along its full width and shown end to end from a locked off position at floor level.

The stored stock checked while it is out, board ends split and mouse damage along the bottom bay, so damaged stock does not go back in.
Surface rust wiped off steel stock and a light oil applied before it returns, before and after shown along one length.

Check the stock while it is out

short.standalone_note: Say this is a workshop material rack and that the gap behind it never gets cleaned because the rack never moves, so the reveal has a reason.

segments.covers: This zone stores the heaviest things in the shop, and the ways they move without warning.
beats: The rack fixed into structural framing rather than just the wall skin, fixing driven on camera, then reloaded heaviest and longest at the bottom with lighter stock above.

The sheet goods failure shown without staging a fall, the scuff arc already on the floor where a sheet has slid before, the shallow lean angle that caused it, and a small panel released at that same angle from a locked off side position.
The corrected storage put in immediately, sheets on edge or leaned steep against the wall, so the Safety pass ends with the fix rather than the hazard.
The second fall, cut, or crush case, a board pulled from the middle of a stack and the stack shifting above it, and the grouping that stops it happening.
The burn or fire question handled directly, a dry offcut bin sitting near a heater, water heater, or extension lead, and the bin relocated on camera, with nothing left stored directly on the floor.

segments.covers: Marks on the rack and on the bin that make the right state readable without thinking.
beats: Lengths marked on the rack rails so stock returns to the right bay rather than the nearest bay.
The size floor written large and permanently on the front of the offcut bin, so the rule outlives the day you set it.
A fill line marked above which the bin counts as full, then the moment of crossing it demonstrated, with the shortest piece coming out as the newest goes in.
The pair explained working together, the size floor governing what comes in and the fill line governing what goes out, which is the whole reason the pile stops growing.

segments.covers: Offcuts get their verdict before the saw gets unplugged.

The trigger given its motion, every offcut going into the bin or into the fire bucket before the saw is unplugged, and never onto the bench, the floor, or the top of the rack.
The rule applied live to fresh cuts against the size floor already written on the bin, so it works at speed rather than only during a reset.
The third destination handled for pieces that cannot burn, coated and treated stock going to its own marked tub rather than the fire bucket, then the plug leaving the socket over a clear floor.

close.standard_beat: Wide of the finished rack, boards lying flat and supported along their length with the longest and heaviest at the bottom, sheet goods standing on edge against the wall, the offcut bin with its size floor written on the front and its fill line marked, nothing stored directly on the floor, and the route from the bench to the door clear along its full width. State the standard, one offcut bin with a written size floor and a fill line, then show the trigger, the saw plug coming out after the last offcut lands.
close.next_zone_teaser: Everything so far has been solid and inert. The last zone in this room is the one that can start a fire with nothing touching it, the finishing and chemical cabinet, and the wall of half used paint inside it.

videos.title: Finishing Cabinet: Dated Lids, Separated Shelves, Rags in a Metal Can
videos.cold_open_problem: Open on the row of part cans, lids crusted shut, masking tape labels naming rooms in a house you no longer live in. Work a lid off to show what is actually inside, a skin across the top and half an inch of solids under it. Name what you are really storing, which is the possibility of a touch up, and that almost none of this will still brush out matching in two years. Then name the second failure hiding in the same zone, the box of condemned paint that will sit by the door for a month, which is the same problem simply relocated.

segments.covers: Open and judge every container, and take the failures to household hazardous waste the same day.
beats: Every container opened on camera and judged by what it does rather than how full it is, with a thick skin or a sour smell being the end of that tin.
Wood glue run out onto a scrap to show it gone stringy or granular, which means it will not hold a joint, which means it is no longer glue.
A half bottle of polyurethane tipped fully and held, with nothing moving, cured solid.

The wall of paint call run properly, keeping only colours currently on a surface in this house, and keeping them well, one small sealed jar of each labeled with the room and the finish rather than the original half empty tin sitting open to the air.
The disposal rule given in full and acted on, all of it to household hazardous waste, never the bin and never the drain, on the same day it gets sorted.

segments.covers: Placement here is entirely about keeping apart the things that must never meet.
beats: Shelves assigned physically, solvents and thinners on their own shelf, water based finishes on another, said out loud as each one lands.
Hardeners carried deliberately away from the resins they cure, with the reason stated as the move happens.
Stir sticks and brushes for each family stored with that family, so the wrong brush never travels between shelves.
The whole layout closed inside the metal cabinet, with a drip tray slid under the solvent shelf as part of the arrangement rather than an afterthought.

Close on hardeners being carried to a separate shelf from their resins.
Close on stir sticks and brushes going into a holder on their matching shelf.
Overhead of a drip tray sliding under the solvent shelf.

short.hook: Two containers get deliberately set down on separate shelves of a metal cabinet, and the hand pauses in the gap between them.
short.standalone_note: Name exactly what is being kept apart and why, solvents from water based finishes and hardeners from the resins they cure, since the pause means nothing on its own.

segments.covers: Cleaning here is what keeps the product usable, starting with the rim of the can.
beats: The rim of a can wiped clear before the lid goes back on, with the mechanism given directly, that a rim packed with dried finish is why the can skinned over in the first place.
A lid seated flush on a clean rim shown against one riding high on a crusted rim, with the gap visible.
Brushes cleaned right through to the ferrule, showing the finish that hides up there and what it does to the bristles by the next job.
The spill tray wiped back to bare metal last, so a fresh drip reads immediately instead of disappearing into old ones.

segments.covers: The rag that heats itself, and the things that must never share space with a flame or a drink bottle.
beats: The fact stated plainly and then respected on camera, that a rag soaked in oil finish generates its own heat as it cures and can ignite with nothing touching it.
Both acceptable endings for that rag shown, into a lidded metal can or spread flat outdoors to dry, alongside the wrong endings, balled in a bin liner or draped over the bench.
The gap between the flammable liquids and the water heater flame walked and measured by hand from a locked off wide, then anything within reach of the pilot relocated.
Ventilation opened as the first action of a finishing job rather than the last, the door and window going wide before a lid comes off.

The poison, choke, or strangle question handled head on, thinner in an unlabeled drink bottle emptied back into a labeled container and the bottle cut open and binned, framed by the line find it, and fix it now. Point to Chapter 22, prevent and prepare.

short.standalone_note: State that oil finish rags generate their own heat while curing and can ignite with nothing touching them, because the closing lid carries the whole message and needs the reason.

segments.covers: Dates on every container and the shelf layout written where you read it while putting things away.
beats: Every container dated with a marker the day it arrives, with the date going onto the lid so it reads from above without anything being lifted.
The shelf layout written on the inside of the cabinet door, and why that spot specifically, because it faces you at the exact moment you are putting things away in a hurry.
A hurried put away run against the written layout, so the solvents and the water based finishes stay apart even when you are not thinking about it.
The standard restated in the zone's own words, original containers, dated lids, incompatibles on separate shelves, and rags in a lidded metal can.

Overhead of a shelf of lids, every date readable from above.
Close on the layout being written onto the inside face of the cabinet door.
Three quarter of a hurried put away with the door layout in frame.

Layout on the inside of the door

short.hook: Overhead on a shelf of finish cans where every lid carries a date written large enough to read without lifting a thing.
short.standalone_note: Say the date goes on the day the container arrives and why it lives on the lid rather than the side, since the overhead only shows the result.

segments.covers: The brush under the tap is what cues the date check and the rag.
beats: The natural end of a finishing job shown first, the brush going under the tap, which is the one thing you already do every single time.
The other two actions attached to it and run in sequence, the can lid date checked and the rag going into the metal can with the lid down.
Why this trigger works rather than a reminder, because washing the brush happens at the exact moment the rag and the can are both already in your hands.
The cabinet closed on the finished state with the layout card facing out, ending the room where it started, on things that cannot hurt you while you are not there.

close.standard_beat: Open the cabinet slowly for the final state, every product in its original labeled container, each lid dated in marker, water based paint on one shelf and solvents and thinners on another, a drip tray under the solvent shelf, the layout written on the inside of the door, and the self closing metal can standing beside it with the lid down. State the standard, then show the trigger once, the brush under the tap with the rag going in the can and the lid dropping.
close.next_zone_teaser: That is all six zones in the workshop, from the glasses at the door to the cabinet that has to be safe while nobody is in the room. The next room in the series is the garage, starting with the bay you cannot park in.
